About the loss: "always predict negative" really is the maximum-likelihood answer. The objective is not broken. It gives a correct answer to the question that you asked. To change the answer, change the question. Use pos_weight in BCEWithLogitsLoss, weight= in CrossEntropyLoss, or resampling. See Chapter 03.

Part 4 · Probability and Loss#

Models output beliefs, not answers#

You cannot improve a discrete answer by a small amount. Also, a step function has a zero derivative at each point where it is defined. Part 2 showed that a zero derivative does not tell you which direction to move. Thus a model gives a belief, $\hat{y} \in (0,1)$. Then an answer can be wrong by different amounts.

Example — why degrees matter
true label: positive (y = 1) model A says 0.51 → correct decision, barely model B says 0.99 → correct decision, confidently model C says 0.10 → wrong A discrete output cannot distinguish A from B, and gives no signal for how far C must move. A probability does both.

The three distributions#

  • Bernoulli, one yes/no result: $P(y \mid p) = p^y(1-p)^{1-y}$.
  • Categorical, one of $K$ classes: $P(y \mid p) = \prod_k p_k^{y_k}$.
  • Gaussian, a real number with noise: $P(y\mid\mu,\sigma^2) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}e^{-(y-\mu)^2/2\sigma^2}$.
Example — the exponent trick
Bernoulli with p = 0.7: y = 1: 0.7¹ × 0.3⁰ = 0.7 × 1 = 0.7 y = 0: 0.7⁰ × 0.3¹ = 1 × 0.3 = 0.3 Categorical, p = [0.2, 0.5, 0.3], true class 1 so y = [0, 1, 0]: P = 0.2⁰ × 0.5¹ × 0.3⁰ = 0.5

The exponents are an if statement in the form of an expression. The branch that does not apply has the power 0, so it becomes 1 and has no effect. An if statement is not differentiable. This expression is.

Likelihood: reading a distribution backwards#

When you read $P(y \mid \theta)$ forward, the parameters are known and the outcomes are uncertain. Training reads it in reverse: you saw the data, and you do not know the parameters. Keep $y$ fixed and let $\theta$ change. Then the same expression is the likelihood of $\theta$. It is not a distribution over $\theta$. It is a score for how well each $\theta$ explains the data that you saw.

Example — the same numbers, read two ways

You flip a coin three times and get heads, heads, tails.

FORWARD (p known), p = 0.5: P(HHT) = 0.5 × 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.125 BACKWARD (outcome known) — score candidate values of p: p = 0.2 : 0.2 × 0.2 × 0.8 = 0.032 p = 0.5 : 0.5 × 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.125 p = 0.67: 0.67 × 0.67 × 0.33 = 0.148 ← highest p = 0.9 : 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.1 = 0.081

The best explanation of "2 heads in 3 flips" is $p = 2/3$, the frequency that you saw. On an easy problem, maximum likelihood gives the obvious answer. That is why you can trust it on a difficult problem.

Why the logarithm is not optional#

Example — the underflow, concretely
64 examples, each assigned probability 0.1 product : 0.1⁶⁴ = 1e−64 → float32 stores this as exactly 0.0 sum of logs : 64 × ln(0.1) = −147.4 → perfectly fine

A zero likelihood has a zero gradient, so training would stop before it started. The logarithm also changes the product into a sum. You can differentiate a sum one term at a time. A product needs the product rule across all $N$ factors.

Change the sign, so that you minimize, and divide by $N$. This gives the negative log-likelihood, which is the loss:

$$\mathcal{L}(\theta) = -\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\log P(y_i\mid x_i,\theta)$$
Key concept Each loss in this book is that formula with a different distribution in it. Bernoulli gives binary cross-entropy. Categorical gives cross-entropy. Gaussian gives mean squared error. They are one procedure with three different inputs.

The losses, derived#

Bernoulli → BCE.

$$\mathcal{L} = -\frac{1}{N}\sum_i\big[y_i\log\hat{y}_i + (1-y_i)\log(1-\hat{y}_i)\big]$$

Categorical → cross-entropy. $y$ is one-hot, so the sum over classes has only one term. That is why nn.CrossEntropyLoss takes integer indices:

$$\mathcal{L} = -\frac{1}{N}\sum_i\log\hat{y}_{i,c_i}$$

Near $p = 1$ the curve is flat. Thus a model that is already correct gets almost no gradient. Near $p = 0$ the curve has no upper limit. Thus the loss for a confident wrong answer has no limit.

Gaussian → MSE. Expand the logarithm of the Gaussian density:

$$-\log P(y\mid\mu,\sigma^2) = \frac{(y-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2} + \tfrac{1}{2}\log(2\pi\sigma^2)$$

The second term does not contain $\mu$. Thus its gradient is zero, and it cannot move the minimum. Remove it. A fixed $\sigma$ is a constant, and the learning rate absorbs it. Thus MSE is not a neutral choice. It assumes symmetric Gaussian noise with a constant width. When that assumption is false, MSE fails exactly as the assumption predicts.

Example — why MSE fails on classification
With ŷ = σ(z) and MSE, the chain rule gives ∂L/∂z = 2(ŷ − y)·σ′(z) truth y = 1, model confidently wrong at z = −8, ŷ = 0.000335 MSE : 2(0.000335 − 1) × σ′(−8) = 2(−0.9997)(0.000335) = −0.00067 BCE : ŷ − y = −0.9997 ratio: about 1,500×

With MSE, the more confident and wrong the model is, the less it learns. Cross-entropy has a structure that cancels the $\sigma'$ factor exactly.

By hand — exercise 00.18 · binary cross-entropy on a batch
example true y predicted ŷ 1 1 0.9 2 0 0.2 3 1 0.4 ln 0.9 ≈ −0.105 ln 0.8 ≈ −0.223 ln 0.4 ≈ −0.916
  1. Write the loss for each example. Remove the term that is multiplied by zero.
  2. Calculate each loss, and then the average.
  3. Which example contributes most, and by how much?
  4. Example 2 is 0.2 from perfect, and example 3 is 0.6 from perfect. That is three times the error. Is the loss three times larger? What does that tell you about which examples control a batch?
Worked solution

1 & 2.

example 1: y=1 → −ln(0.9) = 0.105 example 2: y=0 → −ln(1 − 0.2) = 0.223 example 3: y=1 → −ln(0.4) = 0.916 batch loss = 1.244 / 3 = 0.415

3. Example 3, at 0.916, is 74% of the total.

4. No. It is 4.1× larger for 3× the error. The logarithm makes the loss increase faster than the error. Thus one badly classified example controls the gradient. Usually you want that, because hard examples need attention. Sometimes it is a disaster, because a mislabeled example also gets control. It is the same mechanism that makes MSE sensitive to outliers, seen from the classification side.

Softmax and the cancellation#

$$\hat{y}_k = \frac{e^{z_k}}{\sum_j e^{z_j}} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \boxed{\;\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial z_k} = \hat{y}_k - y_k\;}$$
Example — softmax by hand, and its invariance
z = [2.0, 1.0, 0.0] e² = 7.389, e¹ = 2.718, e⁰ = 1.000, sum = 11.107 ŷ = [0.665, 0.245, 0.090] sums to 1.000 ✓ Now subtract 2 from every logit, z = [0, −1, −2]: 1.000, 0.368, 0.135, sum = 1.503 ŷ = [0.665, 0.245, 0.090] identical Softmax is invariant to adding a constant, because e^c cancels between numerator and denominator. Subtracting the max before exponentiating is therefore free — and it makes overflow impossible.
Key concept Softmax and cross-entropy are a designed pair. Their derivatives cancel, and only the error itself stays, at full size. That is why you give raw logits to nn.CrossEntropyLoss and nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss. If you apply softmax or sigmoid yourself first, you make a silent correctness bug. The loss still runs and the numbers still decrease, but the model trains worse than it should.
The derivation, in full

Let $S = \sum_j e^{z_j}$, so $\hat{y}_k = e^{z_k}/S$. For the diagonal case $k = c$, use the quotient rule:

$$\frac{\partial\hat{y}_c}{\partial z_c} = \frac{e^{z_c}S - e^{z_c}e^{z_c}}{S^2} = \hat{y}_c(1-\hat{y}_c)$$

For the off-diagonal case $k \ne c$, the numerator does not depend on $z_k$:

$$\frac{\partial\hat{y}_c}{\partial z_k} = \frac{0\cdot S - e^{z_c}e^{z_k}}{S^2} = -\hat{y}_c\hat{y}_k$$

With $\mathcal{L} = -\log\hat{y}_c$, we have $\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial\hat{y}_c = -1/\hat{y}_c$. Thus the case $k = c$ gives $\hat{y}_c - 1$, and the case $k \ne c$ gives $\hat{y}_k$. Because $y_c = 1$ and $y_k = 0$, both are $\hat{y}_k - y_k$.

By hand — exercise 00.19 · softmax, cross-entropy, and the gradientMust do
z = [2.0, 1.0, 0.0] true class c = 1 (the middle one) e⁰ = 1.000 e¹ = 2.718 e² = 7.389
  1. Apply the max-subtraction trick. Show that it cannot change the answer.
  2. Calculate $\operatorname{softmax}(z)$ to three decimals.
  3. Calculate the loss. Compare it with a uniform guess.
  4. Calculate $\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial z_k$ for all three logits. Make sure that their sum is zero, and explain why it must be.
  5. Suppose that you add 100 to each logit. What changes in the loss, in the gradients, and in a simple implementation?
Worked solution

1. Subtract 2 to get $[0,-1,-2]$. Because $e^{z_k-m}/\sum_j e^{z_j-m} = (e^{-m}e^{z_k})/(e^{-m}\sum_j e^{z_j})$, the $e^{-m}$ cancels.

2. $\sum = 11.107$, so $\hat{y} = [\mathbf{0.665}, \mathbf{0.245}, \mathbf{0.090}]$.

3. $\mathcal{L} = -\ln(0.245) = \mathbf{1.406}$ nats. A uniform guess over 3 classes costs $-\ln(1/3) = 1.099$. Thus this model is worse than a guess on this example. That comparison is the easiest check on the loss of any classifier.

4.

∂L/∂z₀ = 0.665 − 0 = +0.665 push logit 0 DOWN ∂L/∂z₁ = 0.245 − 1 = −0.755 push logit 1 UP ∂L/∂z₂ = 0.090 − 0 = +0.090 push logit 2 down slightly sum = 0.000

The sum must be zero because the softmax outputs must add to 1. If you change all the logits by the same amount, nothing changes. Thus the gradient can have no component in that direction. The model can learn only the relative logits.

5. Nothing changes in the loss or in the gradients. That is the invariance from part 1, and part 4 is its evidence. The simple implementation changes. $e^{102}$ is satisfactory, but at $+800$ the exponential overflows to inf, and the distribution becomes nan. The mathematics is invariant. The floating-point arithmetic is not.

The information-theoretic reading#

  • Surprisal is $-\log p$.
  • Entropy, $H(p) = -\sum p_k\log p_k$, is the expected surprisal under the true distribution.
  • Cross-entropy, $H(p,q) = -\sum p_k\log q_k$, is the cost to encode reality $p$ with beliefs $q$.
  • The difference is the KL divergence, $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q) = H(p,q) - H(p) \ge 0$.

$H(p)$ depends only on the data. Thus, when you minimize cross-entropy, you also minimize the divergence from the truth. Maximum likelihood and information theory tell the same story in two ways.

Perplexity The perplexity of a language model is $e^{\mathcal{L}}$, for cross-entropy in nats. It is the effective number of choices that the model must select from. Chapter 10 reports a loss of 1.51 over 73 characters. That is a perplexity of 4.5: the model has decreased 73 possible characters to approximately four or five. Loss curves are difficult to read. Perplexity is easy.
By hand — exercise 00.20 · entropy, cross-entropy, and KL

A weather model says that the probability of rain is $q = 0.25$ each day. Really, it rains half the time, $p = 0.5$. Use bits, with $\log_2 3 \approx 1.585$.

  1. Calculate $H(p)$.
  2. Calculate $H(p,q)$.
  3. Calculate $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)$. What does it mean physically?
  4. Calculate $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|p)$. Why is it different?
  5. Training minimizes $H(p,q)$, not $D_{\mathrm{KL}}$. Why is that not a problem?
Worked solution

1. $H(p) = -(0.5\log_2 0.5 + 0.5\log_2 0.5) = \mathbf{1}$ bit. This is a fair coin, which has the maximum uncertainty for a binary event.

2. $\log_2 0.25 = -2$ and $\log_2 0.75 = \log_2 3 - 2 = -0.415$:

H(p,q) = −(0.5(−2) + 0.5(−0.415)) = 1 + 0.208 = 1.208 bits

3. $1.208 - 1 = \mathbf{0.208}$ bits. Physically: if you encode the real weather with the beliefs of this model, you use 0.21 extra bits each day. That is approximately 76 wasted bits each year. It is the cost of a wrong model, measured in message length.

4. $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|p) = 0.25\log_2(0.5) + 0.75\log_2(1.5) = -0.25 + 0.439 = \mathbf{0.189}$ bits. It is different because the two divergences average the error under different distributions. "How surprised will I be" depends on whose expectation you use. This asymmetry is useful. As objectives, forward KL and reverse KL give very different behavior (mass-covering and mode-seeking).

5. $D_{\mathrm{KL}} = H(p,q) - H(p)$, and $H(p)$ depends only on the data. When you subtract a constant from a function, its minimum does not move. Thus to minimize cross-entropy is to minimize divergence from the truth. You cannot calculate the constant, but you do not need it.

Choosing a loss#

TaskFinal layerLossPyTorch
Binary classification1 logitBCEBCEWithLogitsLoss
Multi-class, one label$K$ logitscross-entropyCrossEntropyLoss
Multi-label (tags)$K$ logitsBCE per classBCEWithLogitsLoss
Regression, clean1 linearMSEMSELoss
Regression, outliers1 linearMAE / HuberL1Loss, SmoothL1Loss
Next-token prediction$V$ logitscross-entropyCrossEntropyLoss

Three rules cause more bugs than all the others together:

  • Give logits, not probabilities.
  • Ignore your padding with ignore_index=PAD_IDX.
  • Class imbalance is a likelihood problem. If 95% of labels are negative, "always predict negative" really is the maximum-likelihood answer. Thus reweighting changes the question. It does not fix a bug.
By hand — exercise 00.21 · choosing the loss

There is no arithmetic. For each task, name the loss and use the distribution to explain your choice.

  1. Predict apartment rents. 2% of the data is penthouses at 30× the median.
  2. Tag a photo with any of 20 labels. A photo can have several labels.
  3. Predict the next word from a vocabulary of 50,000 words.
  4. Detect a disease that 0.5% of patients have.
Worked solution

1. MAE or Huber. MSE is the Gaussian NLL, and this data has heavy tails, so the assumption is false. With MSE, the squared errors of the penthouses control the gradient. They make the predictions for normal apartments worse. Huber is usually best: it is quadratic near zero and linear in the tail.

2. BCE for each label over 20 logits, not cross-entropy. Cross-entropy assumes the categorical distribution, where exactly one class occurs. Its softmax makes the 20 outputs share one fixed total probability. Multi-label means 20 independent Bernoulli events. Each one has its own sigmoid and its own BCE term. This error is really common.

3. Cross-entropy over 50,000 logits. This is categorical, because exactly one word comes next. Report perplexity, not raw loss. The uniform baseline is $\ln(50000) = 10.8$ nats.

4. BCE with pos_weight. Report precision and recall, not accuracy. Exercise 00.17 is this question with numbers. The unweighted maximum-likelihood answer is "always predict healthy". It gets 99.5% accuracy, and it is useless.

Part 5 · Recognizing Which Tool Applies#

Parts 1–4 gave you the tools. The more difficult skill is recognition. This skill separates people who can use this material from people who only read it. Recognition means that you see the type of question in front of you before you know what to calculate. Is it a variance question, a base-rate question, or a likelihood question?

With that skill, you can read a paper or the result of a colleague and see if the reasoning is correct. This section is short on purpose. It gives you enough to tell correct reasoning from incorrect reasoning in the next chapters. It is not a statistics course.

The trigger table#

Almost each situation in this book starts with one of seven questions. Learn to hear the question, and then you know the tool.

When you find yourself asking…Reach forBecause
"Will this blow up or shrink as it passes through many layers/steps?"Variance propagation — $\operatorname{Var}(aX)=a^2\operatorname{Var}(X)$, additivityanything applied repeatedly compounds geometrically
"Is this difference real, or noise?"Sample mean and standard errora statistic from $n$ runs is itself random
"What should the model output, and what loss?"Likelihood → negative log-likelihoodthe loss is determined by the distribution, not chosen
"How wrong is this belief, in a unit I can compare?"Entropy, cross-entropy, KLgives an absolute scale and a baseline to beat
"The test says positive — should I believe it?"Bayes and base ratesrarity dominates accuracy
"Are these two quantities related?"Covariance and correlation, and their limitsthey detect linear association only
"Is this number good?"A baseline: $\ln K$, the majority class, the uniform modelno metric means anything alone
Key concept — the one-line diagnostic
  • If you apply something many times, it is a variance question.
  • If you measure something one time, it is a standard-error question.
  • If something is rare, it is a base-rate question.
  • If you select an output, it is a likelihood question.

These four cover most of the situations that you will see. The correct category is most of the work. After that, the arithmetic comes from Parts 1–4.

Guided example 1 — "my deep network won't train"#

Guided

"I stacked 30 layers with torch.randn weights. The loss starts at 2.30 and never moves. More epochs don't help and neither does a bigger learning rate."

Recognize first. Calculate second.

  1. Is something applied many times? Yes: 30 layers, with the same operation each time. That is the variance-propagation trigger.
  2. Is this number good? 2.30 is very close to $\ln 10 = 2.303$. Thus the model gives a uniform distribution over 10 classes. It does not learn badly. It does not learn at all.

Only now, calculate. With torch.randn, $\sigma_w = 1$. Thus, for each layer:

Var(z) = n · σ²_w = n (Part 3, "the two rules") For n = 256: Var multiplies by 256 EVERY layer. After 30 layers: 256³⁰ ≈ 10⁷² — pre-activations are astronomically large, every saturating non-linearity is pinned, every derivative ≈ 0.

Two triggers and two lines of arithmetic make the diagnosis certain. It is not a guess. The fix is $\sigma_w = 1/\sqrt{n}$. Here is the general lesson. "Will not train" plus "the loss stays at $\ln K$" is almost always initialization or a broken gradient path. It is never a hyperparameter that you can tune to fix the problem.

Guided example 2 — "our classifier is 99% accurate"#

Guided

"Our fraud detector hits 99% accuracy on the held-out set. Ship it."

  1. Is something rare? Fraud is rare. That is the base-rate trigger. It makes accuracy the wrong metric before you look at any number.
  2. Is there a baseline? If fraud is 1% of transactions, "always say legitimate" gets 99%. That is the same as the model.
P(fraud) = 0.01 Even a genuinely good model, at 90% recall and 95% specificity: true positives = 0.01 × 0.90 = 0.0090 false positives = 0.99 × 0.05 = 0.0495 precision = 0.0090 / (0.0090 + 0.0495) = 15% 85 of every 100 alerts are wrong — while "accuracy" reads 94.9%.

The claim is not false. It gives no information. To see that, you needed only one question: is the positive class rare? Ask for precision and recall. Also ask for the majority-class baseline next to each accuracy value. This is the most common way that a result that sounds good is really worthless.

Guided example 3 — "the new architecture is better"#

Guided

"Swapping in the new attention variant took us from 84.1% to 84.9% on the test set."

  1. Was it measured one time? Almost certainly. That is the standard-error trigger.
  2. Remember the scale: on a small dataset, the spread between seeds is frequently ±2%.
A 0.8% gap against a ~2% spread is well inside one standard error. With 3 seeds and s ≈ 0.02, SE = 0.02/√3 ≈ 0.012 — larger than the effect. Verdict: the experiment cannot distinguish the two architectures. It is not evidence the variant is worse; it is not evidence of anything.

Note the second trap. The team almost certainly used the test set to select the variant. Thus 84.9% is optimistic, and it is also noisy. Ask for three seeds and a standard error. Also ask if the team used the test set more than one time. If they did, the number is a selection artifact.

By hand — exercise 00.22 · name the tool

For each statement, name the trigger and the tool before you calculate anything. Then say in one line what you would check. You do not need arithmetic.

  1. "I widened d_k from 64 to 256 and the model got worse. Attention is nearly one-hot everywhere."
  2. "Validation loss on my 60-token-vocabulary character model is 3.9. Is that good?"
  3. "Height and shoe size have correlation 0.8 in my data, so I dropped shoe size as redundant."
  4. "My regression targets are house prices; 2% are mansions. Which loss?"
  5. "Dropout at p=0.9 made training unstable rather than just slower."
  6. "The screening test is 99% sensitive, so a positive result means the patient almost certainly has the condition."
Worked solution

1. Applied many times → variance. Dot-product scores have a standard deviation of $\sqrt{d_k}$. Thus four times the $d_k$ gave two times the spread of the attention logits, and the softmax saturated. Its Jacobian term $p(1-p)$ decreased to almost zero, and the layer stopped learning. Check: does the code really apply the $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ scale? (Exercise 00.12.)

2. Is this number good? → baseline. A uniform model over 60 characters gets $\ln 60 = 4.09$. At 3.9, the model has learned almost nothing. Its perplexity is 49, and the baseline is 60. Check: always give $\ln K$ next to a cross-entropy. Perplexity is better, because it is easy to interpret.

3. Related? → correlation, and its limits. There are two cautions. First, correlation finds only linear relations, so 0.8 does not mean that one variable sets the other. Second, for a model, correlated features are not automatically redundant. They can still carry independent signal. To drop one is an experimental question, not an algebra question. Check: measure held-out performance with the feature and without it.

4. Select an output → likelihood. MSE is the Gaussian NLL. House prices have heavy tails, so the assumption is wrong, and the mansions will control the gradient. Use MAE or Huber. Check: plot the distribution of the residuals. If it is not approximately bell-shaped, MSE assumes something false.

5. Applied many times → variance. Inverted dropout keeps the mean, but it multiplies the variance by $p/(1-p)$. At $p = 0.9$, that is 9×. The result is noise, not slow training. Check: decrease the rate to 0.1–0.5. Above approximately 0.5, the added variance usually costs more than the regularization gives.

6. Rare → base rates. Sensitivity alone tells you nothing about $P(\text{disease} \mid +)$. For that, you need the prevalence and the false-positive rate. At 0.5% prevalence and 95% specificity, a positive result gives only an approximately 9% chance of disease (exercise 00.17). Check: ask for the prevalence and the specificity. Or count people in a population of 10,000.

By hand — exercise 00.23 · spot the flawed claim

A reasonable person could say each of these. One is correct. Find the error in the other three, and name the tool that shows it.

  1. "We ran both models on the same fixed seed to make the comparison fair."
  2. "Cross-entropy went from 0.69 to 0.52 on a binary task, so the model learned something real."
  3. "Our model beats the published baseline, which we ran with its default hyperparameters while tuning ours."
  4. "We used the validation set to pick the architecture and the learning rate, then reported the test set once."
Worked solution

1. Incorrect — standard error. A shared seed removes one unwanted difference. But it tells you nothing about the spread. You have one sample from each model, and you do not know if the gap is larger than the variation between runs. A fair comparison needs matched conditions and repeated measurements. The fix is several seeds, not the same seed.

2. Correct — baseline. $\ln 2 = 0.693$ is exactly the loss of a uniform guess on a binary task. Thus 0.69 means "knows nothing", and 0.52 is real progress. The baseline makes the claim possible to check, and this claim includes it indirectly.

3. Incorrect — the untuned baseline. This comparison measures the tuning effort, not the architecture. This is the most common way for honest work to reach a wrong conclusion, and you cannot see it in the table of results. Tune the baseline with the same budget as your own method, and state that budget.

4. Incorrect, but not obviously — repeated selection. It is correct to report the test set one time. But the team used the validation set to select both the architecture and the learning rate. Thus the validation number is now an optimistic selection artifact, and each claim that uses it is too strong. The test value is correct. But do not also show the validation score as an unbiased estimate.

A deliberately small dose This is not a statistics course. It is the minimum that you need to read the rest of this book critically. With it, you can see when a loss curve, an ablation or a benchmark claim does not support the conclusion. The reading guide applies the same instincts to papers. Chapter 12's projects ask you to meet the same standard yourself.

Exercises 00.22 and 00.23 stop at the diagnosis on purpose, because people skip the step of naming the category. But a diagnosis is not very useful if you cannot act on it. Thus the last two exercises take a problem through all the steps: identify, set up, calculate, decide.

Two problems, end to end#

Each exercise above practices one idea. These last two exercises are different. Each one gives you a situation of the type that really occurs. You must find which tools apply before you use them. This chapter exists to teach that step of recognition. Nobody can teach it to you by explanation alone.

By hand — exercise 00.24 · a network that will not train, end to endMust do

"I built a 12-layer classifier over 10 classes, width 256, ReLU, initialized with torch.randn(256, 256) * 1.0. The loss starts at 2.30 and does not move. Learning rates from 1e-5 to 1e-1 all behave the same."

Stage 1 — identify

  1. Two of the four triggers apply here. Which ones? Which words show them?
  2. Before you do any other analysis, what does the number 2.30 tell you?

Stage 2 — set up

  1. Write the expression for $\operatorname{Var}(z)$ at one layer. Use the fan-in $n$ and the weight standard deviation $\sigma_w$.
  2. ReLU sets half of its input to zero. What does that do to the variance? What is the multiplier for each layer of this network?

Stage 3 — compute

  1. Calculate the multiplier. Then calculate the variance after 12 layers.
  2. Find the $\sigma_w$ that makes the multiplier exactly 1.

Stage 4 — decide and verify

  1. Write the fix in one line of code. Give one measurement that would confirm the fix before training.
  2. The learning-rate sweep found nothing. Explain why that result was certain.
Worked solution

1. Applied many times: "12 layers" with the same operation each time, so the variance grows exponentially. And is this number good?: the statement gives a loss with no baseline.

2. $\ln 10 = 2.3026$. The model gives a uniform distribution over the 10 classes. It does not learn badly. It gives no information at all. That is a much stronger clue than "the loss is high".

3. From Part 3, with inputs of variance $v$ and independent zero-mean weights:

$$\operatorname{Var}(z) = n\,\sigma_w^2 \cdot v$$

4. ReLU keeps the positive half and sets the rest to zero. This approximately halves the variance. Thus the multiplier for each layer is

c = n · σ²_w · ½ = 256 × 1.0 × 0.5 = 128

5. Each layer multiplies the variance by 128:

after 12 layers: 128¹² = 2⁸⁴ = 1.93 × 10²⁵ Starting from variance 1, activations reach a scale of about sqrt(1.93e25) ≈ 4.4 × 10¹² before the final layer.

The logits are extremely large. The softmax saturates completely, and the gradient underflows to zero. (In float32, the forward pass can give inf. Then the loss would be nan, not 2.30. The loss is exactly $\ln 10$. This suggests that the logits are large but finite, and that the softmax is one-hot on an arbitrary class.)

6. Set the multiplier to 1 and solve:

n · σ²_w · ½ = 1 σ²_w = 2/n σ_w = sqrt(2/256) = sqrt(0.0078) = 0.0884

That is He initialization, $\sqrt{2/n}$. You derived it here; you did not just remember it. Note that it is the ReLU version of Xavier because of the factor of $\tfrac12$ in stage 2.

7. The fix:

nn.init.kaiming_normal_(layer.weight, nonlinearity='relu')
# or simply use nn.Linear's default, which is already scaled by fan-in

The measurement, before you train anything: put one batch through the network, and print the variance of the activations at each layer. It must stay near 1. If it increases by a constant factor at each layer, that factor is the multiplier from stage 4. You can read $\sigma_w$ directly from it. This costs one forward pass, and it answers the question completely.

8. The learning rate multiplies the gradient, and the gradient here is zero. Each output is saturated, so $\sigma'$ or the ReLU derivative gives nothing to propagate. Any multiple of zero is zero. A sweep can help only when there is a signal with the wrong magnitude. It cannot make a signal. Learn the difference between "wrong magnitude" and "no signal". It saves you the afternoon that the sweep would cost.

By hand — exercise 00.25 · is the result real, end to endRecommended

"Our new architecture reaches 71.2% on the rare-event detection task, against 69.6% for the baseline. It also has 96% accuracy overall. Positives are 4% of the data."

Stage 1 — identify

  1. Two triggers apply, to two different claims in that statement. Name both.

Stage 2 — set up

  1. The comparison: what would you need to say that the gap of 1.6 points is real? Write the quantity and its formula.
  2. The 96%: what does a model that always predicts "negative" get? What does that tell you about the metric?

Stage 3 — compute

You ask for more data, and you get three seeds for each model:

new : 71.2, 68.9, 70.3 baseline : 69.6, 70.1, 68.4 useful: sqrt(3) = 1.732
  1. Calculate each mean, each sample standard deviation and each standard error.
  2. Calculate the gap between the means. Calculate the combined standard error $\sqrt{\text{SE}_1^2 + \text{SE}_2^2}$.
  3. The detector works on 4% positives at 96% overall accuracy. Recall is 60% and specificity is 97.5%. What is the precision?

Stage 4 — decide

  1. What can you claim about the architecture? Write the sentence that you would put in a report.
  2. If the gap of 1.6 points is real, what would you need to prove it?
Worked solution

1. Measured one time: the statement compares two single numbers, so it is a standard-error question. And rare: positives are 4%, so "96% accuracy" is a base-rate question.

2. You need the standard error of each mean, $\text{SE} = s/\sqrt{n}$ over several seeds. Then see if the gap is larger than approximately two times the combined standard error.

3. "Always negative" gets 96%. That is the same as the reported value. Thus accuracy gives no information here. A model that learned nothing would get the same value.

4.

new mean = (71.2+68.9+70.3)/3 = 70.13 deviations +1.07, −1.23, +0.17 s = sqrt((1.145+1.513+0.029)/2) = sqrt(1.343) = 1.159 SE = 1.159/1.732 = 0.669 baseline mean = (69.6+70.1+68.4)/3 = 69.37 deviations +0.23, +0.73, −0.97 s = sqrt((0.053+0.533+0.941)/2) = sqrt(0.764) = 0.874 SE = 0.874/1.732 = 0.505

5.

gap = 70.13 − 69.37 = 0.76 points combined SE = sqrt(0.669² + 0.505²) = sqrt(0.447+0.255) = 0.838 0.76 < 2 × 0.838 = 1.68 -> well inside the noise

Note also that the first claim, 71.2 against 69.6, compared the best seed of one model with an average seed of the other. The real gap over three seeds is 0.76, not 1.6.

6. In 1,000 examples, 40 are positive and 960 are negative.

true positives = 40 × 0.60 = 24 false positives = 960 × 0.025 = 24 precision = 24 / (24 + 24) = 50%

Half of the alerts are false, from a model with a reported accuracy of 96%.

7. For example:

Over three seeds, the new architecture has a mean of 70.1% and the baseline has 69.4%. The gap is 0.8 points and the combined standard error is 0.8, so we cannot tell the two apart. We do not report overall accuracy. With a positive rate of 4%, it gives no information: the majority class alone gets 96%. At the measured operating point, precision is 50% at 60% recall.

That claim is weaker than the original, and it is much more useful, because it is the claim that stays true under examination.

8. Standard error decreases as $1/\sqrt{n}$. To resolve a gap of 0.76 points, you need a combined SE of approximately 0.38. That is a factor of 2, so you need approximately four times as many seeds: twelve for each model. Before you spend that compute, ask if a difference of 0.8 points would change a decision. Usually the honest action is to find a larger effect. Do not use more compute to chase a small one.

Feel for the numbersMust do

Each loss in this book is the logarithm of a probability. Thus each one has a minimum that you can calculate, and a chance-level value that you can compare with. Learn these six, and you can read a training log without running anything. All values are in nats ($\ln$), because PyTorch reports nats.

QuantityFloorTypicalCeilingRead it as
Cross-entropy, $K$ classes0$\ln K$ at chanceunboundedcompare to $\ln K$ first, always
Binary cross-entropy00.693unboundedchance is $\ln 2$, not 0.5
Perplexity $e^{\mathcal{L}}$1$K$ at chance$K$the effective number of choices left
Entropy $H(p)$0—$\ln K$0 is certainty, $\ln K$ is total ignorance
$D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)$0—unbounded0 only when the distributions match
$-\ln q$ for one example00.69 at $q=0.5$unbounded$q = 0.01$ costs 4.6; confident and wrong is expensive

Now do these on paper. Where you can, do them in your head. You can use a calculator for the logarithms. The goal is to know which number to use.

  1. A 10-class classifier trained for an hour. It reports a loss of 2.30. Is it learning?
  2. A character model with a vocabulary of 73 characters reports 1.51 nats. What is its perplexity? What has it ruled out?
  3. A binary classifier reports loss 0.69 and accuracy 50%. These are two numbers. How many independent facts do they give?
  4. One example gets probability 0.05 on the correct class. What does it add to the loss? Compare that with the chance-level average for $K = 10$.
Answers

1. $\ln 10 = 2.303$. The loss is exactly at chance. An hour of compute gave nothing, and the loss number alone did not tell you that.

2. $e^{1.51} = 4.53$. The model went from 73 possible characters to approximately four and a half. Note how much easier that is to read than "1.51".

3. One. $\ln 2 = 0.693$, so both numbers say the same thing: chance. They do not confirm each other.

4. $-\ln 0.05 = 3.00$, against a chance level of 2.30. The model predicts that one example worse than a guess. A model can have a good average loss and still do this on a full subpopulation.

The habit. Before you read a loss curve, calculate $\ln K$ and draw it on the axis. If you cannot compare a loss with chance, it is not yet information.

Say it backRecommended

Explain this to your favorite LLM, in your own words: why is minimizing cross-entropy the same thing as maximizing likelihood? Then ask it to correct you. Ask it to question each part where you were vague, not only the parts where you were wrong, because the gaps are in the vague parts. Do not use the words cross-entropy, likelihood or loss in your first two sentences. The paraphrase is the full exercise. If you cannot start without those words, you are only repeating them.

What a good answer covers — open this afterwards, not before
  1. A model gives a distribution, not an answer. Likelihood is the probability that the model gave to the data that really occurred.
  2. A product of many probabilities underflows, and it is difficult to differentiate. A logarithm changes the product into a sum.
  3. To maximize log-likelihood is to minimize its negative. That is the average of $-\log q$ at the true class.
  4. That average is cross-entropy $H(p,q)$ when $p$ is the one-hot truth.
  5. $H(p,q) = H(p) + D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)$, and the data fixes $H(p)$. Thus, when you minimize cross-entropy, you minimize divergence from the truth.

Most common miss. Most answers write the formula and stop. The formula is the result of the decision that the model gives beliefs. If your explanation would also justify MSE, it has not said anything yet.

Notebook Open 00_math_foundations/prompt.ipynb. In it, you will do these tasks:
  • Verify the linear algebra rules in code, and read a network diagram as matrices.
  • Run each broadcasting example from this chapter. See two silent bugs, a (N, 1) minus (N,) loss and a mask on the wrong axis, and fix each one.
  • Check the derivative rules, and the partial-derivative rules, with finite differences.
  • Measure variance propagation through a deep stack. See it explode and collapse with the wrong initialization.
  • Confirm the $\sqrt{d_k}$ argument with experiments.
  • Implement BCE, softmax and cross-entropy from their definitions.
  • Get the $\hat{y}-y$ gradient in three independent ways.
It trains no real model. (One cell fits a single weight, to show what the broadcasting bug does to training.) It is only about the mathematics.
Where this goes next Chapter 01 uses all four parts at the same time. Matrix multiplication gives the forward pass. The BCE loss comes from this chapter. The chain rule gives each gradient. The variance argument explains why weights start random and small. That is backpropagation. After this chapter, it adds no new mathematics.

Chapter 01 · notebook 01_nn_from_scratch

A Neural Network from Scratch#

This chapter uses one network, four training examples and no framework. At the end of it, you will calculate a forward pass, a loss and each gradient in a two-layer network with only arithmetic. You will derive backpropagation and gradient descent with only the derivative rules from Chapter 00. You will also know exactly which line of PyTorch replaces each step.

XOR: the smallest problem that needs a hidden layer#

The exclusive-or function is the traditional first problem, and there is a good reason. It is the smallest dataset that a network without a hidden layer cannot learn. There is a proof of this.

$x_1$$x_2$$y$
000
011
101
110

Plot those four points. The two points with label 1 are on one diagonal. The two points with label 0 are on the other diagonal. A model of the form $\hat{y} = \sigma(w_1x_1 + w_2x_2 + b)$ can divide the plane with only one straight line. The decision boundary is exactly where $w_1x_1 + w_2x_2 + b = 0$. No straight line separates one diagonal from the other. More training does not help. It is a geometric impossibility. This observation stopped most neural network research in the 1970s.

The fix is a hidden layer. It is a first transformation that bends the space, so that a straight line works in the new coordinates. Learn this idea exactly, because each layer of each deep network does it.

Key concept A neural network is a stack of linear maps (matrix multiplications, Chapter 00) and elementwise non-linearities, one after the other. The linear maps rotate, scale and shear the space. The non-linearities fold it. When you repeat the two, they bend the input space until the classes become linearly separable. Then the last layer draws the straight line. Without the non-linearity between them, two linear maps become one linear map ($W_2(W_1x) = (W_2W_1)x$). Then the extra layer gives you nothing.
Example — watching the fold happen

Use two hidden units with these weights. Put all four XOR inputs through them. Unit 1 is on when "at least one input is on". Unit 2 is on when "both inputs are on".

unit 1: z = 20x₁ + 20x₂ − 10 unit 2: z = 20x₁ + 20x₂ − 30 x₁ x₂ │ z₁ a₁=σ(z₁) │ z₂ a₂=σ(z₂) │ y ──────┼─────────────────┼─────────────────┼──── 0 0 │ −10 0.00 │ −30 0.00 │ 0 0 1 │ 10 1.00 │ −10 0.00 │ 1 1 0 │ 10 1.00 │ −10 0.00 │ 1 1 1 │ 30 1.00 │ 10 1.00 │ 0

In the original coordinates, the two classes are on opposite diagonals, and no line separates them. In the new $(a_1, a_2)$ coordinates, there are three different points: $(0,0)$ for label 0, $(1,0)$ for label 1, and $(1,1)$ for label 0. The line $a_1 - a_2 = 0.5$ separates them cleanly. The hidden layer did not classify anything. It moved the points until a straight line was sufficient. Each hidden layer in each network does this.

Architecture and shapes#

We use two inputs, four hidden units and one output. The network processes all four training examples at the same time, as a batch. Thus each operation is a matrix multiplication.

TensorShapeMeaning
$X$(4, 2)4 examples, 2 features each
$W_1$(2, 4)input → hidden weights
$b_1$(1, 4)hidden biases
$W_2$(4, 1)hidden → output weights
$b_2$(1, 1)output bias
$Y$(4, 1)4 targets

The shape of a weight tells you what a layer does. (2, 4) means "takes 2 features and makes 4". The batch dimension is always first, and it never changes. If you learn only one debug habit from this book, learn this one: when something breaks, print the shapes.

The forward pass#

$$Z_1 = XW_1 + b_1 \qquad A_1 = \sigma(Z_1) \qquad Z_2 = A_1W_2 + b_2 \qquad A_2 = \sigma(Z_2)$$

That is four lines, and $A_2$ is the prediction. Before we look at the mechanics, learn the names. They are not arbitrary, and nothing later makes sense without them.

Why each layer has two names

A layer does two things. Each thing gets its own letter, because the backward pass needs both of them separately.

Z "pre-activation" what the matrix multiply produced, before anything was squashed Z1 = X W1 + b1 A "activation" the same numbers after the sigmoid A1 = sigma(Z1)

The subscript is the layer: $Z_1, A_1$ for the hidden layer, and $Z_2, A_2$ for the output. $A_2$ has a second name. It is also $\hat{y}$, the prediction, because there is nothing more to do to it.

Why keep both, and not overwrite one? Because the backward pass needs each one for a different reason. It needs $Z_1$ to find how steep the sigmoid was here, which is $\sigma'(Z_1)$. It needs $A_1$ because $A_1$ was the input to the next layer, and the gradient of a weight always comes from its input. If the forward pass discards either one, the backward pass must calculate it again. That is exactly why frameworks keep activations, and why memory increases with depth.

Two mechanisms inside those four lines need more explanation.

Every entry is a dot product#

The matrix product $XW_1$ gives a (4, 4) result. Its entry $(i, j)$ is the dot product of the features of example $i$ with the weights of hidden unit $j$. That is all that a linear layer does: each output unit takes a weighted vote over all the inputs. Step through the widget below. See how each output cell comes from one row and one column.

Broadcasting the bias#

$b_1$ has shape (1, 4), but the code adds it to a (4, 4) matrix. NumPy and PyTorch both stretch the length-1 dimension to match. They add the same bias vector to each row, so each example gets the same bias. That is what you want. (Chapter 00 explains the rule, and why the bias gradient becomes a sum.) Broadcasting is convenient, but it also causes many silent bugs. Suppose that you have a (4, 1) where you wanted a (1, 4). It broadcasts into a (4, 4) of incorrect values, and you get no error.

Sigmoid#

$$\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}} \qquad\qquad \sigma'(z) = \sigma(z)\big(1 - \sigma(z)\big)$$

The sigmoid changes any real number into a number in $(0, 1)$. Thus we can read the output as a probability, as Chapter 00 said we must. You can write its derivative with its own output. Thus, during backpropagation, you can use the value that you already calculated. You do not have to calculate an exponential again.

Move the input past $\pm 5$, and see the derivative curve become flat. That is saturation, and it is the main problem of the sigmoid. A unit far from zero stops learning. Each gradient that comes from above is multiplied by a very small number on its way down: 0.0066 at $z = 5$, and 0.000045 at $z = 10$. Note also that the maximum of the derivative is only 0.25. Stack ten sigmoid layers. In the best case, the gradient is multiplied by $0.25^{10} \approx 10^{-6}$ before it gets to the first layer. This is the vanishing-gradient problem. It is why ReLU and GELU replaced the sigmoid in all hidden layers. Change the selector above to compare them. Use the sigmoid only where you really need a probability: at the output.

The loss#

The output is a probability, and the target is binary. Thus Chapter 00 already told us what to use: the Bernoulli negative log-likelihood.

$$\mathcal{L} = -\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\Big[y_i \log a_{2,i} + (1-y_i)\log(1 - a_{2,i})\Big]$$
Numerical trap If the network gives exactly 0 or 1, this becomes $\log 0 = -\infty$, and your loss becomes nan. It stays nan, because nan goes into each gradient and weight after it. From scratch, the fix is to clip: np.clip(a2, 1e-7, 1 - 1e-7). BCEWithLogitsLoss in Chapter 02 removes exactly this hazard, because it never calculates the probability.

All of it, as one expression#

Before you differentiate anything, look at the full calculation written one time. The four forward equations make the calculation easy, but they are not four separate functions. If you put each equation into the next one, you get one expression. That expression is what the loss really is:

$$\mathcal{L}(W_1, b_1, W_2, b_2) \;=\; \text{BCE}\Big(\; \sigma\big(\,\sigma(XW_1 + b_1)\,W_2 + b_2\,\big)\;,\; y \Big)$$

Read it from the inside to the outside. Each step of the forward pass is there, in sequence:

  1. Multiply the inputs by $W_1$ and add $b_1$.
  2. Apply the sigmoid.
  3. Multiply by $W_2$ and add $b_2$.
  4. Apply the sigmoid again.
  5. Compare with $y$.

Nothing is hidden and nothing is shortened. This one line is the network.

Now see what it tells you about differentiation. Exactly four things can change. Each one occurs exactly one time, and each one is inside a different number of operations. That count is all of backpropagation:

Thus $\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial W_2$ will be a short chain, and $\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial W_1$ will be a longer one. The difference between them is not a different idea. It is two extra factors, because $W_1$ is two operations deeper. Each formula in the next section applies that observation.

Backpropagation#

We need $\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial W$ for all four parameter tensors. This section derives each one with only the rules from Chapter 00, Part 2: the logarithm rule, the chain rule, the partial-derivative rules and the sum over paths. Backpropagation is not a new theorem. It is the chain rule, applied in a specific sequence. It keeps intermediate results and uses them again, so that it does not calculate them two times. After the derivation, a smaller XOR network does the same calculation with numbers, entry by entry.

Start at the output#

The loss is the only value that we really care about. Thus the backward pass starts there and moves toward the input. The first question is the simplest possible question: if the prediction $a_2$ was slightly larger, would the loss increase or decrease?

That is only a derivative of the loss formula. Thus, take the loss for one example and differentiate it. Only two terms contain $a_2$:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{one example}} = -\Big[\,y\log a_2 \;+\; (1-y)\log(1 - a_2)\,\Big]$$

The derivative of $\log a$ is $1/a$. By the chain rule, the derivative of $\log(1-a)$ is $-1/(1-a)$. Thus:

dL/da2 = -[ y · (1/a2) + (1-y) · (-1/(1-a2)) ] = -[ y/a2 - (1-y)/(1-a2) ] put the two fractions over the common denominator a2(1-a2): = -[ y(1-a2) - (1-y)a2 ] / [ a2(1-a2) ] expand the top: y - y·a2 - a2 + y·a2 = y - a2 the y·a2 terms cancel = -( y - a2 ) / [ a2(1-a2) ] = ( a2 - y ) / [ a2(1-a2) ] <- flip the sign, tidier

The average over the $N$ examples in the batch puts a $1/N$ in front. That is the source of the factor: it is the "mean" in "mean loss", and nothing more. We also need the derivative of the sigmoid itself, from Chapter 00:

$$\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a_2} = \frac{1}{N}\left(\frac{a_2 - y}{a_2(1-a_2)}\right) \qquad \frac{\partial a_2}{\partial z_2} = a_2(1-a_2)$$

Now multiply them. The chain rule says to do this when you go one more step back: from the prediction $a_2$ to the number $z_2$ that made it. See what happens. The $a_2(1-a_2)$ in the denominator is exactly the $a_2(1-a_2)$ from the sigmoid. Thus they cancel completely:

$$\delta_2 = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial z_2} = \frac{1}{N}(a_2 - y)$$
What $\delta$ is, and why it gets a name

$\delta_2$ is not new notation without a reason. It is a short name for one specific quantity: the derivative of the loss with respect to the pre-activation of a layer, $\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial z$. It is a matrix with the shape of $z$: here (4, 1), one number for each example. Entry $n$ tells you how much the loss changes when $z_2$ of example $n$ increases by a small amount. (This is the $\delta$ of Chapter 00, with $Y = z$.) It gets a name because all the other gradients in that layer come from it:

given delta for a layer, you immediately get: the weight gradient dL/dW = (what came in)^T · delta the bias gradient dL/db = sum of delta over the batch the PREVIOUS layer's delta_prev = (delta · W^T) * sigma'(z_prev)

Thus the backward pass is only this: calculate $\delta$ for the last layer, read its two gradients, and give a $\delta$ to the layer before it. Then do it again. Informally, $\delta$ is "how wrong the output of this layer was, measured in a form that the layer can use". That is why people often call it the error signal. For the output layer, it is exactly the prediction minus the target.

Key concept This is the same cancellation as the softmax/cross-entropy pair in Chapter 00. This is not a coincidence: sigmoid + BCE is the two-class special case of softmax + cross-entropy. The signal that starts the full backward pass is only prediction minus target. It has no saturation factor and nothing makes it smaller. If we used MSE, the $\sigma'(z_2)$ term would stay. It would slow learning exactly when the model is most wrong.

Gradients for the output layer#

Now go one step further back, from $z_2$ to the parameters. Look at one entry: $z_2$ of example $n$ is $\sum_j A_1[n,j]\,W_2[j] + b_2$. With the partial-derivative rules from Chapter 00, $\partial z_2[n]/\partial W_2[j] = A_1[n,j]$, because each other term is a constant. And $\partial z_2[n]/\partial b_2 = 1$. But each weight is used for all four examples, so it has four paths to the loss. The sum over paths adds them. The next section writes that sum entry by entry. The result is:

$$\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W_2} = A_1^{\top}\delta_2 \qquad \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial b_2} = \sum_i \delta_{2,i}$$

Check the shapes, because they are the best proof that you wrote it correctly. $A_1^\top$ is (4, 4) and $\delta_2$ is (4, 1). Thus the product is (4, 1). That is exactly the shape of $W_2$, as a gradient must be. The bias gradient sums over the batch. The same $b_2$ broadcast to all four examples, so all four contributions add together. This is the rule from Chapter 00: the gradient of a broadcast is a sum over the stretched axis.

Rule of thumb The gradient for a weight is always (what came in)ᵀ × (what must change at the output). Each backward formula in this book uses that pattern, also the formulas for attention.

What a gradient actually is#

Be very exact about this point. When people start to type the code, this is where they stop. $\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial W_2$ is not a new type of object, and it is not one number. It is a matrix with exactly the same shape as $W_2$. The entry in row $j$, column $k$ is the ordinary partial derivative of the loss with respect to the one number in row $j$, column $k$ of $W_2$.

$W_2$ is (4, 1): four hidden units go into one output. Thus its gradient has four entries. Here they are in full:

[ W2[0,0] ] [ dL/dW2[0,0] ] W2 = [ W2[1,0] ] dL/dW2 = [ dL/dW2[1,0] ] [ W2[2,0] ] [ dL/dW2[2,0] ] [ W2[3,0] ] [ dL/dW2[3,0] ] shape (4, 1) shape (4, 1) <- always

Each of those four numbers answers one concrete question: if I make this one weight a very small amount larger, and change nothing else, does the loss increase or decrease, and how fast? That is all. The gradient is those four answers, in the same shape as the weights, so that you can subtract one from the other.

You could also calculate each entry from its definition. Entry $j$ of $\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial W_2$ adds two things over each example in the batch: how much the hidden activation $j$ of that example contributed, and how wrong the output of that example was:

$$\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial W_2[j,0]} \;=\; \sum_{n} A_1[n, j]\;\delta_2[n, 0]$$

As a loop, this is what you would type if you did not know about matrix products: 

dW2 = np.zeros_like(W2)                 # (4, 1), same shape as W2
for j in range(4):                      # every hidden unit
    total = 0.0
    for n in range(4):                  # every example in the batch
        total += A1[n, j] * d2[n, 0]
    dW2[j, 0] = total

And this is the reason to write it with matrices: those two loops are a matrix product. The product of $A_1^\top$ and $\delta_2$ calculates exactly that sum, for all $j$ at the same time: 

dW2 = A1.T @ d2                         # identical numbers, one line
Key concept A matrix product is not a new idea that makes this more difficult. It is a short way to write "for each output, sum over the batch of (what came in) times (what must change)". Many backward formulas in this book look like $\text{something}^\top \times \text{something}$. You can always change one back into the loop above and check it entry by entry. When a gradient has the wrong shape, that is how you find the cause.

The bias works the same way, with one axis fewer. $b_2$ is one number that the code adds to the output of each example. Thus a small change to it affects all four examples, and its derivative is the sum of what each example wanted:

dL/db2[0] = d2[0,0] + d2[1,0] + d2[2,0] + d2[3,0] in code: db2 = d2.sum(axis=0) shape (1,) <- same as b2

Propagate to the hidden layer#

The hidden activations affected the loss only through $z_2$. Thus the error goes back through $W_2$, and then through the hidden sigmoid. Do it for one entry first. Two steps of the chain rule give it:

step 1, back through the product z2[n] = sum_j A1[n,j] W2[j] + b2: A1[n,j] occurs only in z2[n], where W2[j] multiplies it dL/dA1[n,j] = delta2[n] * W2[j] one path, one product step 2, back through the sigmoid A1[n,j] = sigma(Z1[n,j]): A1[n,j] depends only on Z1[n,j] delta1[n,j] = dL/dA1[n,j] * sigma'(Z1[n,j]) one path, one product

Step 1 for all entries at the same time is $\delta_2 W_2^\top$: it is the rule "multiply by the other factor, transposed" from the transpose section of Chapter 00. Step 2 is an entry-by-entry product, $\odot$. Thus:

$$\delta_1 = \big(\delta_2 W_2^{\top}\big) \odot \sigma'(Z_1) \qquad\text{where}\qquad \sigma'(Z_1) = A_1 \odot (1 - A_1)$$

$\odot$ is elementwise multiplication. The two factors have different jobs. $\delta_2W_2^\top$ divides the blame: a hidden unit with a large weight gets a large part of it. $\sigma'(Z_1)$ measures how responsive that unit was. A saturated unit has $\sigma' \approx 0$, so it gets nothing, however much blame it deserves.

$$\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W_1} = X^{\top}\delta_1 \qquad \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial b_1} = \sum_i \delta_{1,i}$$

This is the same pattern, one layer lower. That is the full algorithm:

  1. Calculate $\delta$ at the top.
  2. Multiply by a weight matrix to move down one layer.
  3. Multiply by an activation derivative to go through a non-linearity.
  4. At each layer, collect a weight gradient. Then go back to step 2.

And once more, for the hidden layer#

This repeats the steps on purpose, because this is where people stop. $W_1$ is (2, 4): two input features go into four hidden units. Thus its gradient has eight entries, one for each weight, in exactly that shape:

[ W1[0,0] W1[0,1] W1[0,2] W1[0,3] ] W1 = [ W1[1,0] W1[1,1] W1[1,2] W1[1,3] ] shape (2, 4) [ dL/dW1[0,0] dL/dW1[0,1] dL/dW1[0,2] dL/dW1[0,3] ] dL/dW1= [ dL/dW1[1,0] dL/dW1[1,1] dL/dW1[1,2] dL/dW1[1,3] ] (2, 4)

Entry $(i, j)$ asks the same concrete question as before: make a small change to the weight between input feature $i$ and hidden unit $j$; what happens to the loss? You calculate it in the same way, with a sum over the batch:

$$\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial W_1[i,j]} \;=\; \sum_{n} X[n, i]\;\delta_1[n, j]$$ 
dW1 = np.zeros_like(W1)                 # (2, 4), same shape as W1
for i in range(2):                      # every input feature
    for j in range(4):                  # every hidden unit
        total = 0.0
        for n in range(4):              # every example in the batch
            total += X[n, i] * d1[n, j]
        dW1[i, j] = total

dW1 = X.T @ d1                          # the same eight numbers, one line

Compare the two results. The pattern is exact. For $W_2$, the input was $A_1$ and the thing that must change was $\delta_2$. That gives $A_1^\top\delta_2$. For $W_1$, the input was $X$ and the thing that must change was $\delta_1$. That gives $X^\top\delta_1$. It is the same sentence for a different layer. The only work specific to $W_1$ was the calculation of $\delta_1$. From the previous section, that is $(\delta_2W_2^\top)\odot\sigma'(Z_1)$: the two extra factors that the nesting diagram predicted.

The same steps, for any number of layers#

Each layer did the same three things. Thus you can write the backward pass one time, for a network of any depth. Number the layers $l = 1, \dots, k$, and let $A_0 = X$. Each layer calculates $Z_l = A_{l-1}W_l + b_l$ and $A_l = f(Z_l)$.

FORWARD A0 = X for l = 1 .. k: Z_l = A_(l-1) W_l + b_l keep A_(l-1) and Z_l A_l = f(Z_l) L = loss(A_k, Y) BACKWARD delta_k = dL/dZ_k from the loss: (A_k - Y)/N here for l = k down to 1: dL/dW_l = A_(l-1)^T delta_l what came in, transposed, times delta dL/db_l = delta_l.sum(axis=0) b_l was broadcast over the batch if l > 1: delta_(l-1) = (delta_l W_l^T) * f'(Z_(l-1)) * is elementwise UPDATE each parameter <- parameter - eta * its gradient (next section)

Each line of the backward pass comes from one rule in Chapter 00:

  • $\delta_k$ comes from the logarithm rule and the chain rule. The $\sigma'$ cancels, as in Start at the output.
  • The weight gradient comes from the partial-derivative rule (each weight multiplies one input) and the sum over paths (each weight is used for each example).
  • The bias gradient is the gradient of a broadcast: a sum over the batch axis.
  • The next $\delta$ comes from two chain-rule steps: through the matrix product (multiply by the other factor, transposed), then through $f$ (multiply entry by entry by $f'$).
Key concept — why the order is backward

Look at what each $\delta_l$ does. It gives two gradients, and it makes the next $\delta$. Thus each $\delta$ is calculated one time and used three times. Now suppose you calculated $\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial W_1$ separately, from the loss. You must multiply through every layer above it. Then for $\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial W_2$, you must do almost the same product again.

k layers, one chain-rule step per layer crossed each gradient separately: k + (k-1) + ... + 1 = k(k+1)/2 steps (5,050 for k = 100) backward, keeping delta: k steps (100 for k = 100)

The cost of the saving is memory. The backward pass needs each $A_{l-1}$ and each $Z_l$, so the forward pass must keep all of them. That is why training uses much more memory than inference, and why the memory increases with depth and with batch size.

What you are multiplying by, and what it is called#

Each step of the backward pass multiplied the incoming gradient by something. That something has a name. The name occurs frequently from here on, and texts rarely explain it.

When one number depends on one number, the derivative is one number. When a vector of outputs depends on a vector of inputs, there is a derivative for each pair: each output with respect to each input. The natural place to put all of them is a grid:

for an operation taking m inputs to n outputs, the derivative is an n x m matrix, and entry (i, j) is d(output i) / d(input j) that matrix is called the JACOBIAN of the operation.

Thus a Jacobian is not a new type of mathematics. It is a table of ordinary partial derivatives, as in Chapter 00. The table has this arrangement so that you move a gradient back through an operation with one matrix multiplication by that table. That is the only reason it exists. It changes "apply the chain rule to each pair of things" into one product.

Key concept — and why elementwise functions are cheap

Think about the Jacobian of an elementwise function like ReLU or sigmoid. Output $i$ depends on input $i$ and on nothing more. Thus each off-diagonal entry is zero. For example, output 3 does not change when input 7 changes:

Jacobian of an elementwise f, for 3 values: [ f'(z1) 0 0 ] [ 0 f'(z2) 0 ] [ 0 0 f'(z3) ]

A multiplication by a diagonal matrix is the same as a multiplication entry by entry. That is why $f'(Z)$ occurs in the backward pass with a $\odot$, and not with a matrix product. It is also why the backward pass through an activation costs almost nothing. When a later chapter says that a gradient was "multiplied by a Jacobian per step", think of one of these matrices. A later chapter also says that the Jacobian of the softmax is $\operatorname{diag}(p) - pp^{\top}$. Note that the softmax is not elementwise. Thus its off-diagonal entries are not zero, and it costs more.

You can recover every line from the shapes alone

Do this one time. After that, you never have to memorize the backward pass. You can make it again on a whiteboard from only the forward shapes.

$\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial W_2$ must have the same shape as $W_2$, which is (h, K). You have two things: $A_1$ at (N, h) and $\delta_2$ at (N, K). There is exactly one way to multiply them and get (h, K): transpose $A_1$ and put it on the left. In the same way, $\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial A_1$ must be (N, h). The only arrangement of $\delta_2$ (N, K) and $W_2$ (h, K) that gives that shape is $\delta_2 W_2^\top$. The shapes give you no choice. That is why the transpose section of Chapter 00 said that transposes come from the backward pass.

Gradient descent#

Backpropagation gives $\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial\theta$ for each parameter $\theta$. Now use it. This section derives the update rule from two facts in Chapter 00: the gradient and the dot product.

Which direction decreases the loss fastest#

Put all the parameters in one long vector $\theta$. Change them by a small vector $\Delta$. For a small change, each parameter changes the loss by its partial derivative times its own change, and these changes add:

$$\mathcal{L}(\theta + \Delta) \;\approx\; \mathcal{L}(\theta) + \sum_i \frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\theta_i}\,\Delta_i \;=\; \mathcal{L}(\theta) + \nabla\mathcal{L}\cdot\Delta$$

This is the first-order approximation. It is only the definition of the derivative, used for all the parameters at the same time. Check it with the function from Chapter 00, $f(x, y) = x^2y + 3y$, at $(2, 1)$, where $\nabla f = [4, 7]$. Increase $x$ by 0.01. The approximation says that $f$ increases by $4 \times 0.01 = 0.04$. The real change is $f(2.01, 1) - f(2, 1) = 0.0401$.

Now look at the form of the change: $\nabla\mathcal{L}\cdot\Delta$ is a dot product. Chapter 00 showed that $\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b} = \|\mathbf{a}\|\,\|\mathbf{b}\|\cos\phi$, where $\phi$ is the angle between the two vectors. Select a step length $\varepsilon$, so that $\|\Delta\| = \varepsilon$. Then only the angle can change. The dot product is most negative when $\cos\phi = -1$, that is, when $\Delta$ points opposite to $\nabla\mathcal{L}$.

Example — five steps of the same length, five results

Start at $(2, 1)$ with $\nabla f = [4, 7]$ and $\|\nabla f\| = 8.062$. Take a step of length 0.01 in five directions:

direction step predicted real change ∇f · step of f +∇f (uphill) [ 0.00496, 0.00868] +0.0806 +0.0808 −x only [−0.01, 0 ] −0.0400 −0.0399 −y only [ 0, −0.01 ] −0.0700 −0.0700 perpendicular to ∇f [−0.00868, 0.00496] 0.0000 −0.0001 −∇f (downhill) [−0.00496, −0.00868] −0.0806 −0.0804 ← the largest decrease

A step perpendicular to the gradient changes almost nothing. A step along $-\nabla f$ decreases $f$ more than any other step of the same length.

Thus the best step is $\Delta = -\varepsilon\,\nabla\mathcal{L}/\|\nabla\mathcal{L}\|$. Write $\eta = \varepsilon/\|\nabla\mathcal{L}\|$, and you get the update rule:

$$\theta \;\leftarrow\; \theta - \eta\,\nabla\mathcal{L} \qquad\text{one entry at a time:}\qquad W \;\leftarrow\; W - \eta\,\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial W}$$

$\eta$ is the learning rate. It sets the size of the step, and it is the most important number in training. Put the step into the approximation, and you get the predicted change of the loss:

$$\mathcal{L}(\theta - \eta\nabla\mathcal{L}) - \mathcal{L}(\theta) \;\approx\; \nabla\mathcal{L}\cdot(-\eta\nabla\mathcal{L}) \;=\; -\eta\,\|\nabla\mathcal{L}\|^2 \;\le\; 0$$

Two facts follow. First, a small enough step always decreases the loss, unless the gradient is zero. If the gradient is zero, you are at a minimum, a maximum or a flat point, and the method stops. Second, the length of the step is $\eta\,\|\nabla\mathcal{L}\|$. Near a minimum, the gradient becomes small, so the steps become small automatically.

How large the learning rate can be#

The first-order approximation ignores the curvature, so it is correct only for small steps. Add the next term to see the limit. For one parameter, with $\mathcal{L}''$ the second derivative (the curvature):

$$\mathcal{L}(w + \Delta) \;\approx\; \mathcal{L}(w) + \mathcal{L}'\Delta + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}''\Delta^2$$

Put in the step $\Delta = -\eta\mathcal{L}'$:

$$\mathcal{L}(w - \eta\mathcal{L}') - \mathcal{L}(w) \;\approx\; -\eta\mathcal{L}'^2 + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}''\eta^2\mathcal{L}'^2 \;=\; -\eta\,\mathcal{L}'^2\Big(1 - \frac{\eta\,\mathcal{L}''}{2}\Big)$$

The loss decreases only if the factor in brackets is positive. Thus $\boxed{\eta < 2/\mathcal{L}''}$. A sharp valley (large curvature) needs a small learning rate.

Example — one step, by hand
L(w) = (w − 4)² L′ = 2(w − 4) L″ = 2 limit: η < 2/2 = 1 w = 1, η = 0.1: L′(1) = −6 w ← 1 − 0.1(−6) = 1.6 L(1.0) = 9.00 L(1.6) = 5.76 predicted change: −0.1 × 36 × (1 − 0.1) = −3.24 real: 5.76 − 9.00 = −3.24 ✓ w = 1, η = 1.0 (at the limit): w ← 1 + 6 = 7 L(7) = 9 the same loss, on the other side of the minimum

The prediction is exact here, because this loss is a quadratic and has no higher terms. For a real network, it is only an approximation. Also, a network has a different curvature in each direction, and the sharpest direction sets the limit for all of them. That is the problem that Adam solves: it gives each parameter its own effective step size.

Push Step and watch. At a small learning rate, the ball moves downhill reliably but slowly. The left valley has a curvature of approximately 4.4 at its bottom, so the limit is $2/4.4 \approx 0.45$. At 0.5, the ball jumps from one wall of the valley to the other and never settles. Above approximately 0.6, the first step goes too far. The gradient at the new point is larger and points back the other way. Each step goes farther out, and the loss goes to infinity in a few iterations. When the loss is nan five steps into training, this is usually the cause. A lower learning rate is usually the fix.

Note also that this landscape has two minima. The start point and the step size decide which one you get to. From the default start, a learning rate of 0.2 gets to the left minimum, and 0.3 gets to the right one. Real loss surfaces have very many minima. That is why weight initialization is important, and why two runs of the same code give different results. It is also why we initialize $W$ randomly and not at zero. If all the weights are the same, each hidden unit calculates the same thing and gets the same gradient. Thus the units stay the same forever. This failure is called symmetry, and random initialization does the symmetry breaking. Biases can start at zero, because the random weights already break the symmetry.

The algorithm, in full
  1. Do the forward pass. Calculate the loss, and keep each intermediate result.
  2. Do the backward pass. Get $\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial\theta$ for each parameter.
  3. Update each parameter: $\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta\,\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial\theta$.
  4. Do steps 1 to 3 again, until the loss stops decreasing.

The loss is a mean over the examples. Thus, by the sum rule, its gradient is also a mean over the examples. A random batch of examples gives an estimate of that mean, at a much lower cost. Gradient descent with a random batch at each step is stochastic gradient descent (SGD). Chapter 02 uses it.

One full step by hand: XOR, every entry written out#

The derivation above uses letters. This section uses one real network and real numbers, and it does one complete step of training: forward, backward and update. It also makes one idea explicit, and the rest of the book depends on it. You do not need a picture of nodes and arrows to understand a network. A network is a short list of matrices. The backward pass is a second list of matrices, with the same shapes. Each entry of each matrix is one short formula that you can write down and calculate by hand.

Key concept — a network is matrices, and so is its gradient

The forward pass makes five matrices from the input. The backward pass makes six more. Each one has a fixed shape, and each entry has a formula:

FORWARD BACKWARD Z1 = X W1 + b1 (4,2) δ2 = dL/dZ2 (4,1) A1 = sigma(Z1) (4,2) dL/dW2 (2,1) same shape as W2 Z2 = A1 W2 + b2 (4,1) dL/db2 (1,) same shape as b2 A2 = sigma(Z2) (4,1) δ1 = dL/dZ1 (4,2) L = mean BCE scalar dL/dW1 (2,2) same shape as W1 dL/db1 (2,) same shape as b1

A diagram of circles and lines shows the same thing, but it hides the shapes and the formulas. The network diagram in Chapter 00 shows how to read one: each line is one entry of a $W$, and each circle (a "unit" or "neuron") is one column of an activation matrix such as $A_1$. Think in matrices, and backpropagation becomes a list of entries to fill in.

The network and its numbers#

The four XOR examples are the rows of $X$. The targets are the rows of $Y$. The network has two inputs, two hidden units and one output. It is the network in the Chapter 00 diagram. Two hidden units is the smallest number that can solve XOR, and it keeps each matrix small enough to print. (The network in the rest of this chapter has four.) The activation is the sigmoid at both layers, and the loss is binary cross-entropy.

X (4,2) Y (4,1) [ 0 0 ] [ 0 ] example 1 [ 0 1 ] [ 1 ] example 2 [ 1 0 ] [ 1 ] example 3 [ 1 1 ] [ 0 ] example 4 W1 (2,2) b1 (2,) W2 (2,1) b2 (1,) [ 2 2 ] [ -1 -3 ] [ 2 ] [ -1 ] [ 2 2 ] [ -2 ]

These weights are partly trained. Hidden unit 1 has bias $-1$, so it turns on when at least one input is on: it is approximately OR. Hidden unit 2 has bias $-3$, so it turns on only when both inputs are on: it is approximately AND. The output calculates "OR and not AND", which is XOR. But the weights are still too small to make clear decisions.

In this section, indices start at 1, as in mathematics. In code, they start at 0. Thus $W_1[i,j]$ is the weight from input $i$ to hidden unit $j$, and $Z_1[n,j]$ is the pre-activation of hidden unit $j$ for example $n$.

Step 1 — the forward pass, entry by entry#

$Z_1 = XW_1 + b_1$. Each entry is a dot product plus a bias. Here is the formula for each entry, and then the numbers:

Z1[n,j] = X[n,1] W1[1,j] + X[n,2] W1[2,j] + b1[j] j = 1 (OR unit) j = 2 (AND unit) n = 1 0(2) + 0(2) - 1 = -1 0(2) + 0(2) - 3 = -3 n = 2 0(2) + 1(2) - 1 = 1 0(2) + 1(2) - 3 = -1 n = 3 1(2) + 0(2) - 1 = 1 1(2) + 0(2) - 3 = -1 n = 4 1(2) + 1(2) - 1 = 3 1(2) + 1(2) - 3 = 1

$A_1 = \sigma(Z_1)$. The sigmoid acts on each entry separately:

A1[n,j] = sigma(Z1[n,j]) [ sigma(-1) sigma(-3) ] [ 0.2689 0.0474 ] A1 = [ sigma( 1) sigma(-1) ] = [ 0.7311 0.2689 ] [ sigma( 1) sigma(-1) ] [ 0.7311 0.2689 ] [ sigma( 3) sigma( 1) ] [ 0.9526 0.7311 ]

$Z_2 = A_1W_2 + b_2$ and $A_2 = \sigma(Z_2)$. There is one output, so each row gives one number:

Z2[n] = A1[n,1] W2[1] + A1[n,2] W2[2] + b2 n = 1 0.2689(2) + 0.0474(-2) - 1 = -0.5570 A2[1] = 0.3642 target 0 n = 2 0.7311(2) + 0.2689(-2) - 1 = -0.0758 A2[2] = 0.4811 target 1 n = 3 0.7311(2) + 0.2689(-2) - 1 = -0.0758 A2[3] = 0.4811 target 1 n = 4 0.9526(2) + 0.7311(-2) - 1 = -0.5570 A2[4] = 0.3642 target 0

The loss. Each example adds $-\ln \hat{y}$ if its target is 1, and $-\ln(1-\hat{y})$ if its target is 0. The loss is the mean of the four:

example 1: -ln(1 - 0.3642) = 0.4529 example 2: -ln(0.4811) = 0.7317 example 3: -ln(0.4811) = 0.7317 example 4: -ln(1 - 0.3642) = 0.4529 L = (0.4529 + 0.7317 + 0.7317 + 0.4529) / 4 = 0.5923

A random guess gives $\ln 2 = 0.693$. Thus the network has learned something. But examples 2 and 3 are on the wrong side of 0.5, so it still classifies two of the four examples incorrectly.

Step 2 — the backward pass, entry by entry#

The method is the same for each matrix. Write the formula for one entry. Find which numbers that entry affects. Apply the chain rule to that one entry. Then look at the formula again, and recognize the matrix product that calculates all the entries at the same time.

$\delta_2 = \partial L/\partial Z_2$, shape (4, 1). $Z_2[n]$ affects only the loss term of example $n$, and that term has weight $1/4$ in the mean. From Start at the output, the sigmoid and the BCE cancel, and each entry is the error divided by the batch size:

δ2[n] = (A2[n] - Y[n]) / 4 δ2 = [ (0.36425 - 0)/4 ] [ 0.09106 ] too high: push example 1 down [ (0.48107 - 1)/4 ] = [ -0.12973 ] too low: push example 2 up [ (0.48107 - 1)/4 ] [ -0.12973 ] too low: push example 3 up [ (0.36425 - 0)/4 ] [ 0.09106 ] too high: push example 4 down

$\partial L/\partial W_2$, shape (2, 1). $W_2[j]$ occurs in all four rows of $Z_2$, one time for each example. In row $n$, it multiplies $A_1[n,j]$. Thus there are four paths from $W_2[j]$ to the loss, and the sum over paths adds them:

dL/dW2[j] = A1[1,j] δ2[1] + A1[2,j] δ2[2] + A1[3,j] δ2[3] + A1[4,j] δ2[4] dL/dW2[1] = 0.26894(0.09106) + 0.73106(-0.12973) + 0.73106(-0.12973) + 0.95257(0.09106) = 0.02449 - 0.09484 - 0.09484 + 0.08674 = -0.07845 dL/dW2[2] = 0.04743(0.09106) + 0.26894(-0.12973) + 0.26894(-0.12973) + 0.73106(0.09106) = 0.00432 - 0.03489 - 0.03489 + 0.06657 = 0.00111

Now look at the formula. Entry $j$ is column $j$ of $A_1$, dot product with $\delta_2$. Column $j$ of $A_1$ is row $j$ of $A_1^\top$. Thus all the entries together are one matrix product: $\partial L/\partial W_2 = A_1^\top \delta_2$. The matrix product does not add a new idea. It is the sum over the four examples, done for each entry at the same time.

Note the second entry, 0.00111. It is almost zero, but no individual term is small. Examples 2 and 3 want $W_2[2]$ to change in one direction, and examples 1 and 4 want the opposite. A gradient is a sum over the batch, and here the examples almost cancel.

$\partial L/\partial b_2$, shape (1,). $b_2$ is added to each row of $Z_2$ with a multiplier of 1. Thus its gradient is the sum of $\delta_2$:

dL/db2 = δ2[1] + δ2[2] + δ2[3] + δ2[4] = 0.09106 - 0.12973 - 0.12973 + 0.09106 = -0.07734

$\partial L/\partial A_1$, shape (4, 2). Now go one layer down. $A_1[n,j]$ occurs in only one place: row $n$ of $Z_2$, where $W_2[j]$ multiplies it. Thus each entry has one path and one product:

dL/dA1[n,j] = δ2[n] W2[j] [ δ2[1]W2[1] δ2[1]W2[2] ] [ 0.1821 -0.1821 ] dL/dA1 = [ δ2[2]W2[1] δ2[2]W2[2] ] = [ -0.2595 0.2595 ] [ δ2[3]W2[1] δ2[3]W2[2] ] [ -0.2595 0.2595 ] [ δ2[4]W2[1] δ2[4]W2[2] ] [ 0.1821 -0.1821 ]

Each row is $\delta_2[n]$ times the row vector $W_2^\top$. Thus the full matrix is $\delta_2W_2^\top$: a (4, 1) column times a (1, 2) row. The output weight decides how much error each hidden unit gets. Unit 2 has a negative output weight, so its error has the opposite sign.

$\delta_1 = \partial L/\partial Z_1$, shape (4, 2). $A_1[n,j] = \sigma(Z_1[n,j])$ depends only on the one entry $Z_1[n,j]$. Thus the chain rule multiplies each entry by one local derivative, $\sigma'(Z_1[n,j]) = A_1[n,j](1 - A_1[n,j])$. There is no sum here:

δ1[n,j] = dL/dA1[n,j] * A1[n,j] (1 - A1[n,j]) [ 0.1966 0.0452 ] sigma'(Z1) = [ 0.1966 0.1966 ] = A1 * (1 - A1), entry by entry [ 0.1966 0.1966 ] [ 0.0452 0.1966 ] [ 0.1821(0.1966) -0.1821(0.0452) ] [ 0.0358 -0.0082 ] δ1 = [ -0.2595(0.1966) 0.2595(0.1966) ] = [ -0.0510 0.0510 ] [ -0.2595(0.1966) 0.2595(0.1966) ] [ -0.0510 0.0510 ] [ 0.1821(0.0452) -0.1821(0.1966) ] [ 0.0082 -0.0358 ]

In matrix form, $\delta_1 = (\delta_2W_2^\top) \odot \sigma'(Z_1)$. The $\odot$ means entry by entry, because each hidden output depends on only one pre-activation. Note the two entries with 0.0452. There, $|Z_1| = 3$ and the sigmoid is starting to saturate. Thus those entries get approximately four times less gradient than the entries with $|Z_1| = 1$.

$\partial L/\partial W_1$, shape (2, 2). $W_1[i,j]$ occurs in column $j$ of $Z_1$, in all four rows. In row $n$, it multiplies $X[n,i]$. Thus there are four paths, and we add them, exactly as for $W_2$:

dL/dW1[i,j] = X[1,i] δ1[1,j] + X[2,i] δ1[2,j] + X[3,i] δ1[3,j] + X[4,i] δ1[4,j] X has many zeros, so many terms disappear: dL/dW1[1,1] = 0 + 0 + 1(-0.0510) + 1( 0.0082) = -0.0428 dL/dW1[1,2] = 0 + 0 + 1( 0.0510) + 1(-0.0358) = 0.0152 dL/dW1[2,1] = 0 + 1(-0.0510) + 0 + 1( 0.0082) = -0.0428 dL/dW1[2,2] = 0 + 1( 0.0510) + 0 + 1(-0.0358) = 0.0152 [ -0.0428 0.0152 ] dL/dW1 = [ -0.0428 0.0152 ] = X^T δ1

This is the same pattern as $\partial L/\partial W_2 = A_1^\top \delta_2$. The input to the layer, transposed, multiplies the error at the output of the layer. The only difference is the input: $X$ for layer 1, and $A_1$ for layer 2.

$\partial L/\partial b_1$, shape (2,). $b_1[j]$ is added to each row of column $j$ of $Z_1$. Thus its gradient is the sum of column $j$ of $\delta_1$:

dL/db1[1] = 0.0358 - 0.0510 - 0.0510 + 0.0082 = -0.0580 dL/db1[2] = -0.0082 + 0.0510 + 0.0510 - 0.0358 = 0.0580
All six gradients, as formulas and as matrix products
GradientShapeOne entryAll entries
$\delta_2$(4, 1)$(A_2[n] - Y[n])/4$$(A_2 - Y)/4$
$\partial L/\partial W_2$(2, 1)$\sum_n A_1[n,j]\,\delta_2[n]$$A_1^\top \delta_2$
$\partial L/\partial b_2$(1,)$\sum_n \delta_2[n]$column sum of $\delta_2$
$\delta_1$(4, 2)$\delta_2[n]\,W_2[j]\,A_1[n,j](1-A_1[n,j])$$(\delta_2W_2^\top)\odot A_1\odot(1-A_1)$
$\partial L/\partial W_1$(2, 2)$\sum_n X[n,i]\,\delta_1[n,j]$$X^\top \delta_1$
$\partial L/\partial b_1$(2,)$\sum_n \delta_1[n,j]$column sums of $\delta_1$

Read across each row. The "one entry" formula is what the chain rule gives. The "all entries" form is the same formula, written so that a library can calculate it in one call. When a matrix formula confuses you, change it back into the one-entry formula.

Step 3 — one update, and a check#

Take one gradient descent step with $\eta = 1$. Subtract each gradient matrix from its parameter matrix, entry by entry:

W1 <- [ 2 + 0.0428 2 - 0.0152 ] = [ 2.0428 1.9848 ] [ 2 + 0.0428 2 - 0.0152 ] [ 2.0428 1.9848 ] b1 <- [ -1 + 0.0580 -3 - 0.0580 ] = [ -0.9420 -3.0580 ] W2 <- [ 2 + 0.0785 -2 - 0.0011 ]^T = [ 2.0785 -2.0011 ]^T b2 <- -1 + 0.0773 = -0.9227 new predictions: A2 = [ 0.3943 0.5317 0.5317 0.4115 ] targets [ 0 1 1 0 ] new loss: L = 0.5737 was 0.5923

The loss decreased. Also, all four predictions are now on the correct side of 0.5. The step made the OR unit stronger and the AND unit more strict, and it moved the output threshold.

Two more observations:

  • The two rows of $W_1$ stay equal. The two inputs have the same role in XOR, so their gradients are always equal.
