Chapter 04 · notebook 04_rnn_pytorch

Recurrence and Its Limits#

When you average a review, you discard its word order completely. A recurrent network keeps the order. It reads one token at a time and carries a running summary forward. This idea is strictly more powerful than the baseline of Chapter 03. But it fails, and you must understand the reason in detail. The fix for that failure shapes all the chapters after it.

The recurrence#

An RNN processes a sequence one element at a time. It keeps a hidden state $h_t$, which must summarize everything up to position $t$:

$$h_t = \tanh\big(W_{xh}x_t + W_{hh}h_{t-1} + b_h\big) \qquad\qquad y_t = W_{hy}h_t + b_y$$

The important feature is that $W_{xh}$, $W_{hh}$ and $W_{hy}$ do not depend on $t$. The model uses one set of matrices at each step. Thus it can process sequences of any length. There is no parameter for each position, so the model cannot run out of them. A sequence two times as long costs two times the compute, not two times the weights.

Key concept The hidden state is a vector with a fixed size, for example 256 numbers. It must compress the full history. Suppose that the model needs something from token 1 at token 500. That information must stay alive through 499 rounds of multiplication, squashing and mixing with new input. That fixed-width bottleneck is the source of both the elegance of the RNN and its failure.
Example — what the bottleneck costs
"The keys that I left on the kitchen table this morning are ___" To choose "there" over "here", or to get subject-verb agreement right ("keys ... are", not "keys ... is"), the model needs "keys" at step 12. A 256-unit hidden state must therefore hold, simultaneously: - the subject and its number (plural) - the location already mentioned - the tense - the syntactic state (inside a relative clause) - everything else it might still need ...in 256 numbers, rewritten from scratch at every one of 12 steps.

Compare a transformer. When it needs "keys", it looks back at "keys" directly. The RNN must predict at step 2 that "keys" will be important later. Then it must protect "keys" through ten rounds of overwriting. That learning problem is much more difficult than it first seems.

Character-level language modeling#

The notebook trains on Alice's Adventures in Wonderland at the character level. At each position, the task is to predict the next character. This is a $K$-way classification, where $K$ is the size of the alphabet. It trains with cross-entropy, exactly as in Chapter 00.

We use characters, not words, to make the problem simpler on purpose. The vocabulary has 72 symbols, not tens of thousands. There is no tokenization to get wrong, and there are no unknown tokens. The cost is that the model must learn spelling before it can learn anything else. Thus the first samples are random letters. Then they are words that you can say but that do not exist. Then they are real words without grammar. That progression is the most useful part of the exercise.

Backpropagation through time#

To train, unroll the recurrence into a feed-forward graph: $T$ copies of the same cell, one after the other. This is not a metaphor. The dynamic graph of PyTorch (Chapter 02) really builds it as the loop runs. Then backpropagate through the full graph.

The weights are shared. Thus the gradients from all timesteps add into the same tensors:

$$\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W_{hh}} = \sum_{t=1}^{T} \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_t}{\partial W_{hh}}$$

This is the gradient accumulation of Chapter 02, used on purpose and not by accident. It also means that the memory cost of training increases with sequence length. The backward pass needs each intermediate activation at each timestep. For the optimizer, a sequence of 1,000 steps is a network of 1,000 layers.

Why gradients vanish#

Here is the failure. It comes from arithmetic, not from bad luck. To send a gradient from step $t$ back to step $k$, you must go through each cell between them. Each crossing multiplies by the same two factors:

$$\frac{\partial h_t}{\partial h_k} = \prod_{i=k+1}^{t} \frac{\partial h_i}{\partial h_{i-1}} = \prod_{i=k+1}^{t} W_{hh}^{\top} \operatorname{diag}\big(\tanh'(z_i)\big)$$

This is a product of $t - k$ terms that are almost the same. If the typical magnitude of that term is $\lambda$, the gradient changes as $\lambda^{t-k}$. That is exponential in the distance. Also, $\tanh' \le 1$ always, and it is equal to 1 only at zero. Thus, if $W_{hh}$ is not large enough to compensate, $\lambda < 1$.

Set the multiplier to 0.85, and look at 30 steps back. The gradient is $10^{-2}$ of its original size. At 40 steps, the right edge of the plot, it is approximately $10^{-3}$. The information from early tokens is not distorted or noisy. It is absent, and you cannot tell it from zero. More training does not fix this, because there is no signal to train on.

Push the multiplier above 1, and the opposite occurs. The product explodes. It gives gradients of $10^{6}$ and an immediate nan. Exploding gradients are the easier problem, because clipping solves them completely: 

torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), max_norm=1.0)

If the norm of the full gradient vector is more than the threshold, this scales the vector down. It keeps the direction and limits the magnitude. Put it after backward() and before step(). It is standard in each sequence model in this book. Chapter 09 and Chapter 10 both use it.

Asymmetry Clipping fixes explosion, but nothing like it fixes vanishing. You cannot multiply a gradient that is really zero back up to something useful. Vanishing gradients need a fix in the architecture. Chapter 05 gives that fix.

Generating text, and the sampling question#

After training, generation is a loop. Give the model a seed character, and get a distribution over the next character. Select one character, and give it back to the model. All the interesting behavior is in the selection.

The obvious approach is to always take the argmax. It gives the worst output. It is deterministic, so the same seed always gives the same text. Also, it goes into loops almost immediately: "the the the the" is a reasonable greedy continuation. The other extreme is to sample from the full distribution. That gives some nonsense. A distribution over 60 characters has a long tail, and together the tail holds real probability.

The control between the two extremes is temperature. Apply it to the logits before the softmax:

$$p_k = \frac{\exp(z_k / T)}{\sum_j \exp(z_j / T)}$$
  • $T < 1$ makes the distribution sharper, toward the argmax. The output is conservative, repetitive and safe.
  • $T > 1$ makes it flatter. The output is creative and has more errors.
  • $T = 1$ samples from the real beliefs of the model.

Temperature never changes the ranking of the candidates. It changes only how much the top candidates control the result. In practice, 0.7 to 0.9 is the useful range for character models. Chapter 10 adds top-k and nucleus sampling, which cut off the tail and do not reweight it.

By hand — exercise 04.1

Unroll a very small RNN for three steps. Everything is one-dimensional, so all the matrices are scalars.

h₀ = 0.0 W_xh = 1.0 W_hh = 0.5 b = 0.0 inputs: x₁ = 1.0, x₂ = 0.0, x₃ = −1.0 tanh(1.000) = 0.762 tanh(0.381) = 0.364 tanh(−0.818) = −0.674 tanh(0.5) = 0.462
  1. Calculate $h_1$, $h_2$ and $h_3$.
  2. At step 2, the input is zero. Explain what $h_2$ represents, and where its value came from.
  3. Calculate $\partial h_3 / \partial h_2$, then $\partial h_3/\partial h_1$. Use $\tanh'(z) = 1 - \tanh^2(z)$.
  4. If this pattern continued, by what factor would the gradient decrease at each step? After how many steps would it be less than $10^{-3}$?
Worked solution

1. Each step is $h_t = \tanh(1.0 \cdot x_t + 0.5\,h_{t-1})$:

z₁ = 1.0(1.0) + 0.5(0.0) = 1.000 → h₁ = 0.762 z₂ = 1.0(0.0) + 0.5(0.762) = 0.381 → h₂ = 0.364 z₃ = 1.0(−1.0) + 0.5(0.364) = −0.818 → h₃ = −0.674

2. With $x_2 = 0$, the only contribution is $0.5 h_1$. Thus $h_2$ is only memory: a weaker echo of step 1 and nothing more. Note that it already decreased from 0.762 to 0.364 after one step that carried nothing. That decrease is the vanishing problem in the forward pass. The state forgets by itself, before any gradient is involved.

3. $\partial h_t/\partial h_{t-1} = \tanh'(z_t) \cdot W_{hh} = (1 - h_t^2)(0.5)$:

∂h₃/∂h₂ = (1 − 0.674²)(0.5) = (1 − 0.4543)(0.5) = 0.273 ∂h₂/∂h₁ = (1 − 0.364²)(0.5) = (1 − 0.1325)(0.5) = 0.434 ∂h₃/∂h₁ = 0.273 × 0.434 = 0.118

After only two steps back, 88% of the gradient is gone.

4. The factor for each step is at most $W_{hh} \cdot \max \tanh' = 0.5 \times 1 = 0.5$, and usually less. At 0.5 for each step, the gradient gets to $10^{-3}$ in $\log(10^{-3})/\log(0.5) \approx \mathbf{10}$ steps. That is ten characters, which is less than two words. A model like this cannot learn that a quotation mark from forty characters ago needs a closing mark. Real text has many dependencies of exactly that type.

By hand — exercise 04.2

Calculate the effect of temperature. Do not use the slider.

logits over 4 characters: z = [2.0, 1.0, 0.0, −1.0] e^0=1.000 e^1=2.718 e^2=7.389 e^4=54.60 e^6=403.4 e^0.5=1.649 e^{−0.5}=0.607 e^{−1}=0.368 e^{−2}=0.135
  1. Calculate the distribution at $T = 1$.
  2. Calculate it at $T = 0.5$. (Divide the logits by 0.5, which doubles them.)
  3. Calculate it at $T = 2$.
  4. What happens in the limits $T \to 0$ and $T \to \infty$? For each limit, give one concrete failure in text generation.
Worked solution

1. $T=1$: $\sum = 7.389 + 2.718 + 1.000 + 0.368 = 11.475$.

p = [0.644, 0.237, 0.087, 0.032]

2. $T=0.5$: The logits become $[4, 2, 0, -2]$. Thus $\sum = 54.60 + 7.389 + 1.000 + 0.135 = 63.12$.

p = [0.865, 0.117, 0.016, 0.002]

The top character went from 64% to 87%. The last character almost disappeared.

3. $T=2$: The logits become $[1, 0.5, 0, -0.5]$. Thus $\sum = 2.718 + 1.649 + 1.000 + 0.607 = 5.974$.

p = [0.455, 0.276, 0.167, 0.102]

This is much flatter. The least likely character now has a one-in-ten chance at each step.

4. As $T \to 0$, the distribution becomes one-hot on the argmax. Generation is deterministic, and it goes into repetition loops. When the model comes back to a state that it visited before, it must give the same continuation forever. As $T \to \infty$, the distribution becomes uniform. The output is random characters, and it ignores everything that the model learned. The two extremes destroy the usefulness of the model in opposite directions. That is why the interesting values are all in a narrow range near 0.7–1.0.

Feel for the numbersMust do

The full problem of a recurrent network is one number raised to a power. Learn that arithmetic well. Then the vanishing gradient is no longer a slogan. It is something that you can estimate in your head.

QuantityFloorTypicalCeilingRead it as
Per-step gradient factor $\lambda$00.5–0.99$>1$ explodesthe product over $T$ steps is what reaches the start
$\lambda = 0.9$, 50 steps—0.0052—half a percent survives
$\lambda = 0.5$, 20 steps—$9.5\times10^{-7}$—gone well inside one sentence
$\lambda = 1.1$, 50 steps—117—the other failure, and the reason for clipping
Gradient-clip norm0.11.05clips the explosion; does nothing for the vanishing
$\tanh'$01 at $z=0$1the factor is $\lambda = \|W_{hh}\| \cdot \tanh'$

Now do these on paper. Where you can, do them in your head. You can use a calculator for the logarithms. The goal is to know which number to use.

  1. At $\lambda = 0.9$, after how many steps is only 1% of the gradient left?
  2. Answer the same question at $\lambda = 0.99$. What does the comparison tell you about how sharp the cliff is?
  3. Your gradient norm prints $10^{4}$. Is the fix clipping, a lower learning rate, or both? Which one addresses the cause?
Answers

1. $\ln(0.01)/\ln(0.9) = 43.7$, so approximately 44 steps. That is approximately one long sentence.

2. $\ln(0.01)/\ln(0.99) = 458$ steps. A change of 0.09 in $\lambda$ gives ten times the range. The dependence on $T$ is exponential, but the usable range of $\lambda$ is narrow. Thus you cannot tune this away. You would need $\lambda$ to stay near 1 for hundreds of steps, and nothing in a vanilla RNN keeps it there.

3. Clipping prevents the step from destroying the weights. Thus it treats the symptom, and it treats it well. A lower learning rate makes each step smaller, also the steps that were correct. Neither one addresses the cause. The cause is in the architecture, and Chapter 05 changes it.

The habit. When something repeats $T$ times, ask what one repetition multiplies by. Then raise it to the power $T$. This answers almost each stability question in this book.

Say it backRecommended

Explain this to your favorite LLM, in your own words: why does a recurrent network forget, and why is it not something you can fix by tuning? Then ask it to correct you. Ask it to question each part where you were vague, not only the parts where you were wrong, because the gaps are in the vague parts.

What a good answer covers — open this afterwards, not before
  1. The network applies the same weight matrix at each timestep. Thus the backward pass multiplies by a similar Jacobian one time for each step. The Jacobian is the grid of all the partial derivatives of the outputs of a step with respect to its inputs. A multiplication by it moves a gradient back through one step.
  2. A product of $T$ similar factors is exponential in $T$. It vanishes if the factor is less than 1, and it explodes if the factor is more than 1.
  3. No value of the learning rate changes a factor of $\lambda^{T}$. The learning rate scales the step. It does not change the signal that gets to the step.
  4. Clipping fixes only the exploding half. You can limit a gradient that is too large, but you cannot recover a gradient that is already zero.
  5. Thus the fix must be in the architecture: a path from step to step that the network adds to, not multiplies through.

Most common miss. An answer treats vanishing and exploding as one symptom. They have the same cause and completely different fixes. If an explanation gives clipping as the answer to forgetting, it has missed the asymmetry.

Sample at intervals during training, not only at the end. The progression from noise to spelling to grammar is the clearest picture of learning in the full course.
Where this goes next The vanishing gradient is not a tuning problem. Thus Chapter 05 changes the architecture. It gives the cell a memory that the network adds to, not multiplies through. It also puts learned gates in control of what goes into and out of that memory.

Chapter 05 · notebook 05_lstm_pytorch

LSTMs: Gated Memory#

The vanishing gradient of Chapter 04 came from repeated multiplication by the same matrix. The LSTM solves this with a second state. The network mostly adds to this state and does not transform it. Thus gradients can move along it without becoming smaller. The network also learns when to write to it, when to forget, and when to read.

Two states, not one#

An LSTM cell carries a hidden state $h_t$ and a cell state $c_t$. The cell state is the long-term memory. The hidden state is the working output that goes to the next layer and the next timestep. Three gates control the flow between them. Each gate is a small linear layer and a sigmoid. It gives a vector of numbers in $(0,1)$. This is a soft, differentiable switch, with one value for each memory slot.

$$f_t = \sigma\big(W_f[h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_f\big) \qquad \text{forget: what to keep}$$ $$i_t = \sigma\big(W_i[h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_i\big) \qquad \text{input: what to write}$$ $$o_t = \sigma\big(W_o[h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_o\big) \qquad \text{output: what to expose}$$ $$\tilde{c}_t = \tanh\big(W_c[h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_c\big) \qquad \text{candidate content}$$

Then come the two important lines:

$$\boxed{\;c_t = f_t \odot c_{t-1} + i_t \odot \tilde{c}_t\;} \qquad\qquad h_t = o_t \odot \tanh(c_t)$$

Read the boxed equation carefully. Its shape is the full reason for the architecture. The forget gate scales the old cell state, and the new content is added. No weight matrix multiplies $c_{t-1}$. The path from $c_{t-1}$ to $c_t$ goes through one elementwise multiplication and nothing more.

Key concept In a plain RNN, the backward path is $\prod W_{hh}^\top \operatorname{diag}(\tanh')$. That is a product of matrices, and each one makes the signal smaller. In an LSTM, the matching path along the cell state is $\prod f_t$. That is a product of numbers that the network selects. If a memory slot is important, the network can learn $f_t \approx 1$ for it. Then the gradient goes through that slot almost unchanged for hundreds of steps. Vanishing does not become impossible. It becomes optional, and the network controls it.

This is the same widget as in the last chapter, but read it differently. There, $W_{hh}$ and $\tanh'$ set the multiplier. Here, the multiplier is $f_t$, which the network learns. Set it to 1.0, and the gradient stays flat forever. The forget gate can select that regime.

Why the forget-gate bias starts at 1 A common and useful initialization trick is to set $b_f$ to 1, not 0. Then $\sigma(b_f) \approx 0.73$ at step zero. The cell then remembers by default, and it must learn to forget. A start near zero gives the opposite default. Memory decays before the network has learned that anything is worth keeping, and early training becomes much slower. PyTorch does not do this for you.

Reading the gates as behavior#

Gates are vectors. Thus different slots can do different things at the same time. This is one cell, but it is not one memory.

$f$$i$Effect on that slotA use for it
≈1≈0hold the old value, ignore inputremember an open quote across a sentence
≈0≈1discard and overwritereset at a sentence boundary
≈1≈1accumulaterunning count or intensity
≈0≈0clear to zeroend of a phrase, nothing to carry

The output gate is separate for a reason. The cell can hold information that it does not show at that time. Consider a slot that records "we are inside a parenthesis". That slot is important for the closing bracket later. But it is not important for the prediction of the next normal word. $o_t$ lets the cell keep that information but not show it.

The GRU, briefly#

The Gated Recurrent Unit combines the forget gate and the input gate into one update gate ($i_t = 1 - f_t$, so a write is also a forget). It has no separate cell state. It has approximately 25% fewer parameters, and on most tasks its accuracy is similar. If you have an LSTM that works, try a GRU. It usually gives free speed, and the same intuition applies.

Using nn.LSTM#

self.lstm = nn.LSTM(input_size, hidden_size, num_layers=2,
                    batch_first=True, dropout=0.2)

out, (h_n, c_n) = self.lstm(x)   # x: (B, L, input_size)
#   out : (B, L, hidden_size)    -- h_t at every timestep
#   h_n : (num_layers, B, hidden_size)  -- final h per layer
#   c_n : (num_layers, B, hidden_size)  -- final c per layer

Three details cause most of the confusion:

batch_first=True is not the default. The native layout of PyTorch is (L, B, H), with the sequence first. All other code in this book puts the batch first. Thus set it explicitly, and set it consistently. If you mix the conventions, the model runs and trains, but it silently transposes your batch and your sequence.

out or h_n. Use out when you need a prediction at each timestep (language modeling). Use h_n[-1] when you need one summary of the full sequence (classification, or the regression in this notebook). Note that out[:, -1, :] is equal to h_n[-1] for a unidirectional LSTM. It is the same tensor, reached in two ways.

The dropout argument applies only between layers. It has no effect when num_layers=1, and PyTorch warns you about exactly that. It also never applies to the output of the final layer. If you want dropout there, add your own nn.Dropout after the LSTM.

On Apple MPS, nn.LSTM dropout is broken In PyTorch 2.12 on the MPS backend, the dropout argument of nn.LSTM does not work. It is not applied as random dropout, and a stacked LSTM with dropout>0 fails to train. On the sine task of this chapter, the test MSE stays near 0.4, against approximately 0.0002 on the CPU. nn.RNN and nn.GRU are not affected. On a Mac, train a stacked LSTM with dropout on the CPU, or set dropout=0. The notebook does the first.

Bidirectionality#

bidirectional=True runs a second LSTM backward over the sequence and concatenates the outputs. This doubles the output width. It helps a lot for classification, where the full sequence is available. It is impossible for generation, because you cannot read backward from text that does not exist yet. That difference, full context against causal context, comes back in Chapter 09. There it is the main architectural split between the encoder and the decoder.

The task: sine wave prediction#

The notebook changes from text to a regression problem. Given 50 samples of a sine wave, predict the 51st. The target is a continuous number. Thus, by the reasoning of Chapter 00, the loss is MSE, which is the Gaussian negative log-likelihood.

This looks like a toy, but it is a good choice. Here are four reasons:

  • A sine wave has a real long-range dependency: the phase, which continues across the full window.
  • The correct answer is exactly known, so you can see exactly how wrong the model is.
  • It needs no corpus.
  • It shows a failure that text hides. If you run the model autoregressively on its own predictions, small errors grow. After a few dozen steps, the wave moves out of phase. This is the same exposure-bias problem that teacher forcing causes in translation.
By hand — exercise 05.1

Do one step of an LSTM cell. It is one-dimensional, so each gate is a single number.

c₀ = 0.8 h₀ = 0.5 x₁ = 1.0 pre-activations already computed for you: forget gate z_f = 2.0 input gate z_i = −1.0 output gate z_o = 0.0 candidate z_c = 1.0 σ(2.0) = 0.881 σ(−1.0) = 0.269 σ(0.0) = 0.500 tanh(1.0) = 0.762 tanh(0.909) = 0.721
  1. Calculate $f_1$, $i_1$, $o_1$ and $\tilde{c}_1$.
  2. Calculate $c_1$. How much of it came from memory, and how much from the new input?
  3. Calculate $h_1$.
  4. Calculate $\partial c_1 / \partial c_0$. Compare it with the plain-RNN factor of approximately 0.25–0.5 from exercise 04.1.
  5. Suppose that this same $f$ stays for 20 steps. What fraction of $c_0$ stays? What if the network had learned $f = 0.99$?
Worked solution

1. $f_1 = \sigma(2.0) = 0.881$, $i_1 = \sigma(-1.0) = 0.269$, $o_1 = \sigma(0) = 0.500$ and $\tilde{c}_1 = \tanh(1.0) = 0.762$.

2.

c₁ = f₁ c₀ + i₁ c̃₁ = 0.881(0.8) + 0.269(0.762) = 0.705 + 0.205 = 0.909

Memory gives 0.705, and the new input gives 0.205. The gates kept 88% of the old value and let in only 27% of the candidate. That is a cell in "hold" mode.

3. $h_1 = o_1 \tanh(c_1) = 0.5 \times \tanh(0.909) = 0.5 \times 0.721 = \mathbf{0.361}$. Note that $h_1$ (0.361) is much smaller than $c_1$ (0.909). The cell holds more than it shows. That is exactly the job of the output gate.

4. Differentiate $c_1 = f_1c_0 + i_1\tilde{c}_1$ with respect to $c_0$. Treat the gates as fixed:

∂c₁/∂c₀ = f₁ = 0.881

There is no weight matrix and no $\tanh'$. There is only the forget gate. Compare the RNN value of 0.273 from exercise 04.1. The LSTM keeps 3.2 times more gradient at each step. Also, unlike the RNN factor, the network can change it.

5. Over 20 steps at $f = 0.881$: $0.881^{20} = 0.079$. Thus approximately 8% stays. This is decay, but it is slow enough to learn through. At $f = 0.99$: $0.99^{20} = \mathbf{0.818}$. Even at 200 steps, $0.99^{200} = 0.134$. The network can really select to remember something for hundreds of timesteps. Compare the RNN, where $0.5^{20} = 10^{-6}$, and that choice did not exist.

By hand — exercise 05.2

Count the parameters, and find one result of the count.

  1. An LSTM cell calculates four pre-activations. Each one comes from the concatenation $[h_{t-1}, x_t]$. For input size $n$ and hidden size $m$, how many parameters is that in total (weights and biases)?
  2. Calculate it for $n = 1$ and $m = 64$, as in the notebook.
  3. How many parameters does a plain RNN with the same sizes have? What is the ratio, and where does it come from?
  4. The LSTM has 4 times the parameters for each unit. Give one argument why a comparison of an LSTM and an RNN at equal hidden size is not fair. What would you do instead?
Worked solution

1. Each of the four gates has a weight matrix over the concatenated input of width $n + m$. It gives $m$ outputs, and it has $m$ biases:

$$4\big[m(n + m) + m\big] = 4m(n + m + 1)$$

2. $4 \times 64 \times (1 + 64 + 1) = 256 \times 66 = \mathbf{16{,}896}$. (PyTorch reports 17,152. nn.LSTM stores two bias vectors, b_ih and b_hh, so its count is $4m(n + m + 2)$. The second bias is redundant, because the two biases always add.)

3. A plain RNN has one of these blocks, not four: $64 \times 66 = 4{,}224$ (PyTorch: 4,288, for the same reason). The ratio is exactly 4×. It comes from the three gates: the single transformation of the RNN, plus $f$, $i$ and $o$.

4. At equal hidden size, the LSTM has four times the capacity. Thus, if it beats the RNN, that proves little. Some of the gain can come from parameters, not from gating. A fair comparison keeps the parameter count fixed. This means that you give the RNN approximately two times the hidden units ($m_{\text{RNN}} \approx 2m_{\text{LSTM}}$, because parameters increase as $m^2$). The LSTM usually still wins on long sequences, but by less. The gap that stays is the part that really comes from gated memory, not from size. Apply this generally: almost each architecture comparison in the literature is confounded by parameter count, unless it explicitly says otherwise.

Feel for the numbersMust do

The LSTM replaces the fixed $\lambda$ of Chapter 04 with $f_t$, a number that the network selects for each slot at each step. The exponential arithmetic is the same. But now you can ask what value the gate needs to hold a memory for a given span, and check that the gate can get to it.

QuantityFloorTypicalCeilingRead it as
Gate output00.5 at init1a soft switch, one value per memory slot
$\sigma(b_f = 1)$—0.731—the "remember by default" initialization
$\prod f_t$, $f = 0.99$, 100 steps—0.366—a third survives — usable
$\prod f_t$, $f = 0.95$, 100 steps—0.0059—already most of the way gone
$\prod f_t$, $f = 1$—11perfect retention — the regime the gate can select
Cell-state path—one multiply, one add—no weight matrix anywhere on it

Now do these on paper. Where you can, do them in your head. You can use a calculator for the logarithms. The goal is to know which number to use.

  1. To keep half of a memory over 200 steps, what must $f$ be?
  2. At $f = 0.95$, what is the half-life of a memory in steps?
  3. Compare 50 steps of retention with the forget bias at 0 ($f \approx 0.5$) and with a bias of 1 ($f \approx 0.731$). Why is that one line of initialization so important?
Answers

1. $f = 0.5^{1/200} = 0.99654$. Note how close to 1 it must be. Also note that a sigmoid gets to 0.9965 only at a pre-activation of approximately 5.7. Long memory needs the gate to be driven hard. That is a real thing to learn, not a default.

2. $\ln(0.5)/\ln(0.95) = 13.5$ steps. A gate that looks almost fully open loses half its signal within fourteen words.

3. $0.5^{50} = 8.9\times10^{-16}$ against $0.731^{50} = 1.6\times10^{-7}$. That is nine orders of magnitude from one added constant. The network can learn its way out of either one. But only one of them leaves a gradient large enough to learn with.

The habit. When an architecture gives the network control of a quantity, find the value that it needs for the behavior that you want. Then ask if that value is easy to get to. Often the answer explains an initialization trick.

Say it backRecommended

Explain this to your favorite LLM, in your own words: what does the cell state do that a hidden state cannot, and why does that solve Chapter 04's problem? Then ask it to correct you. Ask it to question each part where you were vague, not only the parts where you were wrong, because the gaps are in the vague parts.

What a good answer covers — open this afterwards, not before
  1. The cell state changes by scaling and addition. A weight matrix never multiplies it.
  2. Thus the backward path along it multiplies only by $f_t$, not by a Jacobian at each step.
  3. The network learns $f_t$ for each slot. Thus it can hold a value near 1 for the important slots and forget in the other slots, at the same time.
  4. Vanishing therefore becomes optional and controllable. It is no longer structural. The network can select not to vanish.
  5. The output gate is separate, so the cell can keep something that it does not show at that time. A single hidden state cannot do that.

Most common miss. An answer lists the three gates and their names. The mechanism is the shape of the cell-state update, not the number of gates. If you can name all three but cannot say why addition is more important than gating, you have the words but not the idea.

Read this next, elsewhere

Christopher Olah's Understanding LSTMs (2015) is the best-known explanation of this cell, and it deserves its reputation. It builds the equations one gate at a time, with a separate diagram for each. It is the source of the conveyor belt picture of the cell state: a line along which memory moves, with only small, controlled changes. That picture is a good way to remember the boxed equation in this chapter. The credit for that idea is his.

Read it as an addition to this chapter, not as a repeat. It goes further than this chapter on the variants: peepholes, coupled gates and the derivation of the GRU. It stops before the backward pass. Chapter 07 starts there. The post has no license statement. Thus this book does not copy its diagrams. We drew the figure above for this book.

Where this goes next LSTMs solved the gradient problem, but they kept the sequential bottleneck. The model cannot calculate step $t$ until step $t-1$ is done. Thus training cannot run in parallel across time, and all the information must still go through one fixed-width state. Chapter 06 removes recurrence completely. It lets each position look directly at each other position.

Chapter 06 · notebook 06_self_attention

Self-Attention from Scratch#

Recurrence forces information through a fixed-width state, one step at a time. Attention removes both limits at the same time. Each position reads directly from each other position, in one parallel operation. The mechanism is four lines of algebra, and this chapter derives all four.

The problem with summarizing#

Look at this sentence: "The animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired." To resolve it, the model must link back six words. An LSTM must encode "animal" into its cell state and keep it through six updates. During those updates, it competes with all the other information that the LSTM must remember. It can work, but it is indirect.

Attention makes the link directly. When the model processes it, it calculates a relevance score against each other position. Then it builds a representation weighted by those scores. The path from it to animal is one step long. The six words between them do not change that, and six hundred words would not change it.

Key concept In an RNN, the path length between two positions is the distance between them. Thus gradients decay with distance. In self-attention, each path length is 1. That one property is the reason that transformers replaced recurrent models. Remember it when the notation below becomes dense.
Example — the same dependency, two architectures
"The animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired." ^^^^^^ ^^ position 1 position 7 RNN : information travels 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 → 6 → 7 the gradient is multiplied by ~6 Jacobians on the way back (one matrix of partial derivatives per step — chapter 00). At a typical factor of 0.5 per step: 0.5⁶ ≈ 0.016 — 98% of the signal is gone before it arrives. Attention : position 7 computes q₇ · k₁ directly. One dot product. One step. No attenuation. The distance between them appears nowhere in the computation.

Now make the sentence longer, with 60 words between "animal" and "it". The RNN factor becomes $0.5^{60} \approx 10^{-18}$, which you cannot tell from zero. The attention calculation is exactly the same. Only the size of the score matrix changes. That is the full trade: attention pays $O(L^2)$ compute to get a path length of $O(1)$.

Queries, keys, and values#

Think of attention as a soft dictionary lookup. Each position makes three vectors from its embedding, with three learned linear projections:

VectorProduced byRole
Query $q_i$$x_iW^Q$what position $i$ is looking for
Key $k_j$$x_jW^K$what position $j$ offers as a label
Value $v_j$$x_jW^V$what position $j$ actually contributes

A hard dictionary finds one key that matches exactly, and returns its value. Attention compares the query with all the keys. It changes the similarities into weights, and it returns the weighted average of all the values. It is soft and differentiable. Most important, the model learns what to look for and what to advertise, because $W^Q$, $W^K$ and $W^V$ are parameters.

The separation of keys from values is more important than it first seems. The features that let other positions find a position are not necessarily the features worth retrieving. A token can advertise "I am a noun, singular, animate" in its key, and carry completely different content in its value.

Scaled dot-product attention#

$$\operatorname{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \operatorname{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V$$

There are four steps, and each one has a job.

$QK^\top$: score each pair. $Q$ has shape (L, d_k) and $K^\top$ has shape (d_k, L). Thus the result is (L, L). Entry $(i,j)$ is $q_i \cdot k_j$, the raw affinity of position $i$ for position $j$. This matrix is quadratic in sequence length. That is the one real cost of attention: two times the context needs four times the compute and memory.

Divide by $\sqrt{d_k}$: keep the softmax in its useful range. See below. People skip this step, and then they regret it.

Softmax over the last dimension. Each row becomes a probability distribution. The attention of position $i$ is a normalized allocation over all positions. Each row sums to 1. The columns do not sum to 1, and they do not need to.

Multiply by $V$. (L, L) @ (L, d_v) gives (L, d_v). Each output row is the weighted average of all the value vectors. The weights are the attention of that position.

Why the square-root scaling#

This is the one part of the formula that looks arbitrary but is not. Suppose that the components of $q$ and $k$ are independent, with mean 0 and variance 1. Their dot product is a sum of $d_k$ of these products. Thus:

$$\operatorname{Var}(q \cdot k) = \sum_{i=1}^{d_k}\operatorname{Var}(q_ik_i) = d_k$$

The standard deviation is $\sqrt{d_k}$. At $d_k = 64$, that is 8, so scores are frequently in the range $\pm 20$. A softmax of scores with that spread is one-hot in practice. When the softmax saturates, its gradient is approximately zero, and the attention weights stop learning. (See Chapter 00 again: the softmax Jacobian contains $\hat{y}(1-\hat{y})$, which goes to zero at both ends.) Division by $\sqrt{d_k}$ gives unit variance again, and it keeps the distribution soft.

In the widget above, clear √dₖ scaling and move $d_k$ up to 128. The heatmap becomes a hard, almost diagonal pattern. That is a layer that has stopped learning, shown as a picture.

Multi-head attention#

One attention operation gives one distribution for each position. Thus it can express only one type of relation. But it in our sentence needs two links: a syntactic link (it is the subject of was) and a semantic link (it refers to animal). One softmax must select one of them.

Multi-head attention runs $h$ attention operations in parallel on projections with fewer dimensions. Then it concatenates the results:

$$\operatorname{head}_i = \operatorname{Attention}(XW_i^Q, XW_i^K, XW_i^V)$$ $$\operatorname{MultiHead}(X) = \big[\operatorname{head}_1; \dots; \operatorname{head}_h\big]W^O$$

With $d_k = d_{\text{model}}/h$, the total compute is almost the same. You divide the same budget into independent subspaces; you do not add to it. Each head can specialize, and in trained models they clearly do. Some heads follow syntactic dependencies. Some attend to the previous token. Some attend to rare words. Many attend to nothing in particular, and you can prune them.

The implementation, and the reshape that trips everyone#

def split_heads(self, x):          # (B, L, d_model)
    B, L, _ = x.shape
    return x.view(B, L, self.n_heads, self.d_k).transpose(1, 2)
    #                                                    (B, n_heads, L, d_k)

In practice, you do not run $h$ separate layers. One nn.Linear(d_model, d_model) calculates all the heads at the same time, and a reshape splits the result. The view divides the feature axis into (n_heads, d_k). The transpose moves the heads next to the batch dimension. Then the matrix multiplications that follow treat (B, n_heads) as the batch, and operate independently on each head.

On the way back, you must reverse both operations. The .contiguous() is not optional: 

out = out.transpose(1, 2).contiguous().view(B, L, d_model)

transpose returns a view with changed strides. It does not reorder the memory. view needs contiguous memory. Without .contiguous(), PyTorch gives an error, which is the good result. The bad result comes from reshape. It copies the data without a warning and succeeds. Thus, if your axes were wrong, it hides the error.

Masking#

Two situations need you to block specific attention weights. First, padding positions carry no information. Second, in a decoder, the model must not see future positions. Both use the same method. Add $-\infty$ to the scores before the softmax: 

scores = scores.masked_fill(mask, float('-inf'))
weights = F.softmax(scores, dim=-1)

Because $e^{-\infty} = 0$, those entries get exactly zero weight. The other weights still sum to 1, because the softmax denominator also excludes the masked entries. If you mask after the softmax, the rows are not normalized. That bug makes results worse without a crash, and it is difficult to see.

Select causal mask in the widget, and the upper triangle becomes dark. That is the decoder of Chapter 09 and all of Chapter 10.

The all-masked row Suppose that a full row is masked, for example in a sequence that is all padding. Then each score is $-\infty$, the softmax denominator is zero, and the output is nan. On the next backward pass, the nan goes into each parameter, and the model is destroyed. Prevent empty sequences in your data pipeline. This bug is known for weeks of training before anyone sees it.
By hand — exercise 06.1

Do a complete attention calculation over three tokens with $d_k = 2$. The numbers give easy exponentials.

Q = [[1, 0], K = [[1, 0], V = [[1, 0], [0, 1], [0, 1], [0, 1], [1, 1]] [1, 1]] [1, 1]] e^0 = 1.000 e^{0.707} = 2.028 e^{1.414} = 4.113
  1. Calculate the raw score matrix $QK^\top$: all nine entries.
  2. Scale by $1/\sqrt{d_k} = 1/\sqrt{2} \approx 0.707$.
  3. Apply softmax to row 1 only (the query $[1,0]$).
  4. Calculate the output for position 1: the weighted sum of the value vectors.
  5. Now do step 3 again with a causal mask, so that position 1 can attend only to itself. What is the output, and why is that result certain?
Worked solution

1. Entry $(i,j) = q_i \cdot k_j$:

k₁=[1,0] k₂=[0,1] k₃=[1,1] q₁=[1,0] 1 0 1 q₂=[0,1] 0 1 1 q₃=[1,1] 1 1 2

2. Multiply each entry by 0.707. Row 1 becomes $[0.707,\ 0,\ 0.707]$.

3. Apply the exponential: $[2.028,\ 1.000,\ 2.028]$. The sum is 5.056.

row 1 weights = [0.401, 0.198, 0.401]

Positions 1 and 3 have the same weight, and that is correct. $q_1 = [1,0]$ has dot product 1 with both $k_1 = [1,0]$ and $k_3 = [1,1]$. Position 2 is orthogonal to the query, and it gets the least.

4. The weighted sum of the value rows:

out₁ = 0.401[1,0] + 0.198[0,1] + 0.401[1,1] = [0.401 + 0 + 0.401, 0 + 0.198 + 0.401] = [0.802, 0.599]

Note that the output is not any input row. It is a real mixture. That is the purpose: the new representation of position 1 now contains information from position 3.

5. With a causal mask, the scores at $j > 1$ become $-\infty$. Thus $e^{-\infty} = 0$, and after normalization the row is $[1, 0, 0]$. The output is exactly $v_1 = [1, 0]$.

This is certain, and it is a general fact: the first position of a causal attention layer can only return its own value vector, because it has nothing else to attend to. Attention does not change its representation, however well the model is trained. That is why decoder-only models get so little from their first token. It is also part of the reason that a <SOS> token is useful there: nobody needs the output at that position.

By hand — exercise 06.2

Find the shapes and the cost. You need only multiplication.

B = 32 L = 128 d_model = 256 n_heads = 8
  1. What is $d_k$?
  2. Write the shape after each step: embedding → $W^Q$ → split_heads → $QK^\top$ → softmax → @V → merge heads → $W^O$.
  3. How many floats does the attention weight tensor hold? At 4 bytes each, how much memory is that? How much if $L$ becomes 1024?
  4. Count the parameters of the multi-head attention block (four projections, no biases). Does the count depend on $L$ or on n_heads?
Worked solution

1. $d_k = 256/8 = \mathbf{32}$.

2.

embedding (32, 128, 256) after W^Q (32, 128, 256) after split_heads (32, 8, 128, 32) Q @ Kᵀ (32, 8, 128, 128) ← the quadratic one after softmax (32, 8, 128, 128) @ V (32, 8, 128, 32) merge heads (32, 128, 256) after W^O (32, 128, 256)

3. $32 \times 8 \times 128 \times 128 = 4{,}194{,}304$ floats = 16.8 MB. That is for the attention weights of one layer, in one forward pass. The backward pass needs them, so the model must keep them.

At $L = 1024$: $32 \times 8 \times 1024^2 = 268$M floats = 1.07 GB. Eight times the sequence length needs sixty-four times the memory. Six layers of that use 6.4 GB on attention weights alone, before you count any parameter or activation. That is more than the budget of most laptops, and all of it is for one intermediate tensor. That is why each long-context method aims at exactly this tensor: sliding windows, sparse patterns and the tiling of FlashAttention.

4. There are four projections of $d_{\text{model}} \times d_{\text{model}}$: $4 \times 256^2 = \mathbf{262{,}144}$. The count depends on neither $L$ nor n_heads. Sequence length changes the activations but not the weights. Heads divide a fixed budget; they do not add to it. More heads cost nothing in parameters and almost nothing in compute. That is why 8 or 16 is standard.

In the wild

In production, all of this chapter is one call: 

out = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=True)

It calculates exactly the formula that you just implemented. You can verify that with numbers, and you should, as the notebook does. But where possible, it uses a fused FlashAttention kernel. The difference is not only speed. The simple implementation stores the (B, H, L, L) score matrix in memory. The fused kernel calculates attention in tiles and never stores that matrix at all. Thus memory increases linearly in $L$, not quadratically.

That is the difference between a 4k context and a 128k context. It came from a systems idea, not a modeling idea. Note that, because it shows where progress in this field really comes from. nn.MultiheadAttention also includes the projections, and nn.TransformerEncoderLayer includes the full block from Chapter 08.

Feel for the numbersMust do

In attention, learn an instinct for two quantities. The first is the spread of the raw scores. The second decides if your model fits in memory. You can do the arithmetic for both on a whiteboard while someone proposes an architecture.

QuantityFloorTypicalCeilingRead it as
std of $q \cdot k$, unit-variance inputs—$\sqrt{d_k}$—8 at $d_k = 64$; this is the whole scaling argument
Score range after $\div\sqrt{d_k}$$-3$$\pm 2$3the range where softmax still has a gradient
One attention weight0$1/L$ if uniform11 means the row has collapsed
Row entropy0near $\ln L$ early$\ln L$0 is one-hot; $\ln L$ is attending to everything
Score matrix, fp32—16.8 MB at $B{=}32,H{=}8,L{=}128$1.07 GB at $L{=}1024$per layer, per forward pass, and it is kept for the backward

Now do these on paper. Where you can, do them in your head. You can use a calculator for the logarithms. The goal is to know which number to use.

  1. $d_k = 64$, and you forget the scaling. Approximately what range do the raw scores cover? What does softmax do with numbers of that size?
  2. $L = 128$ with perfectly uniform attention. What is each weight? What is the row entropy?
  3. You double the sequence length. What happens to the memory for the score matrix? What happens to the parameter count?
Answers

1. The standard deviation is 8. Thus $\pm 3\sigma$ is a range of approximately $\pm 24$. The gap between the top score and the next score is then frequently several units. $e^{\text{several}}$ makes the softmax one-hot in practice. Chapter 07 shows what that does to the gradient.

2. Each weight is $1/128 = 0.0078$, and the entropy is $\ln 128 = 4.85$ nats, which is the maximum. An untrained head is near this value. When this number decreases, you see the head decide what it is for.

3. Memory increases four times, because the matrix is $L \times L$. The parameter count does not change at all. The projections are $d_{\text{model}} \times d_{\text{model}}$, and they do not depend on length. Almost everyone first guesses that a longer context needs a bigger model. It needs a bigger activation budget.

The habit. Separate "how many parameters" from "how much memory while the model runs". In attention, they depend on completely different things. When people confuse them, a small model surprises them with an out-of-memory error.

Say it backRecommended

Explain this to your favorite LLM, in your own words: why are there three projections rather than one, and what would break if keys and values were the same vector? Then ask it to correct you. Ask it to question each part where you were vague, not only the parts where you were wrong, because the gaps are in the vague parts. Use each of the words query, key and value only one time. Say what the vectors do.

What a good answer covers — open this afterwards, not before
  1. The query says what a position looks for. The key says what a position offers as a label. The value says what the position really contributes.
  2. The model only compares queries and keys. They make a score, and they never occur directly in the output.
  3. The model only averages values. Values never affect who attends to whom.
  4. Thus the features that let others find a position are not necessarily the features worth retrieving. If keys were tied to values, they would have to be the same.
  5. All positions share the projections. Thus the projections are properties of the model, and the vectors that result are properties of the token.

Most common miss. An answer explains the dictionary analogy but does not say what the separation gives. If your answer would still make sense with $K = V$, it has not found the reason for three matrices and not two.
