Chapter 07 · notebook 07_attention_backprop

Where Q, K and V Come From#

Each explanation of attention derives the forward pass, and almost none derive the backward pass. Thus the question that readers really have stays without an answer. The three projections make queries, keys and values from an embedding. But nothing says where the projections came from. This chapter answers that question in the only honest way: it differentiates the full calculation and follows the result back to each matrix.

The short answer, before the long one#

$W^Q$, $W^K$ and $W^V$ are ordinary parameters. They start at random values. The same optimizer step as each other weight in the model updates them. They train together with everything else, also the feed-forward head, against one scalar loss. There is no separate objective for attention. There is no phase where the projections train before the rest of the network. And nothing in training tells a query what it should look for.

Key concept There is no attention loss. The only quantity that the model ever minimizes is the loss of the end task: next-token cross-entropy, translation cross-entropy or a classification objective. $W^Q$ learns only because a change to it changes that number. Each head that you can interpret in a paper is a by-product. Nobody asked the model for a coreference head. A coreference head is what minimized perplexity.

That answer is correct, but it does not satisfy. It does not explain how a signal from the output turns into a sensible change to a matrix. That signal is thousands of dimensions and a dozen layers away. The matrix decides what position 7 looks at. That is a question about the backward pass. The rest of this chapter is the derivation.

One function, one scalar#

Be exact about what a trained network is, because that exactness makes the rest easy. A transformer is one function:

$$L = \mathcal{L}\big(\theta;\ \text{data}\big) \in \mathbb{R}$$

Here $\theta$ contains each parameter in the model: the embeddings, all four projections in each attention block, both feed-forward layers, each LayerNorm scale and shift, and the output head. The loss is one number. Training asks for $\partial L/\partial\theta$, which is one number for each parameter, and takes a step against it. That is all. It is the same statement as the two-layer network of Chapter 01. Only the length of the chain is different.

Here is the chain for one encoder block, written out:

Example — the path from $W^Q$ to the loss
W^Q ──▶ Q ──▶ S = QKᵀ/√d_k ──▶ P = softmax(S) ──▶ O = PV │ ▼ concat heads, W^O │ ▼ residual add, LayerNorm │ ▼ feed-forward network │ ▼ (× N blocks) ──▶ head ──▶ logits │ ▼ cross-entropy L

There are nine links. The backward pass goes through that list in reverse, and each link gives one multiplication. Nothing in it is special to attention. It is the same chain rule as in all other places. But two of the links behave in ways that decide how the model trains. Those two are the softmax and the residual add. This chapter covers the softmax. Chapter 08 covers the residual add.

The backward pass of scaled dot-product attention#

Use one head, and remove the batch axis. Here is the forward pass, with the shapes from Chapter 06:

$$S = \frac{QK^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_k}}, \qquad P = \operatorname{softmax_{row}}(S), \qquad O = PV$$

$Q$ and $K$ have shape (L, d_k), $V$ has shape (L, d_v), and $S$ and $P$ are square at (L, L). Suppose that the rest of the network already gave us $G = \partial L/\partial O$, with the same shape as $O$. All the results below come from the chain rule and nothing more.

Through the value multiplication. $O = PV$ is a plain matrix product, so it transposes in the usual way:

$$\frac{\partial L}{\partial V} = P^{\top}G, \qquad\qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial P} = GV^{\top}$$

Through the softmax. This is the only interesting step. The softmax acts on each row independently. Thus, take one row: $p = \operatorname{softmax}(s)$, both of length $L$. Write $g = \partial L/\partial p$ for that row. Its Jacobian is $J = \operatorname{diag}(p) - pp^{\top}$. (The Jacobian is the matrix of all the $\partial p_i/\partial s_j$. You multiply by it to move the gradient back across the softmax.) Note that it is not diagonal. A softmax mixes each input into each output. Thus, unlike ReLU, you cannot apply it entry by entry. $J$ is symmetric, so:

$$\frac{\partial L}{\partial s} = Jg = p \odot \big(g - (p \cdot g)\big)$$

Do that for each row, and you have $\partial L/\partial S$. We call it $dS$. Note its form. First, subtract one scalar, $p \cdot g$, from each entry. Then multiply elementwise by $p$. Both halves are important. The next section is about what they do.

Through the scale and the dot products. $S = QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k}$ is again a matrix product, with a constant in front:

$$\frac{\partial L}{\partial Q} = \frac{dS\,K}{\sqrt{d_k}}, \qquad\qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial K} = \frac{dS^{\top}Q}{\sqrt{d_k}}$$

Finally, into the parameters. $Q = XW^Q$, so:

$$\frac{\partial L}{\partial W^Q} = X^{\top}\frac{\partial L}{\partial Q}$$

$W^K$ and $W^V$ have the same form. The input $X$ collects all three contributions, because it went into all three projections:

$$\frac{\partial L}{\partial X} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial Q}W^{Q\top} + \frac{\partial L}{\partial K}W^{K\top} + \frac{\partial L}{\partial V}W^{V\top}$$

That is the complete backward pass of an attention head. It has six lines and no approximations. Each line is a transpose and a multiplication, except the softmax. If you implement those six lines, you get the same values as autograd to floating-point precision. The notebook tells you to do exactly that.

By hand — exercise 07.1

This continues exercise 06.1. It uses the same three tokens, the same $d_k = 2$ and the same matrices:

Q = K = V = [[1, 0], [0, 1], [1, 1]] From 06.1, row 1 of P is p = [0.401, 0.198, 0.401] and the output of position 1 is o₁ = [0.802, 0.599]. Suppose the loss depends only on the first component of o₁, so the gradient arriving from above is g = ∂L/∂o₁ = [1, 0].
  1. Calculate row 1 of $\partial L/\partial P$. (Each entry is $g \cdot v_j$. You ask how much each value vector contributed to the component that you care about.)
  2. Calculate the scalar $p \cdot g$ for that row.
  3. Calculate row 1 of $dS$ with $p \odot (g - (p\cdot g))$. Then add the three entries. What do you get? Why must you get that for each row of each softmax?
  4. Calculate $\partial L/\partial q_1$. Remember the $1/\sqrt{2}$.
  5. Do not calculate it. Which rows of $\partial L/\partial K$ are not zero? Which rows of $\partial L/\partial V$? Explain the difference in one sentence.
Worked solution

1. $(\partial L/\partial P)_{1j} = g \cdot v_j$ with $g = [1,0]$. Thus it selects the first component of each value vector:

v₁ = [1,0] → 1 v₂ = [0,1] → 0 v₃ = [1,1] → 1 ∂L/∂P row 1 = [1, 0, 1]

2. $p \cdot g = 0.401(1) + 0.198(0) + 0.401(1) = 0.802$. This is the output component itself. That is not a coincidence, because $o_{1,0} = \sum_j p_j v_{j,0}$.

3. Subtract 0.802 from each entry, then multiply by $p$:

[1 − 0.802, 0 − 0.802, 1 − 0.802] = [0.198, −0.802, 0.198] × p [0.401, 0.198, 0.401] = [0.0793, −0.1587, 0.0793] sum = 0.0793 − 0.1587 + 0.0793 = 0.0000

The row sums to zero, and it always will: $\sum_j p_j(g_j - p\cdot g) = p\cdot g - (p \cdot g)\sum_j p_j = 0$, because the softmax weights sum to 1. Keep this as a debug check. If you write your own attention backward and a $dS$ row does not sum to zero, the bug is in your softmax gradient and nowhere else.

4. $\partial L/\partial q_1 = \frac{1}{\sqrt 2}\sum_j dS_{1j}k_j$:

0.0793[1,0] + (−0.1587)[0,1] + 0.0793[1,1] = [0.1587, −0.0793] ÷ √2 = [0.1122, −0.0561]

When you ask autograd the same question, it returns [0.112190, -0.056095].

5. All three rows of $\partial L/\partial K$ are not zero, and all three rows of $\partial L/\partial V$ are not zero. But the reasons are different, and the next section is about that difference. Each value vector went into $o_1$ with weight $p_j$. Thus each one gets gradient $p_j g$ directly. Each key was compared with $q_1$. Thus each one gets gradient only through the softmax row. That is why those entries carry the factor $p_j(g_j - p\cdot g)$. They can vanish when the value gradients do not.

Why V learns easily and Q and K do not#

Look at the two paths next to each other. The gradient that gets to $V$ is $P^\top G$. It is a matrix product, linear in the gradient that comes in, and no Jacobian of a non-linearity is in the way. Values are on the easy path. $W^V$ trains approximately as easily as any ordinary linear layer in the network.

The gradient that gets to $Q$ and $K$ must first go through $p \odot (g - (p\cdot g))$, and that expression can fail. Suppose that a row of $P$ has become confident: one weight is near 1, and the others are near 0. For the entry near 1, $p \cdot g \approx g_j$, so the bracket is near zero. Each other entry is multiplied by $p_j \approx 0$. Both terms disappear at the same time. In the limit, this is exact, not approximate. If $p$ is exactly one-hot at index $m$, then $p\cdot g = g_m$. Entry $m$ gives $1 \cdot (g_m - g_m) = 0$, and each other entry gives $0 \cdot (\cdot) = 0$. The row returns exactly zero. $W^Q$ and $W^K$ learn nothing from it, at any learning rate, for as long as it stays that way.

This is the argument for the square-root scale of Chapter 06, now stated in terms of what it protects. Division by $\sqrt{d_k}$ is not about a tidy forward pass. It keeps the attention rows soft enough that the backward pass still has a signal for them. Clear the scale in the widget and increase $d_k$. The row becomes one-hot, and the gradient that it returns disappears.

Measured — and not where you would look for it

The notebook runs this over random heads at $d_k$ from 2 to 256. The first half of the result is what you expect. With the scale, the mean entropy of the attention rows is flat in $d_k$. Without it, the entropy decreases steadily from 2.17 to 0.18 nats. The rows saturate exactly as the algebra predicts.

The second half is not what this chapter originally claimed. At $d_k = 128$, the total $\|\partial L/\partial S\|$ almost does not change: 4.53 with the scale and 3.17 without it. And $\|\partial L/\partial W^Q\|$ is larger without the scale: 283 against 38. On any plot of aggregate gradient norm, the model without the scale looks healthier.

The collapse is there, but it occurs row by row. With the scale, the gradient of the loudest row is approximately $9\times$ the gradient of the quietest row. Without the scale, the spread is twelve orders of magnitude, and 15% of the rows return less than $10^{-4}$. Those rows are dead, but the rows that stay alive are loud enough to keep the average up. This lesson also applies outside attention. A mean or a global norm cannot see a failure that affects only a subset. Plot the distribution.

The same failure, under three names When you can see this term, three pieces of training folklore become one phenomenon. Attention entropy collapse is this row becoming one-hot early and never recovering. Learning-rate warmup helps because it keeps the early updates small. Thus no head becomes sharp before the representation that it attends to is worth attention. QK-LayerNorm normalizes $Q$ and $K$ before the dot product, and it is now standard in large models. It limits the score magnitudes directly. That is the same fix as $\sqrt{d_k}$. But it also works when the weights change scale during training, not only at initialization.
Masking, for free A masked entry has $S_{ij} = -\infty$. Thus $p_{ij} = 0$, and $dS_{ij} = p_{ij}(g_{ij} - p\cdot g) = 0$ exactly. The mask needs no backward implementation at all. A masked position cannot get gradient, because the same zero that removed it from the forward average removes it from the backward sum. That is why Chapter 06 says that you must mask before the softmax. If you mask after it, $p_{ij} \neq 0$, and a future token would silently teach a past position what to look for.

Q and K are only ever a product#

Here is one more structural fact. It is easy to miss, and it is useful. The scores depend on $W^Q$ and $W^K$ only through this expression:

$$S = \frac{X W^Q (W^K)^{\top} X^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_k}}$$

Thus only the product $M = W^Q(W^K)^\top$ affects the function that the model calculates. Multiply $W^Q$ by any $c \neq 0$ and $W^K$ by $1/c$, and the model is identical: the same outputs and the same loss, on each input. The parameterization is redundant. Thus the loss surface has a flat direction through each point.

Differentiate that invariance along $c$ at $c = 1$. This gives a relation that the gradients must satisfy, for any model and any data, at any point in training:

$$\Big\langle \frac{\partial L}{\partial W^Q},\, W^Q \Big\rangle = \Big\langle \frac{\partial L}{\partial W^K},\, W^K \Big\rangle$$

This has two results. First, it is a real test. If you implement attention backward yourself, this equality is true to floating-point noise, and the notebook checks it. Second, it explains a practical problem. The individual norms of $W^Q$ and $W^K$ are not useful quantities to monitor or to regularize. The optimizer can move along the flat direction without a change to anything. Weight decay on both does have an effect: it prefers the balanced point on each flat line. That is a small example of a regularizer that acts on the parameterization, not on the function.

Where the gradient is born#

All the material above assumed that $G = \partial L/\partial O$ came from somewhere. In the end, it comes from one subtraction. Take one position with logits $z$, predicted distribution $\hat{y} = \operatorname{softmax}(z)$ and one-hot target $y$. The gradient of cross-entropy with respect to the logits is:

$$\frac{\partial L}{\partial z} = \hat{y} - y$$

The derivation is in Chapter 00. It is the reason to keep softmax and cross-entropy together. Separately, each one has a difficult Jacobian. Together, they become one subtraction.

What gets updated, and by what#

ParameterShapeWhere its gradient arrives from
$W^V$, $W^O$(d_model, d_model)a linear path — no non-linearity's Jacobian in the way
$W^Q$, $W^K$(d_model, d_model)only through their own layer's softmax; zero if its rows saturate
FFN $W_1$, $W_2$(d_model, d_ff)through ReLU — zero for any unit its input never activates
$\gamma$, $\beta$(d_model,)summed over every token in the batch, so large and low-variance
Token embeddings(V, d_model)only the rows for tokens that appeared; the rest get exactly zero
Learned positions(L_max, d_model)only rows up to the longest sequence in the batch

The last two rows surprise people. The embedding of a rare token changes only on the few steps where the token occurs. At all other steps, nothing changes it. Thus rare-word embeddings stay near their initialization, and a large vocabulary needs more data, not only more parameters. Also, a learned positional table has never seen row 3000 if training never used a sequence that long. That row is still at its initialization, and the model gives confident nonsense there. A fixed formula has no parameters, so it cannot fail that way. Chapter 08 comes back to this trade when it introduces the two options. Note now that the choice between them first shows as a property of the backward pass.

By hand — exercise 07.2

There is no arithmetic. This exercise uses the encoder–decoder of Chapter 09. Its cross-attention takes queries from the decoder, and keys and values from $M$, the output of the encoder. If you have not read Chapter 09, come back to this exercise after it. A translation model has a 6-layer encoder and a 6-layer decoder. You calculate the loss on one target position, the third word of one sentence, and call backward(). For each item below, say whether the gradient is zero or not, and why:

  1. $W^V$ in the self-attention of decoder layer 6.
  2. $W^Q$ in the cross-attention of decoder layer 2.
  3. $W^Q$ in encoder layer 4.
  4. The embedding row for the fifth target token.
  5. The embedding row for a source word in the sentence.
  6. $\gamma$ of the final encoder LayerNorm.
Worked solution

1. Not zero. With the causal mask, position 3 attends to positions 1–3, and their value vectors go into its output.

2. Not zero. Note that it is a decoder parameter, but it is in the sub-layer that talks to the encoder. Its gradient is $H_2^\top(\partial L/\partial Q_2)$, made only from decoder hidden states.

3. Not zero. The route is long: encoder 4 → encoder 5 → encoder 6 → $M$ → the $K$ and $V$ of each decoder layer → the loss. But each link exists, so the chain rule gives something. This answers the question "how does the encoder know anything?". It knows because this path exists, and for no other reason.

4. Zero. The fifth target token is at position 5, and position 3 cannot attend to it. The causal mask gives it exactly zero weight, and a masked entry returns exactly zero gradient. It is also not the target of the position that we scored. Both routes are closed.

5. Not zero. The bidirectional attention of the encoder can see each source token. Each source token gets to the decoder through cross-attention, whichever target position you scored.

6. Not zero, and it will be one of the larger gradients in the model. $\gamma$ is one $d_{\text{model}}$-vector, and it collects a contribution from each source token, not from one position.

The answers are not the useful part. The method is. To decide whether a parameter gets gradient, do not think about what it is for. Look for a path in the graph. Then make sure that no mask or saturated non-linearity sets it to zero on the way.

In the wild

loss.backward() runs all six equations above. PyTorch records the forward operations as a graph. Then it goes through the graph in reverse, and calls the registered backward of each operation. torch.autograd.Function is the interface. The main exercise of the notebook is to write one for attention. 

loss.backward()
for name, p in model.named_parameters():
    if p.grad is None:
        print(name, "received no gradient at all")   # disconnected from the loss
    else:
        print(name, p.grad.norm().item())

For the subject of this chapter, that loop is the most useful debug tool. A None gradient means that the parameter is not on any path to the loss. For example, a head is disconnected, a tensor was rebuilt with .detach(), or a branch was never called. A gradient norm of exactly zero means that a path exists, but a mask or a saturated softmax closed it.

torch.autograd.gradcheck compares an analytic backward with finite differences in double precision. It is the correct way to trust your own Function. It hides two things that you should know. First, autograd stores the (B, H, L, L) attention matrix for the backward pass. That is the memory cost of exercise 06.2 in Chapter 06. Second, FlashAttention does not store it. It calculates $P$ again during the backward pass from $Q$ and $K$. It trades arithmetic for memory, and it calculates the same six equations both ways.

Feel for the numbersMust do

Gradients have expected magnitudes and exact invariants, and you can check both. The invariants are especially useful. When you debug your own backward pass, a quantity that must be exactly zero is the most useful thing that you can have.

QuantityFloorTypicalCeilingRead it as
Sum of a $dS$ row000exactly zero, every softmax, always
$\langle \partial L/\partial W^Q, W^Q\rangle - \langle \partial L/\partial W^K, W^K\rangle$000exactly zero — $W^Q$ and $W^K$ appear only as a product
Gradient at a masked entry000exactly zero; the mask needs no backward code
Attention row entropy, $L = 16$0≈2.35 healthy2.77$\ln 16 = 2.77$
Per-row $\|dS\|$ spread, scaled—≈9×—measured in the notebook
Per-row $\|dS\|$ spread, unscaled, $d_k=128$—≈$10^{12}$×—measured; the aggregate norm hides it
p.grad is None———not on any path to the loss at all

Now do these on paper. Where you can, do them in your head. You can use a calculator for the logarithms. The goal is to know which number to use.

  1. A row of $P$ is exactly one-hot. What is the gradient to each score in that row? Is that approximate or exact?
  2. You write your own attention backward, and one $dS$ row sums to $0.03$. Where is the bug? Where is it certainly not?
  3. Each logged gradient norm looks healthy, but one head has clearly stopped learning. Which statistic did you not examine?
Answers

1. Exactly zero, at each entry. For the hot index, $p \cdot g = g_m$, so the bracket $(g_m - p\cdot g)$ is zero. For each other index, $p_j = 0$ multiplies the bracket. Both terms disappear, and no learning rate recovers the row.

2. In the softmax gradient, and nowhere else. The row sum is $\sum_j p_j(g_j - p\cdot g) = p\cdot g - (p\cdot g)\sum_j p_j = 0$ for any $g$. Thus a wrong $dP$, a wrong $V$ or a wrong scale cannot cause a sum that is not zero. Those errors would give a wrong answer that still sums to zero.

3. The distribution. The largest entries control a Frobenius norm. Thus a few loud rows keep the average up while other rows return $10^{-13}$. Plot a histogram of the entropy of each row or the gradient norm of each row. A mean cannot show you a failure that affects only a subset.

The habit. Find quantities that must be exactly zero or exactly equal, and assert them. An approximate expectation finds careless code. An exact invariant finds the bug.

Say it backRecommended

Explain this to your favorite LLM, in your own words: an encoder–decoder's encoder has no loss of its own. So how does it learn anything? (This question uses Chapter 09. If you have not read it, come back to this question after it.) Then ask it to correct you. Ask it to question each part where you were vague, not only the parts where you were wrong, because the gaps are in the vague parts.

What a good answer covers — open this afterwards, not before
  1. The loss uses only decoder outputs. The encoder is in the graph only through the memory that it makes.
  2. The only edges out of the memory are the cross-attention key and value projections of each decoder layer.
  3. There is no query term, because cross-attention makes its queries from decoder hidden states. Thus no gradient comes back that way.
  4. Each decoder layer contributes. The contributions add into one tensor before they get to the encoder.
  5. Thus the encoder learns to be useful for lookups. "End-to-end" means that the gradient found a path. It does not mean that anything had direct supervision.

Most common miss. The answer "through backpropagation" only repeats the question. The content is which edges exist. If you cannot say why there is no $W^Q$ term, you have not followed the graph.

Notebook Open 07_attention_backprop/prompt.ipynb. You will do these tasks:
  • Implement the six backward equations by hand. Check them against autograd to floating-point agreement.
  • Verify the invariant $\langle \partial L/\partial W^Q, W^Q\rangle = \langle \partial L/\partial W^K, W^K\rangle$.
  • Measure how the attention rows saturate as $d_k$ increases, with and without the $\sqrt{d_k}$ scale, and find where the damage to the gradient appears.
  • Build a two-layer encoder–decoder, then cut the edge from the memory to the decoder. Do this one carefully. You will see that the encoder learns only through the cross-attention $K$ and $V$ projections.
Read this next, elsewhere
  • Andrej Karpathy, Yes you should understand backprop. This is the general case of the argument of this chapter. If you treat autograd as a black box, saturating non-linearities seem mysterious, not obvious.
  • Xiong et al., On Layer Normalization in the Transformer Architecture (2020). This gives the full gradient analysis of pre-norm and post-norm. It also explains why one needs warmup and the other does not.
  • Zhai et al., Stabilizing Transformer Training by Preventing Attention Entropy Collapse (2023). This measures the failure that the widget above shows, at scale. It also gives the fix that became QK-LayerNorm.
Where this goes next You can now differentiate an attention head from end to end. You need that before you can stack heads. Chapter 08 does the stacking: positional encoding, residual connections and normalization. It also explains why a deep stack of these blocks trains at all, and that argument is only about the backward pass that you just derived. Much later, Chapter 11 freezes most of these parameters and trains a low-rank correction. That only makes sense when you can say exactly which gradients you decide not to calculate.

Chapter 08 · notebook 08_transformer_pytorch

The Transformer Encoder#

Attention alone is not a model. It cannot see order, it is shallow, and a simple stack of it does not train. This chapter adds three components that change the mechanism of Chapter 06 into an architecture: positional encoding, residual connections with layer normalization, and a position-wise feed-forward network.

Attention is permutation-equivariant#

Start with the gap. Take the attention formula and permute the input rows. Each $q_i$, $k_j$ and $v_j$ moves with its token, and each pairwise score stays the same. The output rows are permuted in exactly the same way, and their contents do not change.

Thus "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" give the same set of representations. For a task where word order carries meaning, which is every task, that is fatal. An RNN gets order automatically from the sequential recurrence. Attention removed recurrence, so we must tell it the order.

Positional encoding#

The fix is to add a vector that depends on position to each token embedding, before the first attention layer. The original transformer uses fixed sinusoids:

$$PE_{(pos,\,2i)} = \sin\!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}}}\right) \qquad PE_{(pos,\,2i+1)} = \cos\!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}}}\right)$$

Even dimensions get sines, and odd dimensions get cosines. The wavelength increases exponentially with the dimension index, from $2\pi$ at $i=0$ up to $10000 \cdot 2\pi$ at the top.

The picture explains the design better than the formula. The columns on the left oscillate quickly, and they tell neighboring positions apart. The columns on the right oscillate slowly, and they encode the approximate location in the sequence. Together they make a multi-resolution code. It is much like a binary counter, where the low bit changes at each step and the high bit changes one time for each half of the sequence. Each position gets a different fingerprint, and positions near each other get similar fingerprints.

Here is the really clever property. For any fixed offset $k$, $PE_{pos+k}$ is a linear function of $PE_{pos}$. It is a rotation, by the angle-addition identities for sine and cosine. Thus a model can learn to attend "three positions back" as one linear operation, applied in the same way at each position. It does not need to memorize each absolute pair. The model can learn relative position.

Why add rather than concatenate It seems that an addition of position to content would damage the content, and you could reasonably expect concatenation. There are two answers. In practice, concatenation costs dimensions that you would prefer to use for meaning. In structure, a high-dimensional space lets a learned embedding keep the two types of information in subspaces that are almost orthogonal, and trained models do exactly that. Modern alternatives mostly perform better than sinusoids. One is learned absolute embeddings. Another is rotary embeddings (RoPE), which rotate $Q$ and $K$ by an angle that depends on position, inside each attention layer. Current large language models use RoPE.

Residual connections#

The model does not apply each sub-layer directly. It wraps each one:

$$x \leftarrow \operatorname{LayerNorm}\big(x + \operatorname{Sublayer}(x)\big)$$

The x + is a residual connection, and it makes depth possible. Differentiate it: $\partial(x + f(x))/\partial x = 1 + f'(x)$. Thus the gradient that gets to the input is the gradient from above plus a correction. Even if $f'$ is very small, the 1 stays. Thus gradients have a clear path from the loss to each layer, however deep the stack is.

Key concept This is the same structural idea as the LSTM cell state in Chapter 05: an additive path where gradients do not go through repeated multiplication. The LSTM puts a gate on it. The transformer leaves it open. Each deep architecture that trains successfully has some version of this. The problem of the product of Jacobians in Chapter 04 (one matrix of partial derivatives for each step, all multiplied together) is universal. It is not specific to recurrence.
Example — 24 layers, with and without the skip

Suppose that the Jacobian of each sub-layer has a typical magnitude of $f' = 0.8$. That is not an extreme value. It is only slightly contractive.

WITHOUT residuals: the gradient scales as 0.8²⁴ = 0.0047 layer 1 receives 0.5% of the signal. WITH residuals: each factor is (1 + f′) instead of f′. Even if every f′ were exactly 0, the product of the 1-terms is 1 — layer 1 still receives 100%.

The exact arithmetic is not the point. The structure is. The additive term makes 1 the minimum, not the maximum. Without it, depth multiplies the signal away. With it, depth cannot starve any layer. That is why networks stopped at approximately 20 layers before residual connections, and went past 150 layers immediately after. Nothing else about the training changed.

There is a second way to read it. Each sub-layer calculates a correction to the running representation. It does not replace it. A block that learned nothing useful can give approximately zero, and then it is the identity. Thus more layers are almost harmless. That is why transformer depth scales so easily.

Layer normalization#

For each token independently, normalize across the feature dimension:

$$\operatorname{LN}(x) = \gamma \odot \frac{x - \mu}{\sqrt{\sigma^2 + \epsilon}} + \beta$$

$\mu$ and $\sigma^2$ come from the $d_{\text{model}}$ features of that token. $\gamma$ and $\beta$ are a learned scale and shift for each feature. Repeated addition of attention outputs to residuals lets the magnitude of the activations drift. Layer norm sets the scale again at each step. This keeps the network in the range where both its non-linearities and its optimizer behave well.

Compare it with batch normalization. Batch norm calculates statistics across the batch for each feature. Thus the output of each example depends on the other examples in its batch. It needs different behavior in training and in evaluation, and it becomes much worse at small batch sizes. Layer norm looks only at the features of one token. Batch size has no effect, sequence length has no effect, training and evaluation are the same, and inference on one example works without a change. For sequence data with variable length, that is the deciding factor.

Post-norm and pre-norm#

The formula above is post-norm, as in the original paper. Modern models almost always use pre-norm:

$$x \leftarrow x + \operatorname{Sublayer}\big(\operatorname{LayerNorm}(x)\big)$$

The difference is whether the residual path goes through a normalization. In pre-norm, it does not. The skip connection is a completely clear path from input to output. Thus deep stacks train without learning-rate warmup, and much more stably. With careful tuning, post-norm sometimes gets slightly better final quality. The notebook uses post-norm to match the original paper. The GPT of Chapter 10 uses pre-norm, as GPT-2 and later models do.

The residual stream is the road back#

That is what residual connections do in the forward direction. What makes them necessary is what they do in the backward direction, so look at it now. In a twelve-layer model, there are approximately fifty sub-layers between the loss and the weights of layer 1. At an addition $y = x + f(x)$, the gradient divides into two parts. It does not go through a bottleneck:

$$\frac{\partial L}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial y} + f'(x)^{\top}\frac{\partial L}{\partial y}$$

The first term carries the gradient forward without a change. Expand that across $N$ blocks. One of the terms that results is the pure identity path: the loss gradient gets to layer 1, and nothing multiplied it on the way. Attention blocks and feed-forward blocks add their corrections to that stream. They are not gates that it must go through.

LayerNorm's backward is a projection#

One sub-layer does interfere with the stream, and you should know exactly how. Let $\hat{x} = (x - \mu)/\sigma$ over the $d$ features of a token, and write $u = \partial L/\partial \hat{x}$. Then the gradient with respect to the input is:

$$\frac{\partial L}{\partial x} = \frac{1}{\sigma}\Big(u - \operatorname{mean}(u) - \hat{x}\,\operatorname{mean}(u \odot \hat{x})\Big)$$

The two subtractions are projections. The first removes the component of the gradient along the all-ones direction. The second removes the component along $\hat{x}$ itself. Thus LayerNorm discards each part of the gradient that only wants to shift the mean of a token or change its length. That is correct, because normalization would cancel such a change. But it means that each normalization really loses gradient information. It does not only rescale it.

That is the argument for pre-norm in one line. In post-norm, the output of each block goes through this projection on the residual path itself. Thus the identity term above is not really an identity. It is $1/\sigma$ times a projection, $N$ times. In pre-norm, the normalization is inside the branch, and nothing touches the stream. That is why post-norm transformers need learning-rate warmup and pre-norm transformers mostly do not. It is the full difference between the two formulas above.

The feed-forward network#

$$\operatorname{FFN}(x) = W_2\,\operatorname{ReLU}(W_1x + b_1) + b_2$$

The model applies it in the same way, independently, at each position. It is really a (1×1) convolution. By convention, the inner dimension is $4d_{\text{model}}$: expand, apply a non-linearity, and project back.

Why is it there at all? Apart from its softmax weights, attention is a linear operation on values. It moves and mixes information, but it does not transform it non-linearly. A stack of attention layers without an FFN is an expensive linear map. The FFN gives the non-linear processing at each position. It also holds approximately two thirds of the parameters in a transformer block ($8d^2$ against $4d^2$ for attention). Recent interpretability research reads it as a key-value memory. The first matrix detects patterns, and the second writes learned facts related to them.

The full encoder block#

class TransformerEncoderLayer(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model, n_heads, d_ff, dropout=0.1):
        super().__init__()
        self.attn  = MultiHeadAttention(d_model, n_heads)
        self.ff    = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(d_model, d_ff), nn.ReLU(),
                                   nn.Linear(d_ff, d_model))
        self.norm1 = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)
        self.norm2 = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)
        self.drop  = nn.Dropout(dropout)

    def forward(self, x, mask=None):
        attn_out, _ = self.attn(x, x, x, mask)          # self-attention: Q=K=V=x
        x = self.norm1(x + self.drop(attn_out))
        x = self.norm2(x + self.drop(self.ff(x)))
        return x

That is the full architecture. Stack $N$ of these. Add embeddings and positional encoding at the bottom, and put a task head on top. Each transformer that you know is this block, repeated, at scale. The new ideas since 2017 are about efficiency, position encoding, the location of normalization, and data. They are not about the block.

Note self.attn(x, x, x). The query, the key and the value all come from the same sequence. That is what makes it self-attention. In Chapter 09, the cross-attention of the decoder gives a different tensor for the query. That one change turns the block into a translator.

Pooling for classification#

The encoder gives one vector for each token. Classification needs one vector for each sequence. The simple option is a mean over the positions that are not padding, and it works well. BERT adds a [CLS] token at the start and uses its final representation. This is reasonable, because attention lets that position collect information from all positions. It also gives the model a dedicated place for a summary, so the model does not have to use an average.

Pool with the mask x.mean(dim=1) also averages over padding. Thus a 10-token review padded to 200 gets 95% of its representation from <PAD> embeddings. Multiply by the mask, and divide by the true length. This bug silently decreases accuracy. The model still trains, but it trains worse, and nothing in the output tells you why.
By hand — exercise 08.1

Do layer normalization on one token with four features.

x = [2.0, 4.0, 4.0, 6.0] γ = [1, 1, 1, 1] β = [0, 0, 0, 0] ε ≈ 0
  1. Calculate the mean $\mu$ and the variance $\sigma^2$ across the four features.
  2. Normalize each feature.
  3. Make sure that the result has mean 0 and variance 1.
  4. Now let $\gamma = [2,2,2,2]$ and $\beta = [1,1,1,1]$. What is the output? Why would a network ever want to cancel the normalization that it just did?
  5. Suppose that you had applied batch norm to a batch with this token and three others. Which numbers would have gone into the mean? What fails at inference on one example?
Worked solution

1. $\mu = (2+4+4+6)/4 = 4$. The squared deviations are $4, 0, 0, 4$, so $\sigma^2 = 8/4 = 2$ and $\sigma = 1.414$.

2.

(2 − 4)/1.414 = −1.414 (4 − 4)/1.414 = 0.000 (4 − 4)/1.414 = 0.000 (6 − 4)/1.414 = 1.414

3. Mean $= (-1.414 + 0 + 0 + 1.414)/4 = 0$ ✓. Variance $= (2 + 0 + 0 + 2)/4 = 1$ ✓.

4. Output $= 2 \times [-1.414, 0, 0, 1.414] + 1 = \mathbf{[-1.828, 1, 1, 3.828]}$.

Now the reason. Unit variance for each representation is a strong constraint. Sometimes the correct answer really needs a feature with a large magnitude or a mean that is not zero. $\gamma$ and $\beta$ let the network get back any scale and shift that it needs. Thus normalization makes training stable without a decrease in what the model can express. In the extreme case, the network can learn $\gamma = \sigma$ and $\beta = \mu$ and cancel the operation completely. Normalization is a useful default, not a restriction.

5. Batch norm would average feature 0 across all four tokens in the batch: $x_0$ of token 1, $x_0$ of token 2, and so on. It makes four means, one for each feature. At inference on one example, there is no batch to calculate statistics from. Thus batch norm must use running averages from training. That is why it needs different behavior in training and evaluation. Layer norm does not have this problem. The statistics come from inside the token, so one example works exactly like a thousand.

By hand — exercise 08.2

Calculate positional encoding directly.

d_model = 4, so dimension pairs are i = 0 (dims 0,1) and i = 1 (dims 2,3) PE(pos, 2i) = sin(pos / 10000^{2i/4}) PE(pos, 2i+1) = cos(pos / 10000^{2i/4}) 10000^{0} = 1 10000^{0.5} = 100 sin 0 = 0 cos 0 = 1 sin 1 = 0.841 cos 1 = 0.540 sin 2 = 0.909 cos 2 = −0.416 sin 0.01 = 0.010 cos 0.01 = 1.000 sin 0.02 = 0.020 cos 0.02 = 1.000
  1. Calculate $PE(0)$, $PE(1)$ and $PE(2)$. Each one is a 4-vector.
  2. Which dimensions clearly tell position 1 from position 2? Which ones almost do not change?
  3. At what position does dimension 2 complete a full cycle back to $\sin = 0$?
  4. Explain what would go wrong with $d_{\text{model}} = 4$ and a sequence of length 50,000.
Worked solution

1. For $i = 0$ the divisor is 1. For $i = 1$ it is 100.

PE(0) = [sin 0, cos 0, sin 0, cos 0 ] = [0.000, 1.000, 0.000, 1.000] PE(1) = [sin 1, cos 1, sin 0.01, cos 0.01 ] = [0.841, 0.540, 0.010, 1.000] PE(2) = [sin 2, cos 2, sin 0.02, cos 0.02 ] = [0.909, −0.416, 0.020, 1.000]

2. Dimensions 0 and 1 change sharply: the cosine goes from 0.540 to −0.416 between two neighboring positions. Dimensions 2 and 3 almost do not move (0.010 → 0.020, and 1.000 → 1.000 to three decimals). Fast dimensions resolve local position, and slow dimensions carry global position, exactly as the widget above shows.

3. Dimension 2 has $\sin(pos/100)$. Thus a full cycle needs $pos/100 = 2\pi$, which is $pos \approx \mathbf{628}$.

4. Here, the slowest dimension has a wavelength of only approximately 628, and the fast dimensions repeat every 6.3 positions. Over 50,000 positions, many pairs of positions far apart get almost the same code. For example, positions 100 and 13,923 have codes that agree to approximately two decimal places in all four dimensions. The model could not tell them apart. Thus $d_{\text{model}}$ must be large enough that the slowest wavelength ($2\pi \times 10000 \approx 62{,}800$ at realistic sizes) is more than your longest sequence. This also shows why it is difficult to extend the context window of a trained model. The model has never seen the position codes past the training range.

Feel for the numbersMust do

The parameter count of a transformer block is one formula. If you know it, you can size a model, or check a claim about one, without opening a file. It is $12d^2$ for each block, and you derive it from four numbers that you already have.

QuantityFloorTypicalCeilingRead it as
Attention block—$4d^2$—four projections; independent of heads and length
Feed-forward, $d_{ff} = 4d$—$8d^2$—twice the attention block — the FFN is where the parameters are
One whole block—$12d^2$—3.15M at $d = 512$; 7.08M at $d = 768$
LayerNorm parameters—$2d$—negligible, and often forgotten in counts
LayerNorm output, per tokenmean 0—var 1by construction, before $\gamma$ and $\beta$
Embedding table—$V \cdot d$—compares against all the blocks together

Now do these on paper. Where you can, do them in your head. You can use a calculator for the logarithms. The goal is to know which number to use.

  1. GPT-2 small has $d = 768$ and 12 layers. How many parameters are in the transformer blocks?
  2. What fraction of one block is the feed-forward network?
  3. People say that GPT-2 small has 124M parameters. Add the token embedding ($V = 50{,}257$) and the learned position table (1024 slots). Does the total agree?
Answers

1. $12 \times 768^2 = 7.08$M for each block. Multiply by 12 layers to get 84.9M.

2. $8/12 = 67\%$. Two thirds of each transformer is the part with no attention in it. Remember this when someone describes these models as "attention-based".

3. The token embedding is $50{,}257 \times 768 = 38.6$M. The positions are $1024 \times 768 = 0.8$M. The total is $84.9 + 38.6 + 0.8 = \mathbf{124.3}$M. It agrees. The output head adds nothing, because GPT-2 ties it to the input embedding. If you can do this, you can check any model card that someone gives you.

The habit. Calculate again the published parameter count of a model that you did not build. When it agrees, you understand the architecture. When it does not agree, you found the part where you were wrong.

Say it backRecommended

Explain this to your favorite LLM, in your own words: why can you not just stack attention layers — what do the residual connection and the normalization each contribute? Then ask it to correct you. Ask it to question each part where you were vague, not only the parts where you were wrong, because the gaps are in the vague parts.

What a good answer covers — open this afterwards, not before
  1. Attention alone is permutation-equivariant. Thus something must add position before the first layer.
  2. The residual connection puts an identity term, which nothing touches, on the gradient path from the loss to each layer. Thus depth no longer makes the signal smaller.
  3. Normalization sets the activation scale again. Without it, repeated additions would let the scale drift.
  4. The model uses LayerNorm, not BatchNorm, because LayerNorm looks only at the features of one token. Thus batch size and sequence length have no effect, and training and evaluation behave the same.
  5. The feed-forward sublayer holds most of the parameters and does most of the calculation for each position. Attention moves information between positions. The FFN transforms it in place.

Most common miss. An answer says that residuals "help with vanishing gradients" but does not give the mechanism. The point is specific, and you can prove it. When you differentiate $x + f(x)$, a 1 stays. Thus there is a path where nothing multiplies the gradient.

Notebook Open 08_transformer_pytorch/prompt.ipynb. You will implement positional encoding, build the encoder layer, and stack it into a sentiment classifier. Then you will compare it with the baseline of Chapter 03 and with plain self-attention (Chapter 06) on the same reviews. With 2,000 reviews, do not expect the transformer to win. It needs the most data of the three. Even when you train it until it fits the training set, it gets approximately 75% test accuracy, against approximately 81% for the bag of embeddings. To see that in an experiment is more useful than to see it win.
Where this goes next Chapter 09 adds a second stack and turns this encoder into a translator. That brings a full new category of problems. They start as soon as a model must generate a sequence, not label one.

Chapter 09 · notebook 09_seq2seq_translation

Encoder–Decoder Translation#

Each model until now mapped a sequence to one label or number. Translation maps a sequence to another sequence. That sequence has a different length, a different language and a different word order. This chapter builds the architecture that does it. It also faces the new problem that generation causes: the model must use its own output as input.

The same thing, three names This chapter says encoder–decoder, because that name tells you the parts. You will see the name seq2seq much more frequently for the same architecture. It is short for sequence-to-sequence, from the 2014 paper of that name by Sutskever, Vinyals and Le. That paper did this with LSTMs, before transformers existed. Papers also say sequence transduction, which is the name in "Attention Is All You Need". All three names mean a model that reads one full sequence and writes another. The lesson folder is 09_seq2seq_translation because you will see that term in real work. There is no difference between them. If someone asks whether your model is seq2seq, they ask whether it has this shape.

Two stacks with different jobs#

The encoder reads the source sentence. It makes one contextual vector for each source token. Together, these vectors are the memory. The encoder is exactly the encoder of Chapter 08, with no change. It uses bidirectional (unmasked) attention, because the full source is available at the same time.

The decoder generates the target sentence one token at a time. It is different from the encoder in two ways, and both are necessary:

  1. Its self-attention has a causal mask: position $t$ cannot see $t+1$. At generation time, those tokens do not exist yet.
  2. It has a third sub-layer, cross-attention. This is how the source sentence gets in.
Encoder layerDecoder layer
Self-attentionbidirectionalcausally masked
Cross-attention—Q from decoder, K/V from memory
Feed-forwardyesyes
Sub-layers23

Causal masking#

The mask is an upper-triangular boolean matrix. True means "block this": 

def make_causal_mask(L, device):
    return torch.triu(torch.ones(L, L, dtype=torch.bool, device=device), diagonal=1)

diagonal=1 starts the triangle one place above the main diagonal. Thus position $t$ can attend to itself and to each position before it, but to nothing after it. Apply it as scores.masked_fill(mask, float('-inf')) before the softmax, as in Chapter 06.

Select causal mask. The upper triangle becomes dark, and the weights that stay in each row normalize again to sum to 1.

Key concept Masking lets the decoder train in parallel. Without it, you would have to run the decoder one time for each output position: $T$ sequential forward passes for each example. With it, the model calculates all $T$ positions in one pass. Each position sees exactly the prefix that it will have at generation time. The mask makes a parallel calculation simulate a sequential one. It is the reason that transformers train orders of magnitude faster than RNNs.
Example — counting the forward passes
A batch of 64 sentences, each 18 tokens long. WITHOUT masking you would have to run the decoder once per output position, feeding it a progressively longer prefix each time: 18 sequential forward passes per batch. WITH the causal mask, all 18 positions go through in ONE pass. Row t of the attention matrix sees exactly tokens 1..t — the same prefix that pass number t would have supplied. 64 × 18 = 1,152 supervised predictions, one forward pass.

The mask is not a restriction added to attention. It is the method that lets the model calculate a sequential objective in parallel. Generation is still sequential, and it always will be. But training, which uses most of the compute, is not.

Cross-attention#

This one line makes the model a translator: 

ca_out, _ = self.cross_attn(tgt, memory, memory)   # Q=tgt, K=V=memory

The query comes from the decoder. It asks: what do I need to make the next French word? The keys and the values come from the memory of the encoder. The attention matrix that results has shape (B, heads, T_tgt, S_src). It is a soft alignment between target positions and source positions.

No mask applies here, and a mask here would be wrong. The full source sentence is known from the start. Also, word order is different between languages. To make the first French word, the model can need the last English word. Statistical machine translation spent two decades on explicit alignment models. Cross-attention learns alignment as a side effect of learning to translate, and you can read the alignment directly from the attention weights. The notebook plots exactly this.

Teacher forcing#

Training a generator has a chicken-and-egg problem. To predict token $t$, the decoder needs tokens $1..t-1$. But early in training, the tokens of the model are garbage. Thus it would learn to continue nonsense.

Teacher forcing gives the decoder the true prefix instead. The implementation is a shift of one token: 

logits = model(src, tgt[:, :-1])              # input:  <SOS> w1 w2 ... w_{T-1}
loss   = criterion(logits.reshape(-1, V),
                   tgt[:, 1:].reshape(-1))    # target: w1 w2 ... w_{T-1} <EOS>

The decoder input is the target shifted right, with <SOS> at the start. The prediction target is the target shifted left, with <EOS> at the end. Position $t$ of the input aligns with position $t$ of the output. The causal mask makes sure that no position can see its own answer.

Exposure bias Training always gives a perfect prefix. Generation never does. Thus the model has never seen its own errors, and it does not know how to recover from them. After one wrong token, it is in a state that never occurred in training. This is exposure bias. It is why an undertrained translation model often goes into loops ("de la session de la session…"). Train the notebook model for only a few epochs, and you will see it. Some fixes exist: scheduled sampling, sequence-level objectives and beam search. But the mismatch is part of teacher forcing, and each autoregressive model in production has it.

Autoregressive decoding#

memory  = model.encode(src)          # once — the source never changes
tgt_ids = [SOS_IDX]
for _ in range(max_len):
    out = model.decode(torch.tensor([tgt_ids]), memory)
    next_token = model.fc_out(out)[0, -1].argmax().item()
    tgt_ids.append(next_token)
    if next_token == EOS_IDX:
        break

Note three points:

  • The encoder runs one time. People often calculate it again at each step, and that is an expensive error.
  • The loop uses only the logits of the last position. The earlier positions predict again the tokens that the loop already selected.
  • Generation stops at <EOS>, and the model must learn to give it. Thus <EOS> must be in the training targets. A model that never learns it will run to max_len each time.

This loop also does a quadratic amount of wasted work. At step $t$, it encodes the full prefix $1..t-1$ again, but those representations have not changed. Chapter 10 fixes that with a KV cache.

Greedy versus beam search#

If you take the argmax at each step, that is greedy decoding. It sees only the next step. The best token now can lead to a poor sentence overall. Beam search keeps the $k$ best partial sequences, ranked by total log-probability, and expands all of them at each step. It reliably improves translation quality by one or two BLEU points. But it usually makes open-ended generation worse: there it gives bland, repetitive text. Translation has approximately one correct answer. Storytelling does not.

Evaluating a translation#

Cross-entropy measures how well the model predicts the reference when it gets a perfect prefix. That is not the same as a good translation, and you cannot compare it across vocabularies. BLEU is the standard alternative. It compares the $n$-gram overlap between the hypothesis and the reference for $n = 1..4$, and takes a geometric mean. Then it applies a brevity penalty, so that it does not reward an output of three safe words.

BLEU is a crude tool. It does not know about synonyms or grammar. But in aggregate, it correlates well enough to be useful. For a model of this size, the honest evaluation is to read twenty outputs yourself.

A dataset trap worth remembering The comtrans corpus of NLTK has three alignment files: German–English, German–French and English–French. If you call comtrans.aligned_sents() with no argument, it concatenates all three. Thus a model that seems to learn English→French really trains on three language pairs at the same time. It will give English where you expected French. Always name the file: aligned_sents('alignment-en-fr.txt'). Check your data: print a few pairs and read them. This lesson is general. Almost each corpus has a trap like this, and to print ten examples is the cheapest bug detector in machine learning.
By hand — exercise 09.1

Masking and shifting are the two bookkeeping steps most likely to cause problems.

target sentence: <SOS> le chat dort <EOS> indices: 1 7 12 23 2
  1. Write the decoder input and the prediction target after the shift.
  2. Draw the $4 \times 4$ causal mask for the decoder input (True = blocked).
  3. For each of the four decoder positions, list which target tokens it can attend to, and what it must predict.
  4. Suppose that you forgot the shift. You gave the full target as decoder input and predicted the same full target. What loss would you get after a few epochs? Why is it useless?
Worked solution

1.

decoder input = tgt[:-1] = [<SOS>, le, chat, dort] = [1, 7, 12, 23] prediction tgt = tgt[1:] = [le, chat, dort, <EOS>] = [7, 12, 23, 2]

2. The upper triangle above the main diagonal:

j=0 j=1 j=2 j=3 i=0 False True True True i=1 False False True True i=2 False False False True i=3 False False False False

3.

pos 0: sees [<SOS>] → predicts "le" pos 1: sees [<SOS>, le] → predicts "chat" pos 2: sees [<SOS>, le, chat] → predicts "dort" pos 3: sees [<SOS>, le, chat, dort] → predicts <EOS>

Each position sees exactly the prefix that it will have at generation time. That match is the full reason for the mask.

4. Without the shift, the input at position $t$ contains the token that it must predict. The causal mask lets a position attend to itself. Thus the model learns the identity function: copy the input to the output. The loss goes to almost zero within one or two epochs.

That is exactly why this bug is dangerous. Almost zero training loss looks like a great success. Here is the sign: validation loss also looks very good (the same trick works there), but the generated output is garbage. At generation time, the input is not the answer, and the model learned nothing else. Each time the loss of a sequence model decreases unrealistically fast, check your shift first.

By hand — exercise 09.2

Calculate a cross-attention alignment, and then interpret it.

source (English): [ the, red, house ] encoder memory keys give these raw scores for the decoder query at target position 2 (generating the word after "la"): score(la → the) = 0.0 score(la → red) = 2.0 score(la → house) = 1.0 d_k = 4, so the scale factor is 1/√4 = 0.5 e^0 = 1.000 e^0.5 = 1.649 e^1 = 2.718
  1. Apply the scale, and calculate the attention distribution over the three source words.
  2. The correct French is "la maison rouge". With that word order, is this alignment sensible for the word that the decoder will make next?
  3. The value vectors are $v_{\text{the}} = [1,0]$, $v_{\text{red}} = [0,1]$ and $v_{\text{house}} = [1,1]$. Calculate the cross-attention output.
  4. The self-attention of the decoder has a mask. Why is it correct that no causal mask applies here?
Worked solution

1. The scaled scores are $[0.0, 1.0, 0.5]$. Apply the exponential: $[1.000, 2.718, 1.649]$. The sum is 5.367.

weights = [0.186, 0.506, 0.307]

2. French puts the adjective after the noun: "la maison rouge". Thus, after "la", the next word must be "maison", which aligns to house, not red. This distribution puts the most weight (0.506) on red. Thus the model would probably make "rouge" next and give "la rouge maison": English word order with French words. That is a known failure of an undertrained translation model. You diagnose it exactly by reading cross-attention weights.

3.

out = 0.186[1,0] + 0.506[0,1] + 0.307[1,1] = [0.186 + 0 + 0.307, 0 + 0.506 + 0.307] = [0.493, 0.813]

4. The mask prevents a position from seeing information that it will not have at generation time. The own future tokens of the decoder are exactly that type of information. The source sentence is not. The model gets all of it before generation starts. A mask on it would stop the model from using source words that come later than the current output position. That makes no sense across languages with different word orders. This exercise is an example: to make the second French word, the model needs the third English word.

In the wild

PyTorch includes the full architecture of this chapter: 

model = nn.Transformer(d_model=256, nhead=8,
                       num_encoder_layers=3, num_decoder_layers=3,
                       batch_first=True, norm_first=True)

out = model(src_emb, tgt_emb,
            tgt_mask=nn.Transformer.generate_square_subsequent_mask(T),
            src_key_padding_mask=(src == PAD_IDX))

Note what you must still supply: the embeddings, the positional encoding, the causal mask, the padding masks, the output projection, the teacher-forcing shift and the decode loop. The module is the easy half. Each bug in this chapter is in the half that the library does not cover: the shift, the padding mask, ignore_index, and the <EOS> that never comes. That is exactly why it is worth an afternoon to build it one time by hand.

How the decoder's loss reaches the encoder#

One question is left, and it decides how this architecture trains at all. The model calculates the loss only on the output of the decoder. The encoder has no loss of its own: no reconstruction objective, no auxiliary head, nothing. Thus, by what route does it learn anything?

There is exactly one route. Write $M$ for the memory, which is the output of the top encoder layer. In decoder layer $\ell$, cross-attention makes:

$$Q_\ell = H_\ell W_\ell^{Q}, \qquad K_\ell = M W_\ell^{K}, \qquad V_\ell = M W_\ell^{V}$$

Here $H_\ell$ is the hidden states of the decoder. In the computational graph, $M$ has edges out to $K_\ell$ and $V_\ell$, and to nothing else. Thus the gradient that it gets is:

$$\frac{\partial L}{\partial M} = \sum_{\ell=1}^{N}\left( \frac{\partial L}{\partial K_\ell}W_\ell^{K\top} + \frac{\partial L}{\partial V_\ell}W_\ell^{V\top}\right)$$

That sum is the full training signal of the encoder. Three results follow. They are usually left implicit, so here they are explicitly:

  • There is no $W^Q$ term. The query projections of cross-attention are decoder parameters, trained from $H_\ell$. The source sentence never gives a query. Thus no gradient goes back to the encoder along that edge. The asymmetry in cross_attn(tgt, memory, memory) is not a convention. It decides which half of the model each of those three matrices belongs to.
  • Each decoder layer contributes, and the contributions add. This is the fan of arrows in the stack diagram above, read in reverse. The top encoder layer gets one summed gradient, built from all $N$ decoder layers. That is also why an encoder–decoder is difficult to pipeline across devices. The encoder cannot take its optimizer step until each decoder layer has finished its backward pass.
  • The self-attention of the decoder sends the encoder nothing directly. It contributes only by changing $H_\ell$, which changes $\partial L/\partial K_\ell$. In a real sense, the encoder learns to be useful for lookups. The only feedback that it ever gets is how well its output worked as keys and values.
Key concept This is the general shape of end-to-end training, and you should take the phrase literally. No component of a transformer has a target of its own. Encoders learn representations, heads learn to specialize, and embeddings learn geometry. All of it is a result of one scalar at the far end of the graph, sent back along the edges that exist. When you design a new architecture, ask "what gradient does this part get, and along which edges?". That question usually tells you more than "what is this part supposed to do?".

Teacher forcing severs the recurrence#

There is one more difference from the recurrent models of Chapter 04, and it is larger than it looks. With teacher forcing, the input of the decoder is the true prefix. That is a constant, with no gradient of its own. Thus there is no path from the prediction at position $t$ back to the input at position $t+1$. The forward pass connects the positions through causal self-attention. But the graph has no edge at all from the output of one timestep to the input of the next.

The result is that a transformer has no backpropagation through time. Its graph depth is the number of layers, and nothing more. It is not layers times sequence length. An RNN over 200 timesteps multiplies 200 Jacobians on the way back: 200 matrices of partial derivatives, one for each step. A 6-layer decoder over 200 timesteps multiplies 6 sub-layer Jacobians, and it does all 200 positions in parallel. Attention pays $O(L^2)$ memory for this. It gets the short path length of Chapter 06. It also gets a backward pass whose cost does not grow with sequence length.

The severed edge is also the problem When you cut that edge, exposure bias grows in its place. No gradient ever goes from one generated token to the next. Thus the model never gets a penalty for a token that makes the rest of the sentence difficult. It gets a penalty only for a token that is wrong after a perfect prefix. To restore the edge, you must give the model its own output again. But the argmax that selects that token has a zero derivative almost everywhere. That one fact is why sequence-level training needs tools from a completely different area: policy gradients, Gumbel-softmax relaxations and minimum-risk training. It is also why none of these is a small change to the training loop.
Feel for the numbersMust do

Translation is the first task in this book whose metric is not a probability. Thus it is the first place where you need a second set of reference points. It is also the first place where a number can look excellent for a bad reason.

QuantityFloorTypicalCeilingRead it as
BLEU020–30 usable40+ near-humanbelow 10 is not a working system
Cross-entropy, $V = 10{,}000$02–3 trained9.21 at chance$\ln 10{,}000 = 9.21$
Teacher-forced vs free-running loss—TF always lower—the gap is exposure bias
Sentence length, MT corpora520–30100sets the padding waste and the memory
Cross-attention matrix—$T_{\text{tgt}} \times S_{\text{src}}$—not square — an alignment, not a self-attention

Now do these on paper. Where you can, do them in your head. You can use a calculator for the logarithms. The goal is to know which number to use.

  1. Validation loss is 2.0 over a vocabulary of 10,000 words. What is the perplexity? How does it compare with chance?
  2. Teacher-forced loss is a healthy 1.8, but generated sentences loop: "de la session de la session…". What does that loss not measure?
  3. A colleague reports BLEU 65 on their dev set. Should you believe it?
Answers

1. $e^{2.0} = 7.4$, against a chance perplexity of 10,000. The model decreased ten thousand options to seven. That is really good, and it is much easier to read than "loss 2.0".

2. Its own errors. The data gave a perfect prefix for each number in that loss. The model never got a score on a state that it made itself. Thus nothing in training gave a penalty for a loop. A low teacher-forced loss and broken generations are completely consistent.

3. No. BLEU 65 is higher than the agreement between most human translators. The most probable explanations are test data that leaked into training, or an evaluation on the training split. A number that is too good tells you about your pipeline, not about your model.

The habit. For each metric, learn three reference values: the chance value, the usable value, and the value that is too good to be true. The third one has saved more projects than the second.

Say it backRecommended

Explain this to your favorite LLM, in your own words: how does the source sentence actually get into the decoder, and why is teacher forcing both necessary and a problem? Then ask it to correct you. Ask it to question each part where you were vague, not only the parts where you were wrong, because the gaps are in the vague parts.

What a good answer covers — open this afterwards, not before
  1. The encoder makes one vector for each source token. Together they are the memory. The model uses only the output of the top encoder layer.
  2. Cross-attention takes its query from the decoder, and its keys and values from that memory. That asymmetry makes it a translator and not a language model.
  3. Teacher forcing gives the true prefix. Thus the model can score all target positions in one parallel pass, not one at a time.
  4. It is necessary because, early in training, the output of the model is noise. If the model learns to continue noise, it learns nothing.
  5. It is a problem because the model never gets a score on its own errors. Thus it cannot learn to recover from one. That is exposure bias.

Most common miss. An answer describes teacher forcing as "just faster training". The speed is a result. The reason for it is that the alternative has no useful signal early in training. The cost is a specific, named failure at generation time.

Then you will show the cross-attention alignments. On this small corpus, the model starts to overfit after approximately epoch 11. Thus the training loop keeps the weights with the best validation loss, as exercise 02.7 recommends.
