Chapter 10 · notebook 10_gpt_from_scratch

GPT: A Decoder-Only Model#

Remove the encoder. Remove cross-attention. What stays is a stack of causally masked transformer blocks that predict the next token. Make that several thousand times larger, and it is each large language model that you have used. This chapter builds one. Then it examines the two things that separate a trained model from a useful one: how you sample from it, and how fast you can do that.

Why the encoder was optional#

Chapter 09 needed two stacks because it had two sequences: an English source to read and a French target to write. Cross-attention connected them.

Text continuation has only one sequence. The context is the prefix of the text that you generate, and causal self-attention already reads it. There is no second sequence. Thus cross-attention has nothing to attend to, and the encoder has no input. Both disappear, and the architecture becomes simpler, not more complex.

Seq2seq (Ch. 09)GPT (this chapter)
Stacksencoder + decoderdecoder only
Self-attentionbidirectional / causalcausal throughout
Cross-attentionyesnone
Objectivepredict the target tokenpredict the next token
Labels requiredparallel translationsnone — the text is the label
Key concept The last row is why language models scale and translation models do not. Parallel corpora are expensive and limited. Raw text is neither. Each position in each document is a free supervised example. Because of the causal mask, a document of 1,000 tokens gives 1,000 examples in one parallel forward pass. The only limits are compute and data. Under exactly that condition, scaling laws become interesting.

Pre-norm, and why this differs from Chapter 08#

Chapter 08 used post-norm, as in the original 2017 paper. GPT-2 and later models use pre-norm, and so does the notebook here:

$$\text{post-norm:}\quad x \leftarrow \operatorname{LN}\big(x + F(x)\big) \qquad\qquad \text{pre-norm:}\quad x \leftarrow x + F\big(\operatorname{LN}(x)\big)$$

The difference is what the residual path goes through. In post-norm, each skip connection goes through a normalization. Thus the "clear path" for gradients has an interruption at each layer. In pre-norm, the path really has no interruption. From the loss to layer 1, the gradient can move by pure addition.

The practical results are large. Pre-norm trains deep stacks without learning-rate warmup. It tolerates higher learning rates, and it is much less likely to diverge. With careful tuning, post-norm sometimes gets slightly better final quality. That is why the original paper used it. But almost no model trained since 2019 uses it.

Three details in the model#

Learned positional embeddings#

GPT does not use the fixed sinusoids of Chapter 08. It uses an ordinary nn.Embedding(block_size, n_embd), and gradient descent selects the position codes. This is simpler, and it works at least as well. But it sets an absolute limit on the context length. There is no embedding vector for position block_size. Thus a longer input does not become slowly worse. It gives an error.

That hard limit is why the extension of the context window of a trained model is a research problem, not a configuration change. It is also why rotary embeddings (RoPE) have mostly replaced both approaches in current models. RoPE encodes relative position. It rotates $Q$ and $K$ inside each attention layer.

Weight tying#

self.lm_head.weight = self.tok_emb.weight

The input embedding maps token → vector. The output head maps vector → token scores. These are two inverse views of one relation, so they share a matrix. This saves $V \times d$ parameters. That is very few at $V = 73$ characters, but approximately 38 million at a vocabulary of 50k and $d = 768$. It also usually improves perplexity. It does not only save memory. The symmetry is real. It is not a convenient trick.

Depth-scaled initialization#

Each block adds to the residual stream. With $N$ blocks, each one adds independent noise, so the variance of the stream increases linearly with depth. To cancel this, scale the initialization of the residual projections by $1/\sqrt{2N}$. Then the activations stay in the same range at layer 1 and at layer 48.

A one-line sanity check worth building the habit around The first loss of a correctly initialized model must be almost exactly $\ln(V)$, the loss of a uniform distribution. The 73-character model of the notebook starts within a few thousandths of $\ln 73 = 4.290$. (The exact value changes a little with the seed.) If the initial loss is much higher, the model starts confident and wrong, not uniformly uncertain. Almost always, this means that the standard deviation of the initialization is too large. This check costs one forward pass. It finds a full class of bugs before you waste an hour on training.

Decoding: where the character of the output is decided#

Training decides what the model believes. Sampling decides what it says. The same model can give anything from robotic repetition to incoherence, and only this choice causes the difference.

Temperature divides the logits before the softmax. It reweights the full distribution, but it never cuts it off. Each token keeps some probability. Thus, over hundreds of steps, the model will eventually sample from the absurd tail. Increase the temperature, and watch the flat tail rise.

Top-k keeps the $k$ tokens with the highest probability and normalizes again. It cuts the tail, which fixes that problem. But it uses a fixed pool size that ignores the context. Set $k = 5$ in the widget. Then think of two situations. After "the", the model is really uncertain across dozens of possible nouns. After "Alice was beginning t", it is 99% certain of "o". Top-k treats both in the same way.

Nucleus sampling (top-p) keeps the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability is more than $p$. The pool adapts. It is wide where the model is uncertain, and narrow where the model is confident. Decrease $p$ to 0.9, and watch the pool size change as you also change the temperature. That is why top-p at 0.9, with a temperature of approximately 0.8, is the default almost everywhere.

Greedy decoding and the repetition trap If you always take the argmax, generation is deterministic. For open-ended generation, that is fatal. When the model comes back to a state that it visited before, it must give the same continuation forever. The notebook sample at $T = 0.1$ shows this clearly: "the was to go the trees the was on the same to the…". Compare translation, where beam search (a more thorough relative of greedy) really helps. Translation has approximately one correct answer. Storytelling does not. If you search harder for "the most likely continuation", you find bland text.

The KV cache#

The simple generation loop of Chapter 09 wastes work. At step $t$, it runs the full model over all $t$ previous tokens. But their keys and values do not change, because the causal mask makes sure that the representation of a past token never depends on a future one.

A KV cache stores $k$ and $v$ for each layer, and it adds one column at each step. Thus each step processes exactly one token. Generation divides into two phases. Production inference servers describe it in exactly this way:

  • Prefill: run the full prompt through in one batched pass, and fill the cache. This phase is limited by compute. It is parallel and efficient.
  • Decode: one token at a time. Read the cache and extend it. This phase is limited by memory bandwidth. It is sequential, and almost all the time of a long generation goes here.
Key concept — a result the notebook gets "wrong"

On the 0.8M-parameter model of the notebook, the KV cache measures slower than the loop without the cache. That is a real result, not a broken implementation. It teaches more than a clean speedup would.

Count operations, not seconds. Without the cache, each new token pushes 128 positions through the stack. With the cache, it pushes one. The cache does approximately two orders of magnitude less arithmetic. But at this size, each GPU kernel launch costs more than the arithmetic that it does. The version without the cache does its 128 positions in one well-batched call. The cached version makes the same number of very small calls, which are mostly overhead.

The algorithmic saving is real, and it increases linearly with context length. Whether you can see it depends on whether your kernels are large enough to be larger than their own launch overhead. At production scale they are, by a very large amount. That is why each serving stack uses a cache. Optimization results that are true asymptotically but reverse at small scale are common. This is a cheap way to learn not to trust a single benchmark.

The cache also costs memory. It holds $2 \times n_{\text{layer}} \times n_{\text{head}} \times T \times d_k$ floats for each sequence. That increases linearly with context, and with the number of concurrent users. For a large served model, the KV cache, not the weights, decides how many requests you can serve at the same time. That is why methods that make it smaller get so much attention: multi-query attention, grouped-query attention and cache quantization.

What this model is, and is not#

The model of the notebook gets to a validation loss of approximately 1.51 nats. That is a perplexity of 4.5, against a uniform baseline of 73. It has learned spelling, capital letters after full stops, matched quotation marks, and the dialogue punctuation of Carroll. It has learned very little about meaning. That is exactly what 145k characters of training data predict.

The gap between this model and a frontier model is only a matter of quantity. A frontier model has more parameters, much more data, and subword tokenization instead of characters. It also has a post-training phase (instruction tuning, RLHF or DPO) that this course does not cover. The architecture in the notebook is the real architecture. Think about that for a moment. It is really surprising, and it is why the scaling-law literature reads the way it does.

By hand — exercise 10.1

Do causal attention and next-token prediction from start to end, on a three-token sequence with $d_k = 1$ (so each vector is one number).

tokens: "the" "cat" "sat" queries: q = [1.0, 2.0, 1.0] keys: k = [1.0, 1.0, 2.0] values: v = [0.0, 4.0, 8.0] d_k = 1, so the scale factor is 1/√1 = 1 — no scaling to apply. e^0 = 1.000 e^1 = 2.718 e^2 = 7.389 e^{-1} = 0.368
  1. Calculate the full $3 \times 3$ score matrix $q_i k_j$.
  2. Apply the causal mask, then apply softmax to each row.
  3. Calculate the attention output at each of the three positions.
  4. The output of position 3 goes into a language-model head with weight $W = [0.5, -0.5]^\top$ and no bias. This gives two logits for a vocabulary of two words, {"down", "up"}. Calculate the logits and the predicted distribution.
  5. The true next word is "up". Calculate the loss and the gradient on both logits.
Worked solution

1. Entry $(i,j) = q_i k_j$:

k=1.0 k=1.0 k=2.0 q=1.0 1.0 1.0 2.0 q=2.0 2.0 2.0 4.0 q=1.0 1.0 1.0 2.0

2. Mask all entries above the diagonal. Then apply softmax to each row over the entries that stay.

row 1: [1.0, −∞, −∞] → [1.000, 0, 0] row 2: [2.0, 2.0, −∞] → e^2, e^2 tie → [0.500, 0.500, 0] row 3: [1.0, 1.0, 2.0] → [2.718, 2.718, 7.389] / 12.825 → [0.212, 0.212, 0.576]

3. The weighted sums of $v = [0, 4, 8]$:

out₁ = 1.000(0.0) = 0.000 out₂ = 0.500(0.0) + 0.500(4.0) = 2.000 out₃ = 0.212(0.0) + 0.212(4.0) + 0.576(8.0) = 5.456

Position 1 can only return its own value, as exercise 06.1 showed. Position 3 uses itself most (0.576) because its key is the largest. But it really mixes in the earlier context.

4. Apply the head to the scalar 5.456:

z = [0.5 × 5.456, −0.5 × 5.456] = [2.728, −2.728] difference = 5.456, so softmax([2.728, −2.728]) = softmax([5.456, 0]) e^5.456 ≈ 234.1, e^0 = 1 → sum 235.1 ŷ = [0.9957, 0.0043] ("down" 99.6%, "up" 0.4%)

5. The truth is "up", index 1, so $y = [0, 1]$:

L = −ln(0.0043) = 5.45 nats ∂L/∂z = ŷ − y = [0.9957 − 0, 0.0043 − 1] = [+0.996, −0.996]

The loss is 5.45 nats, against a uniform-guess baseline of $\ln 2 = 0.69$. The model is confident and badly wrong. Thus the gradient is close to its maximum magnitude of 1. This is the $\hat{y} - y$ cancellation doing exactly what it was designed to do. No saturation term slows the correction. Note also that the two gradients sum to zero, for the same reason as in exercise 00.19.

By hand — exercise 10.2

Do the sampling arithmetic. Which tokens really stay after each strategy?

probabilities over six tokens, already softmaxed at T = 1: the 0.40 a 0.25 my 0.15 one 0.10 seven 0.07 purple 0.03
  1. Which tokens stay with top-k at $k = 3$? What is the probability of "the" after normalization?
  2. Which tokens stay with top-p at $p = 0.8$? Show the running cumulative sum.
  3. Now suppose that the model is much more certain, with probabilities $[0.97, 0.01, 0.01, 0.005, 0.003, 0.002]$. Which tokens stay with top-k at $k = 3$? Which stay with top-p at $p = 0.8$?
  4. Use part 3 to state, in one sentence, what top-p gives you that top-k cannot.
Worked solution

1. The three highest: the, a, my, with a total of $0.40 + 0.25 + 0.15 = 0.80$. After normalization, "the" becomes $0.40 / 0.80 = \mathbf{0.50}$. Note that the cut makes the tokens that stay more likely. That is a second effect of both methods, and people often miss it.

2. Add from the top until the sum gets to 0.8:

the 0.40 cumulative 0.40 a 0.25 cumulative 0.65 my 0.15 cumulative 0.80 ← reaches p, stop here one 0.10 excluded

These are the same three tokens. On this distribution, the two methods agree by chance.

3. Top-k with $k=3$ keeps the, a, my. That is still exactly three. The second and third have probability 0.01 each, which the model considers almost impossible. Top-p with $p=0.8$ stops at the first token, because 0.97 is already more than 0.8. Thus the pool is {the} alone.

4. Top-p changes the pool size to match the real confidence of the model, wide when the model is really uncertain and as narrow as one token when it is not. Top-k always keeps the same number of candidates. Thus, depending on the distribution, it either lets in almost impossible tokens or discards real ones.

In the wild

Here is the same model in the ecosystem that people will really give you: 

from transformers import GPT2Config, GPT2LMHeadModel

model = GPT2LMHeadModel(GPT2Config(
    vocab_size=50257, n_positions=1024,
    n_embd=768, n_head=12, n_layer=12))

out = model(input_ids, labels=input_ids)   # out.loss is the shift, done for you
model.generate(ids, do_sample=True, temperature=0.8, top_p=0.9,
               use_cache=True)             # your sampling loop and KV cache

Match it to what you built. GPT2Block is your Block. use_cache is your CachedAttention. labels= does the same one-token shift. The config fields are the hyperparameters that you selected by hand. GPT-2 is this notebook at 124M parameters. Think about that. The gap is scale, data and a BPE tokenizer, not architecture.

The library is useful at inference. It gives batched generation, beam search, stopping criteria, quantized loading, and a KV cache that is correct at the boundaries where yours is not (see the block_size assertion in the notebook). Use it. But know what each argument does, because that separates configuring a model from understanding one.

Feel for the numbersMust do

The numbers for language models cover many orders of magnitude. Thus they are easy to quote and difficult to check. These reference values let you tell a possible claim from an impossible one.

QuantityFloorTypicalCeilingRead it as
Char-level perplexity, $V = 73$14–6 trained73 at chanceChapter 10's model lands near 4.5
BPE perplexity, $V \approx 50{,}000$120–4050,257 at chance$\ln 50257 = 10.82$ nats at chance
Training FLOPs—$6ND$—$N$ parameters, $D$ tokens; the 6 is fwd + bwd
Tokens per parameter—≈20—the Chinchilla ratio for compute-optimal training
KV cache per token—$2 \cdot n_{\text{layers}} \cdot d \cdot 2$ bytes—fp16; this is what limits context at serving time
Sampling temperature0 = greedy0.7–1.0$>1.5$ incoherentan inference knob; no gradient passes through it

Now do these on paper. Where you can, do them in your head. You can use a calculator for the logarithms. The goal is to know which number to use.

  1. A BPE model reports a validation loss of 3.0. What is the perplexity? What fraction of the chance-level perplexity is that?
  2. GPT-2 small (124M) trained on 300B tokens. Approximately how many FLOPs is that? Can one person afford it?
  3. Your character model reports a validation perplexity of 1.02. Are you happy?
Answers

1. $e^{3.0} = 20.1$, against a chance perplexity of 50,257. That is approximately 0.04% of it. The model went from fifty thousand possible next tokens to twenty.

2. $6 \times 1.24\times10^{8} \times 3\times10^{11} = 2.2\times10^{20}$ FLOPs. At a realistic 50 TFLOP/s sustained on one good GPU, that is approximately 50 GPU-days. It is expensive, but it does not need an institution. The same formula for a 70B model and 15T tokens gives $6\times10^{24}$. That is four orders of magnitude more, and far out of reach. With that one formula, you can tell the two situations apart without asking anyone.

3. No. Be alarmed. Perplexity 1.02 means that the model is almost perfectly certain of each next character, and no language model should be. Almost certainly, your validation set leaks into training, or you evaluate on the training split.

The habit. Change each loss to perplexity before you quote it, and always give the chance value next to it. A loss without its baseline is not a result.

Say it backRecommended

Explain this to your favorite LLM, in your own words: what actually changes between the translator of Chapter 09 and a decoder-only GPT, and why does the supervision become free? Then ask it to correct you. Ask it to question each part where you were vague, not only the parts where you were wrong, because the gaps are in the vague parts.

What a good answer covers — open this afterwards, not before
  1. The encoder and the cross-attention sublayer are removed. What stays is causally masked self-attention and a feed-forward network.
  2. The target is the input shifted by one. Thus each position is both an input and a label at the same time.
  3. Thus the model needs no labeled pairs. Any text is training data, and that is the source of the scale.
  4. The causal mask makes it legitimate to score each position in one parallel pass, without a position seeing its own answer.
  5. Generation is the same type of process as in Chapter 09: one token at a time, with $O(L^2)$ wasted work if there is no cache.

Most common miss. An answer describes it only as a simpler architecture. The interesting result is economic. Without the encoder, "we need aligned sentence pairs" becomes "we need text". That is the reason these models became large.

Chapter 11 · notebook 11_quantization_and_lora

Quantization, LoRA, and Fitting in Memory#

Each chapter until now assumed that the model fits. This chapter is about what to do when it does not. Its two techniques are the reason that a laptop can run and adapt models that are much too large for it.

The number that decides everything#

Before any technique, do the arithmetic. To train one parameter with Adam in float32, you need four tensors:

TensorBytes per parameter
weight4
gradient4
Adam first moment $m$4
Adam second moment $v$4
total16

That is sixteen bytes for each parameter, plus activations. A model with one billion parameters needs 16 GB before any activation exists. Take the memory of your machine, and subtract what the operating system already uses. Assume that you can really allocate approximately 70% of the rest. Full fine-tuning has a limit of approximately that value divided by sixteen bytes. On most laptops, that is less than a billion parameters.

Inference is very different: 4 bytes for each parameter in fp32, 2 in fp16, and 0.5 at 4-bit. The gap between those two cases is the full subject of this chapter.

Move the parameter count to 7B, and change between the modes. Full fine-tuning is impossible by two orders of magnitude. 4-bit inference is comfortable. Quantization plus LoRA takes you from one to the other.

Quantization#

Represent a tensor of floats with a small set of integer levels at equal spacing. The simplest scheme is symmetric quantization:

$$s = \frac{\max|W|}{2^{b-1}-1} \qquad q = \operatorname{round}(W/s) \qquad \hat{W} = q\cdot s$$
Example — 8-bit, worked
w = [0.00, 0.15, −0.42, 0.98, −0.07, 0.31] max|w| = 0.98, and at 8 bits qmax = 2⁷ − 1 = 127 s = 0.98 / 127 = 0.007717 w w/s q q·s error 0.00 0.0 0 0.0000 0.0000 0.15 19.44 19 0.1466 0.0034 −0.42 −54.42 −54 −0.4167 0.0033 0.98 127.00 127 0.9800 0.0000 −0.07 −9.07 −9 −0.0694 0.0006 0.31 40.17 40 0.3087 0.0013 every error is below s/2 = 0.00386 ✓

Six floats (24 bytes) became six int8 values plus one float scale (10 bytes). The largest weight has no error, because it sets the scale.

Key concept The error is at most $s/2$, and the single largest magnitude in the tensor sets $s$. One outlier weight stretches the grid for each other weight that shares its scale. That one sentence is the reason for almost every technique in modern quantization research.

Turn on the outlier with a wide clip range, and watch the normal weights become coarser. Turn it off, or clip it, and the error becomes very small.

Per-channel scales#

The direct fix is to use one scale for each output row, not one scale for the full tensor. Then an outlier makes only its own row worse.

Example — what the overhead actually costs
a 4096 × 4096 weight matrix = 16,777,216 weights per-tensor : 1 scale = 4 bytes of metadata per-channel : 4096 scales = 16,384 bytes → 0.1% overhead In the notebook's 64 × 128 test with one outlier, per-channel cuts RMSE by roughly 7.5x for 256 bytes on 8,192 weights (3% overhead).

You get a large gain in accuracy for almost no cost. That is why per-channel is the default everywhere. The production version of the same idea is LLM.int8(). It keeps a few outlier channels in fp16 and quantizes everything else.

Where quality actually breaks#

The notebook sweeps bit-widths across the full model and measures validation loss. The shape of the result is consistent across models. Know it before you start to tune:

  • 8-bit costs almost nothing. In the notebook, the loss changes only in the fourth decimal place. That is why int8 inference is routine, not remarkable.
  • 4-bit per-channel has a real cost (0.05 nats in the notebook), but it is usable. Per-tensor at 4 bits costs approximately four times as much. Most quantized models that "run on a laptop" use 4-bit with small groups of weights that share a scale.
  • Below 4 bits, per-tensor quantization fails: at 3 bits it adds 1.1 nats. Per-channel lasts approximately one more bit (0.28 nats at 3 bits), and at 2 bits both schemes fail. The gap between the two schemes increases exactly where you need it most.
Fake quantization The notebook quantizes weights to integers and immediately changes them back to float. This measures the accuracy cost exactly, because it reproduces the numerical error. But it gives neither of the practical benefits, because the tensors and the arithmetic are still float32. To get real memory and speed savings, you need integer kernels that keep the weights packed (torch.ao.quantization, GGML, MLX). Fake quantization is the standard way to answer "is this worth doing?" before you do the engineering. Research papers report it.

LoRA#

Fine-tuning calculates $W' = W + \Delta W$, where $\Delta W$ is a full-size matrix. LoRA assumes that $\Delta W$, the change that adapts a pretrained model, has a much lower intrinsic rank than $W$ itself. Thus it writes $\Delta W$ as a product of two thin matrices:

$$W' = W + \frac{\alpha}{r}BA \qquad B \in \mathbb{R}^{d\times r},\ A \in \mathbb{R}^{r\times d},\ r \ll d$$

Freeze $W$ completely. Train only $A$ and $B$.

Example — the parameter arithmetic
d = 4096, r = 8 full fine-tune : d² = 16,777,216 parameters per matrix LoRA : 2dr = 65,536 parameters per matrix 256x fewer and the optimizer state shrinks by the same factor: full : 16.8M × 12 bytes (grad + m + v) = 201 MB per matrix LoRA : 65k × 12 bytes = 786 KB per matrix

The second block is what really makes this fit in memory. LoRA removes 12 of the 16 bytes for each parameter. You must still store the weights themselves.

Three details that make it work#

$B$ starts at zero. Thus $BA = 0$ at step 0, and the adapted model is exactly the base model. Fine-tuning starts from the pretrained behavior, not from a random change to it. A random change would discard part of what pretraining gave, before the first gradient step.

$A$ starts at random values. If both were zero, the gradient of each one would be proportional to the other, and both would stay zero forever. Exactly one of them can start at zero, and it must be the one on the output side.

The $\alpha/r$ scale keeps the update magnitude approximately constant when $r$ changes. Thus, when you change the rank, you do not have to tune the learning rate again.

Key concept The adapter is a separate, very small file. The base model never changes. Thus one copy of it serves each task, and to change the task you load a few megabytes, not a few gigabytes. That is why adapter-based deployment won. It turns "one fine-tuned model for each customer" from a storage problem into no problem.

The rank sweep, and what it tests#

The main claim of LoRA comes from experiments, not from a proof. Thus test it. The notebook adapts a model trained on Carroll to Shakespeare at ranks 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32. It measures the gain against the unadapted baseline of 2.499 nats:

rank $r$trainableval lossgain% of the $r{=}32$ gain
10.37%2.0990.39958%
20.73%2.0350.46367%
41.46%1.9750.52376%
82.92%1.9160.58385%
165.84%1.8650.63492%
3211.68%1.8100.688100%

Read that honestly. Rank 1, with three thousand parameters (0.37% of the model), already gets much more than half of the benefit. Rank 8 gets 85%, with a quarter of the parameters of rank 32. That strongly supports the low-rank hypothesis. If adaptation really needed a full-rank update, one direction would give almost nothing.

But the curve has not become flat. Rank 32 is clearly better than rank 8, and it shows no sign that it has stopped improving. The honest statement is steep diminishing returns, not saturation. You get most of the benefit cheaply, and you can continue to buy a little more without a limit. Where you stop is a budget decision. It is not a point where more rank stops helping.

Why this regime may flatter high ranks This is a 0.8M-parameter model, adapted for 500 steps between two very different authors. All three of those facts make it need more rank than a realistic setting. A small model has less redundant capacity to use again. A short run has not converged at any rank. A large domain shift is a bigger change than typical fine-tuning. Published results on large models become flat much earlier, because the base already contains most of what the target task needs. Treat the shape of this curve as real, and its exact position as specific to this experiment.

Catastrophic forgetting#

The notebook measures something that is easy to skip. After adaptation to Shakespeare, the model is worse on Alice than it was. Adaptation to a new domain costs performance on the old one. This is not a defect specific to LoRA. Full fine-tuning forgets more.

But it is a strong argument to keep adapters as separate files that you can swap, and not to merge them permanently. If you merge, you trade one capability for another. If you keep them separate, you have both.

QLoRA: both at once#

  1. Quantize the frozen base to 4 bits.
  2. Keep the LoRA adapters in full precision.
  3. Let gradients go through the quantized weights to the adapters.
Key concept — why quantizing a frozen base is safe Quantization error in a frozen base is a fixed bias. The model is only a slightly different, slightly worse fixed function. The adapters train on top of that function, and they can partly compensate for its errors. In a full fine-tune, the weights change at each step. Thus quantization error would come back at each step and interact with the optimizer state. It would accumulate, not stay in one place. Frozen-and-quantized is stable in a way that trainable-and-quantized is not. That asymmetry is the full reason that QLoRA works.

Nothing must backpropagate into the quantized values, only through them. At the scale of the notebook, the memory saving is very small. At 7B parameters, it is 28 GB against 3.5 GB. On the machine that this course targets, that is the difference between impossible and routine.

What actually runs you out of memory#

Here is a result from the notebook that you should remember, because it is the opposite of what most people expect. For a 0.8M-parameter model, here is the activation memory at different sequence lengths. The model has 4 layers and 4 heads, and the batch is 64 sequences. Each head in each layer stores its own $L \times L$ attention matrix:

Sequence lengthHidden statesAttention matricesTotal
12817 MB67 MB84 MB
51267 MB1.07 GB1.14 GB
2048268 MB17.2 GB17.4 GB
4096537 MB68.7 GB69.3 GB

Hidden states increase linearly. Attention increases quadratically and becomes the largest part by far. At 4096 tokens, this 0.8-million-parameter model needs more memory than the full machine has. But the model itself is 3 MB. The parameter count has nothing to do with the memory problem.

That is why flash attention and sliding-window attention exist. (Flash attention tiles the calculation, so it never stores the $L \times L$ matrix.) For long-context work, they are more important than any weight-compression technique.

The rest of the toolkit#

TechniqueSavesCosts
Mixed precision (bf16)~50% memory, faster matmulsless mature on MPS than CUDA
Gradient checkpointingactivations by ~√N~30% extra compute
Gradient accumulationeffective batch sizewall-clock time
Flash attentionthe $L^2$ matrix entirelynothing — use it
Distillationeverything, permanentlya full training run
Structured pruningreal dense speedupaccuracy, and retraining

In production code, use F.scaled_dot_product_attention, not an attention that you wrote by hand. It uses a flash implementation where one exists. Chapter 06 writes attention by hand so that you understand it. If you ship the hand-written version, you lose performance.

By hand — exercise 11.1 · quantize a vector
w = [0.10, −0.30, 0.80, −0.05, 0.45] Quantize symmetrically to 4 bits, so qmax = 2³ − 1 = 7.
  1. Calculate the scale $s$.
  2. Calculate $q$ for each weight. Round to the nearest integer.
  3. Dequantize, and calculate the error on each weight.
  4. Make sure that each error is at most $s/2$.
  5. Now add an outlier of 8.0, and calculate $s$ again. What is the new quantized value of the original 0.10? How much worse is its error?
Worked solution

1. $\max|w| = 0.80$, so $s = 0.80/7 = \mathbf{0.11429}$.

2 & 3.

w w/s q q·s error 0.10 0.875 1 0.1143 0.0143 −0.30 −2.625 −3 −0.3429 0.0429 0.80 7.000 7 0.8000 0.0000 −0.05 −0.437 0 0.0000 0.0500 0.45 3.937 4 0.4571 0.0071

4. $s/2 = 0.0571$, and the largest error is 0.0500 ✓. Note that $-0.05$ quantized to zero. At 4 bits, small weights disappear completely. With many such weights, this is a real loss of information. It is one reason that 4-bit needs per-channel scales to work at all.

5. With the outlier, $\max|w| = 8.0$ and $s = 8.0/7 = 1.1429$. That is ten times larger.

0.10 / 1.1429 = 0.0875 → rounds to q = 0 → ŵ = 0.0000 error = 0.10, up from 0.0143 — 7x worse and −0.30, 0.45 also collapse to 0. Four of the five original weights are now identically zero.

One unrelated weight destroyed the representation of each other weight. This is the outlier problem at its most extreme. It is exactly why per-channel scales (which would isolate the outlier in its own row) are not optional at low bit-widths.

By hand — exercise 11.2 · LoRA budgets

A transformer has 12 layers and $d_{\text{model}} = 768$. You adapt the four attention projections ($W^Q, W^K, W^V, W^O$) in each layer.

  1. How many parameters are in those projections in total?
  2. With LoRA at $r = 8$, how many parameters do you train? What percentage is that?
  3. Compare the optimizer memory (gradient + $m$ + $v$, 12 bytes for each trainable parameter) for full fine-tuning and for LoRA.
  4. You want to serve 50 customers, each with their own adapter. How much storage do 50 full fine-tunes need, and how much do 50 adapters need, at 4 bytes for each parameter? (Use 110M parameters for the full model.)
Worked solution

1. Each projection is $768 \times 768 = 589{,}824$. There are four in each layer, over 12 layers:

589,824 × 4 × 12 = 28,311,552 ≈ 28.3M parameters

2. Each LoRA pair is $2dr = 2(768)(8) = 12{,}288$:

12,288 × 4 × 12 = 589,824 trainable parameters 589,824 / 28,311,552 = 2.08% of the adapted projections 589,824 / 110,000,000 = 0.54% of the whole model

3.

full : 28.3M × 12 bytes = 340 MB LoRA : 0.59M × 12 bytes = 7 MB 48x less

Note that this is only the optimizer state. The frozen weights still use their 440 MB in fp32. QLoRA attacks that next.

4.

50 full fine-tunes : 50 × 110M × 4 bytes = 22.0 GB 50 LoRA adapters : 1 × 110M × 4 = 440 MB (shared base) + 50 × 0.59M × 4 = 118 MB = 558 MB 39x less

The practical difference is larger than the ratio shows. With adapters, the base model stays in memory, and a change of customer costs a 2.4 MB load. 50 full models cannot all be in memory at the same time, so each change is a 440 MB load. That is the real reason that adapter-based serving won.

By hand — exercise 11.3 · will it fit?

You need only multiplication. You have 17 GB of usable memory.

  1. Can you do a full fine-tune of a 1.5B-parameter model with Adam in fp32?
  2. Can you run inference on it in fp16?
  3. Can you do a LoRA fine-tune of it, with an fp16 frozen base and $r=8$ adapters on 1% of the weights? (Assume that activations add 30% of the size of the base weights.)
  4. Which single change gives the most: a 4-bit base, gradient checkpointing, or half the sequence length? State what you would need to know to answer correctly.
Worked solution

1. $1.5\text{B} \times 16 = \mathbf{24\text{ GB}}$ for weights, gradients and Adam state, before activations. No, and not by a small amount.

2. $1.5\text{B} \times 2 = 3\text{ GB}$ of weights, plus the KV cache and activations. That is approximately 3.5 GB. Yes, easily.

3.

frozen base fp16 : 1.5B × 2 = 3.00 GB LoRA weights : 15M × 4 = 0.06 GB LoRA grad + m + v : 15M × 12 = 0.18 GB activations (~30%) : = 0.90 GB ─────── 4.14 GB yes, easily

It goes from 24 GB (impossible) to 4.1 GB (routine), because you freeze the base and make the optimizer state smaller.

4. It depends on which term is largest. You cannot answer without the sequence length and the batch size. In part 3, the weights are largest, at 3.0 GB against 0.9 GB of activations. Thus 4-bit is the best single change (3.0 → 0.75 GB). But at a long sequence length, the attention matrices are larger than everything else. Remember the table above: a 3 MB model needed 69 GB of activations at 4096 tokens. There, half the sequence length gives a quadratic saving that nothing else can match. Measure before you optimize. The correct answer reverses, depending on a number that nobody has told you.

In the wild

You implemented both techniques from their definitions. Here are the same two ideas as one-line calls, and what each library adds to your version. 

# quantization — PyTorch native, CPU only, and you must pick a backend first
import torch.ao.quantization as tq
torch.backends.quantized.engine = 'qnnpack'   # 'none' by default on Apple silicon
qmodel = tq.quantize_dynamic(model, {nn.Linear}, dtype=torch.qint8)

# LoRA — the peft library, the de facto standard
from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model
model = get_peft_model(base, LoraConfig(
    r=8, lora_alpha=16, target_modules=["qkv", "proj"], lora_dropout=0.05))
model.print_trainable_parameters()   # your `trainable / total` line
model.save_pretrained("adapter/")    # a few MB, not a few GB
YoursProductionWhat it adds
quantize_symmetrictorch.ao.quantizationreal int8 kernels, so the memory and speed savings are actual rather than simulated
per-channel scalesbitsandbytes LLM.int8()keeps outlier channels in fp16 — the production form of your outlier experiment
4-bit fake quantNF4 (QLoRA), GPTQ, AWQa non-uniform grid matched to a normal distribution; calibration on real activations
LoRALinearpeftadapter save/load/merge, hot-swapping, and every layer type
fake quant + LoRAQLoRA in bitsandbytes+peftpaged optimizers and double quantization of the scales themselves

Here are three honest notes. We found all of them when we ran this code. First, torch.ao.quantization needs an explicit backend. On this build, the engine is 'none' by default. If you do not set it, the first quantized operation fails with NoQEngine, and that error does not clearly mean "select a backend". Second, the module is deprecated in current PyTorch, and the separate torchao package replaces it. Read its migration notes before you build on it.

Third, bitsandbytes is CUDA-first. It will not give you 4-bit kernels on Apple silicon at all. Here, MLX and llama.cpp/GGUF are what really work. The pattern in all three notes is the same lesson as the KV cache in Chapter 10: a technique that works is not necessarily a technique that works on your hardware. We built these by hand for a practical reason. When a 4-bit model becomes worse, the useful question is "which tensor has the outlier, and is my grid per-channel?". You cannot ask that question if quantization is only a flag that you passed.

Feel for the numbersMust do

In this chapter, arithmetic decides whether something runs at all. You should be able to give each number here on a whiteboard when someone asks if a model will fit.

QuantityFloorTypicalCeilingRead it as
7B weights, fp32—26.1 GiB—weights alone, before anything else
7B weights, fp16/bf16—13.0 GiB—the usual serving default
7B weights, int8—6.5 GiB—fits a 16 GB laptop with room to work
7B weights, int4—3.3 GiB—QLoRA territory
int8 range$-128$—127symmetric quantization uses $-127..127$
LoRA $r=8$ on a $768^2$ matrix—2.08%—$2rd$ against $d^2$
Adam optimizer states—2× the trainable params—why freezing the base model saves more than it looks

Now do these on paper. Where you can, do them in your head. You can use a calculator for the logarithms. The goal is to know which number to use.

  1. You have a 16 GB laptop. Which of those four precisions fit the weights of a 7B model? What did you forget to include in the budget?
  2. LoRA at $r = 16$ on a $768 \times 768$ matrix. What fraction of the original is that? What fraction of the optimizer state?
  3. Why does the $B$ matrix of LoRA start at zero while $A$ is random? What would happen if both were random?
Answers

1. fp32 is not close. fp16 at 13.0 GiB fits on paper, but it is a trap. It leaves approximately 3 GB for the operating system, your editor and all the activations. In practice, it will not run. int8 at 6.5 GiB and int4 at 3.3 GiB are the two that really work. You forgot: activations, the KV cache (which increases with context and batch), gradients and optimizer states if you train, and fragmentation, which makes the practical limit lower than the arithmetic limit. The measurement in this chapter shows that sequence length, not parameter count, is usually what really uses all the budget.

2. $2 \times 16 \times 768 = 24{,}576$ against $768^2 = 589{,}824$, so 4.17%. But the saving in optimizer state is larger. Adam keeps two moments for each trainable parameter. Thus, when you freeze the base model, you also remove approximately 96% of that state. That is why LoRA decreases memory much more than the parameter fraction suggests.

3. So that $BA = 0$ at step 0, and the adapted model is exactly the base model. Thus training starts from the pretrained function, not from a random change to it. If both were random, the adapter would add noise to each layer before it learned anything. That is exactly the damage that fine-tuning must prevent. If both were zero, it would be even worse. The gradient to $A$ is proportional to $B$, so nothing would ever move.

The habit. Before you ask whether a model is good enough, find out whether it fits. Bytes for each parameter times the parameter count is thirty seconds of arithmetic. It rules out most proposals immediately.

Say it backRecommended

Explain this to your favorite LLM, in your own words: quantization and LoRA both make a model cheaper. What is each one actually trading away, and why do they compose? Then ask it to correct you. Ask it to question each part where you were vague, not only the parts where you were wrong, because the gaps are in the vague parts.

What a good answer covers — open this afterwards, not before
  1. Quantization gives up precision. It stores the same parameters in fewer bits, and it accepts the rounding error that results.
  2. LoRA gives up expressiveness. It freezes the parameters and learns a low-rank correction. Thus the model can make only changes inside that subspace.
  3. Thus one decreases the cost of having the weights, and the other decreases the cost of changing them. These are different budgets, and that is why they stack.
  4. QLoRA keeps a quantized frozen base and trains full-precision adapters on top. Thus the optimizer never accumulates the rounding error.
  5. Both assume that the part that they discard (low-order bits, high-rank directions) carried little of what was important. Both assumptions come from experiments. Neither is guaranteed.

Most common miss. An answer describes both as "making the model smaller". They decrease different quantities. If an explanation does not separate storage from adaptation, it cannot explain why the combination helps.

  • Implement LoRALinear, and verify its zero-init property.
  • Adapt a model trained on Carroll to Shakespeare, and train less than 3% of its parameters.
  • Run a rank sweep.
  • Combine both techniques into QLoRA.

Chapter 12 · notebook 12_capstone_projects

Capstone Projects#

Each chapter until now gave you an architecture and asked you to complete it. This chapter gives you five specifications and no solutions. There is a gap between "I finished the tutorial" and "I can build this". These projects exist to close exactly that gap.

How to choose, and how to scope#

Select one project and finish it correctly. A completed translator teaches more than five prototypes that are half built. The last 20% is evaluation, error analysis and the honest write-up. That is where you learn the things that you will remember.

Each project below has a minimum viable version and a set of extensions. Make the minimum work from start to end before you touch an extension. This is not only good discipline. A working baseline is the only thing that tells you whether an extension helped.

Key concept — scoping

These projects usually do not fail because they are difficult. They fail because someone builds three components, never connects them, and has nothing to show. First, build the ugliest possible pipeline from start to end: hard-coded hyperparameters, a very small subset of the data and no evaluation. Get one bad output from the far end. Then improve it.

Here is a specific version for any model that generates. Get one sequence out, however bad, before you tune anything. Generation bugs hide completely behind a good loss curve: the teacher-forcing shift, an <EOS> that never comes, an off-by-one error in position indexing. If you find them after a long training run, it is very discouraging.

Project 1 — A translator#

Builds on 06, 08, 09.

Beat the Chapter 09 baseline on English→French. Be able to say why with a number, not an impression. The minimum is an encoder–decoder transformer trained with teacher forcing, greedy decoding, and a corpus BLEU score on a held-out set.

Here are the most valuable extensions, approximately in sequence:

  • Beam search. It is worth 1–3 BLEU. Remember length normalization, or the model will prefer short outputs.
  • Subword tokenization. This attacks the real problem: a word-level vocabulary gives many <UNK>s on French morphology.
  • Label smoothing at 0.1. It is standard in translation for a reason.
  • Length bucketing from Chapter 03. It gives free speed.

Expect overfitting, because the filtered corpus has fewer than 10,000 pairs. Thus use best-checkpoint restore from the first run. Do not wait to add it after you see the problem.

Project 2 — A text generator#

Builds on 04, 10.

Train a language model on an author that you select, and generate text in a style that people can recognize as theirs. The minimum is a decoder-only transformer, a recorded validation perplexity, and four sampling configurations compared next to each other.

The first real judgment call is characters or words. The notebook gives you a survey of the corpus to help you decide. Below approximately 200k characters, word-level vocabularies overfit almost immediately. Above approximately 1M, word-level trains much faster, because each token carries more information.

Evaluating a generator honestly Perplexity measures next-token prediction, not quality. A model can have excellent perplexity and generate boring text. The two are most different at exactly the settings that you would want to ship. Use three signals together: perplexity for calibration, distinct_n for repetition, and your own reading of twenty samples. The third is not optional, and you cannot automate it away.

Project 3 — A domain-adapted assistant#

Builds on 10, 11.

Train one base model. Then make several specialized variants as LoRA adapters, and show hot-swapping. Load the base one time, attach adapter A, generate, detach it, and attach adapter B. This is how adapter-based deployment really works. When you build it one time, the full approach becomes concrete in a way that reading cannot give you.

One design decision is more important than the others: train the base on a corpus outside all three target domains. If the base trains on the same data that you adapt to, the experiment cannot show what the adapters add. The base already knows each domain. If it also saw your test text, each perplexity looks better than it really is. The notebook suggests a neutral corpus for exactly this reason.

The most interesting extension is the forgetting matrix: the perplexity of each adapter on each domain, also the domains that it did not train on. It shows catastrophic forgetting as a number, not as a warning. It is also the clearest reason to keep adapters separate and not merge them.

The question worth sitting with In Chapter 11, an adapter is approximately 100 KB, and the base is 3.3 MB. A full fine-tune stores a full model for each task, but LoRA stores almost nothing. So what is really in that 100 KB, and why is it enough? The honest answer connects back to the rank sweep of Chapter 11. Almost all of what the model knows is already in the base. Adaptation is a small, low-rank adjustment of capabilities that it already has.

Project 4 — An architecture bake-off#

Builds on 03–08.

Compare the bag-of-embeddings baseline, an LSTM and a transformer on one task. Make the conditions fair enough that the result means something. This project is not the most difficult technically. It needs the most rigor, and that is the point.

Two requirements make it worth doing:

  • Matched parameter counts, within approximately 10%. If they do not match, you compare capacity, not architecture. The notebook gives a binary-search helper for exactly this.
  • Three random seeds, with the standard deviation reported.
Why three seeds is the minimum On 2,000 movie reviews, the seed alone frequently changes accuracy by ±2%. If architecture A beats B by 1% on one run, you measured noise and reported it as a result. This failure is not hypothetical. It is the most common error in informal ML comparisons, and it costs almost nothing to prevent.

The most useful extension is the learning-curve study. Train each architecture again at 10%, 25%, 50% and 100% of the training data. The ranking will probably change with dataset size. Try to understand why. The transformer has the weakest inductive bias, so it needs the most data. The baseline does not model order at all. That is a very strong prior, and it stops hurting only when there is enough data to learn order from. This study connects Chapter 03 and Chapter 08 better than either chapter does alone.

Project 5 — Reproduce a paper#

Builds on everything, plus the reading guide.

This project builds most directly the skill that the others only approach. Take a published result, implement it again, and write what you found. It is also the clearest thing that you can show to someone who evaluates your work. It shows three skills at the same time: reading, implementing and honest reporting.

Select something small and self-contained that this course has prepared you for. Here are good candidates, approximately in sequence of effort:

PaperClaim to reproduceWhy it is tractable here
Iyyer et al. (2015), deep unordered compositionaveraged embeddings plus depth rival far more complex models on sentimentCh. 03 is the shallow version of exactly this
Holtzman et al. (2019), nucleus samplingtop-p beats beam search on repetition metricsyour Ch. 10 model plus distinct_n
LoRA (2021), §7.2low rank suffices; rank beyond a point adds littlethe rank sweep in Ch. 11, extended
Xiong et al. (2020), pre-normpost-norm needs warmup; pre-norm does notone flag in your Ch. 08/10 block, two training runs
Press & Wolf (2017), weight tyingtying improves perplexity, not just sizeone line in your Ch. 10 GPT

The method#

  1. State the claim as a number before you start. You can test "pre-norm trains stably at a learning rate where post-norm diverges". You cannot test "pre-norm is better".
  2. Implement from the paper, not from someone's code. If you cannot continue, that is the interesting part. Write exactly which detail the paper did not specify. Each paper has several.
  3. Reproduce at your scale, not theirs. You test whether the mechanism works. You do not try to match a number from a thousand GPUs. Say this explicitly in the write-up.
  4. Run three seeds, and report the spread. Half of the failed reproductions are really seed variance.
  5. Write it in two pages: the claim, your setup, the result with error bars, where you did something different from the paper, and what you could not test.
Key concept — the most valuable outcome is not "it worked"

A reproduction that confirms the claim is satisfactory. Sometimes a reproduction finds that the claim is true only under conditions that the paper did not state. That result is much more valuable, and it is common. Examples are sensitivity to the learning rate, to the initialization, to the dataset size, or to a preprocessing detail in an appendix.

That is a real contribution. You can publish it as a blog post or a workshop note. It is exactly the type of work that shows judgment, not only output. Write it carefully and generously. The goal is to inform, not to win a point against the authors.

The checklist#

Most of the items below are failures that look like successes. Thus check them deliberately. Do not trust that you would see them.

StageCheckWhy it matters
DataVocabulary built from the training split onlythe classic leak; inflates every number
Ten examples decoded from the tensors and readcatches encoding bugs nothing else will
<UNK> rate measureda high rate caps quality regardless of model
ModelInitial loss ≈ $\ln(\text{n classes})$one forward pass; catches bad init
Eight examples overfitted to ~zero lossproves the pipeline can learn at all
TrainingBest checkpoint restored, not the lastval loss often turns up long before the end
Learning rate printed for the first epochsschedulers fail silently
EvaluationTest set touched exactly oncerepeated peeking is slow-motion overfitting
Three seeds, standard deviation reportedotherwise you are reporting noise
A baseline to compare against"80% accuracy" means nothing alone
ReportingA statement of what you cannot concludethe difference between a result and a claim

After this#

The course ends here. But the material clearly continues in several directions, and you are now ready for all of them.

  • Subword tokenization. Implement BPE from scratch. It is the last major component of a modern language model that this course does not build.
  • RLHF and DPO. This is how a base language model becomes an assistant. It is a different idea from everything here, and it is the natural next step after Chapter 10.
  • Retrieval augmentation. Embed a corpus, retrieve by nearest neighbor, and condition generation on what you retrieved.
  • MLX. This is the array framework of Apple, designed around unified memory. If you implement the GPT of Chapter 10 again in it, you see clearly what PyTorch hides from you.
  • The papers. Attention Is All You Need (2017), LoRA (2021) and QLoRA (2023) are all easy to read now, in a way that they were not before Chapter 00. You have implemented most of what they describe.
Say it backRecommended

Explain this to your favorite LLM, in your own words: what does your capstone actually show, and where would a skeptical reader attack it first? Then ask it to correct you. Ask it to question each part where you were vague, not only the parts where you were wrong, because the gaps are in the vague parts.

What a good answer covers — open this afterwards, not before
  1. What the model maps to what, in shapes: the inputs, the outputs, and what one training example really is.
  2. Why you used that loss for that output type, in one sentence, with the distribution that it assumes.
  3. What the baseline is, and what it scores. Not "a simple model", but a number, from a baseline that you tuned at least a little.
  4. What result would have proved your claim false. State it before you look at whether it did.
  5. What you cannot conclude from what you ran: the confound that you did not control, the seed variance that you did not measure, the split that you used again.

Most common miss. Each version of this that skips the last point. A project that cannot name its own limitation is not modest. It is not finished. And a skeptical reader will find that limitation first.

Back matter

Appendix#

This appendix collects reference material in one place: notation, tensor-shape conventions, a glossary, and the failures that you will really see. After that, three sections look past the end of the course. From scratch to the library maps each component that you built by hand to its production equivalent. Reading the literature shows how to find the real contribution of a paper. The modern stack covers the approximately eight changes between the transformer of Chapter 08 and a current frontier model. You can read all of them with the mathematics that you now have.

Making it fast on Apple silicon#

Unified memory is the defining feature of Apple Silicon. The CPU and the GPU share one pool. Thus .to('mps') costs much less than a PCIe transfer to a discrete GPU. But it also means that your model shares the same pool with the operating system and everything else. There is no separate VRAM value to watch. A discrete NVIDIA card gives you a fixed budget that is only yours, and it tells you when you go over it.

  • Measure before you optimize. MPS is asynchronous. Thus, if you time a forward pass with a clock, you measure only the queueing. Call torch.mps.synchronize() before you stop the clock.
  • Batch size is the first control. Small models are limited by launch overhead. A change from batch 16 to 128 frequently costs almost no time and gives a large gain in throughput.
  • Watch for silent CPU fallback. With PYTORCH_ENABLE_MPS_FALLBACK=1, operations without MPS support run on the CPU. The result is correct, but each one forces a synchronization. One fallback operation in your inner loop can cost more than everything else together.
  • torch.compile is not the answer here. Its MPS support is much less mature than its CUDA support. At these model sizes, it usually costs more in compile time than it gives back.
  • float16 halves memory, and MPS supports it well. But the Apple backend does not have the mature autocast and GradScaler support that CUDA has. Use float16 freely for inference. For training, treat it as an experiment (see Chapter 11).

LetterDimensionTypical
$B$batch size32–128
$L$, $T$, $S$sequence length (input / target / source)16–512
$C$, $d$channels / features / model width64–768
$V$vocabulary size60–50,000
$H$number of attention heads4–16

Shapes through each architecture#

LayerInOutWatch for
nn.Linear(i, o)(B, …, i)(B, …, o)weight is stored (o, i)
nn.Embedding(V, d)(B, L) ints(B, L, d)set padding_idx
nn.Conv1d(c, f, k)(B, c, L)(B, f, L−k+1)channels before length — transpose
nn.LSTM(i, h)(B, L, i)(B, L, h), $(h_n, c_n)$needs batch_first=True
Multi-head attention(B, L, d)(B, L, d)internally (B, H, L, d/H)
Attention weights—(B, H, L, L)quadratic in $L$ — the memory hog
nn.LayerNorm(d)(…, d)(…, d)normalizes the last dim only
CrossEntropyLoss(N, C), (N,)scalarreshape sequences to (B·L, V)

The output-size formula#

$$L_{\text{out}} = \left\lfloor\frac{L_{\text{in}} + 2p - k}{s}\right\rfloor + 1$$

Here $p$ is the padding, $k$ is the kernel size and $s$ is the stride. With $p = 0$ and $s = 1$, it is $L - k + 1$. Set $p = (k-1)/2$ with an odd $k$ and $s = 1$, and the length stays exactly the same. This is "same" padding.

Glossary#

AutogradPyTorch's automatic differentiation. Records operations into a graph during the forward pass, traverses it in reverse on backward(). Ch. 02
BackpropagationThe chain rule applied layer by layer, caching intermediate results. Not a separate algorithm from the chain rule. Ch. 01
BLEU$n$-gram overlap metric for translation, with a brevity penalty. Blunt but comparable. Ch. 09
BroadcastingAutomatic stretching of size-1 dimensions to match. Convenient; a rich source of silent bugs. Ch. 00
Causal maskUpper-triangular $-\infty$ added before the softmax so position $t$ cannot see the future. Ch. 09
Cross-attentionQ from the decoder, K and V from encoder memory. The bridge in a seq2seq model. Ch. 09
Cross-entropy$-\sum p\log q$; the negative log-likelihood of a categorical model. Ch. 00
DropoutRandomly zero activations during training, scaling survivors. Off at eval. Ch. 03
EmbeddingLearned dense vector per token; a lookup table equivalent to a linear layer on a one-hot. Ch. 03
Exposure biasA model trained on perfect prefixes has never seen its own mistakes and cannot recover from them. Ch. 09
Gradient clippingRescale the gradient vector if its norm exceeds a threshold. Fixes explosion, not vanishing. Ch. 04
KV cacheStored keys and values so each generation step processes one token instead of $t$. Ch. 10
Layer normNormalize across features within one token. Batch-size independent, unlike batch norm. Ch. 08
LogitA raw unbounded score before softmax or sigmoid. Pass these to the loss, not probabilities. Ch. 00
LoRAFreeze $W$, train a low-rank $BA$ alongside it. $B$ starts at zero. Ch. 11
Nucleus (top-p)Sample from the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds $p$. Ch. 10
Perplexity$e^{\mathcal{L}}$: the effective number of choices the model is deciding between. Ch. 00
Positional encodingPosition information added to embeddings, because attention is order-blind. Ch. 08
Pre-norm / post-normWhether LayerNorm sits inside or outside the residual path. Pre-norm trains deeper, more stably. Ch. 10
QuantizationRepresenting weights on a coarse integer grid. Error is bounded by half the step size. Ch. 11
Residual connection$x + F(x)$. Gives gradients an unobstructed additive path to every layer. Ch. 08
FlashAttentionTiled attention with an online softmax; the $L\times L$ matrix is never materialized, so memory is linear in $L$. Modern stack
GQA / MQAHeads share key/value projections, in groups or entirely. Shrinks the KV cache, which is what limits concurrent users. Modern stack
GRPOGroup Relative Policy Optimization: preference optimization without a value network, normalizing advantages within a sampled group. Used for reasoning training. Modern stack
MLAMulti-head latent attention: cache a low-rank latent instead of full K and V. Chapter 11's factorization, applied to the cache. Modern stack
MoEMixture of experts: many feed-forward blocks, a router picking top-$k$ per token. Total parameters grow; active parameters do not. Modern stack
RMSNormLayerNorm without the mean subtraction or shift — scale only. Modern stack
RoPERotary position embedding: rotate $q$ and $k$ by an angle proportional to position, making the dot product depend on relative offset. Ch. 08
Speculative decodingA small draft model proposes tokens; the large model verifies them in one parallel pass. Same output distribution, faster. Modern stack
SwiGLUA gated feed-forward block — the LSTM gating idea applied to the MLP. Better per parameter. Modern stack
SoftmaxLogits to a distribution. Invariant to adding a constant — which is why you subtract the max. Ch. 00
Teacher forcingFeed the ground-truth prefix during training rather than the model's own output. Ch. 09
TemperatureDivide logits before softmax: below 1 sharpens, above 1 flattens. Never changes the ranking. Ch. 04
Vanishing gradientA product of many sub-1 factors decaying geometrically with depth or time. Ch. 04
Weight tyingSharing the embedding matrix with the output head. Saves parameters, usually improves quality. Ch. 10

Apple silicon notes#

These notes are specific to Apple Silicon. They apply when PyTorch selects the Metal backend, which each notebook does automatically on an M-series Mac. If you use CUDA or the CPU, this section does not apply to you, and nothing in the course changes. We lost time to find each one.

MPS silently returns zeros for out-of-range embedding indices

This is the most dangerous problem in the backend. It caused a real bug while we wrote Chapter 10. Cached generation went past block_size, so the code used an index for pos_emb that was out of range. 

e = nn.Embedding(128, 8)
e(torch.tensor([200]))                            # cpu : IndexError
e.to('mps')(torch.tensor([200], device='mps'))    # mps : a row of zeros

The model continued to run with a zero position embedding. It gave fluent text for a hundred tokens, and then it changed to noise. There was no error and no warning. Nothing showed in the loss, because it occurs at inference time. When the MPS output looks wrong but the CPU output does not, run it again on the CPU. That is the fastest way to change a silent corruption into a stack trace.

  • nn.LSTM dropout is broken. With dropout>0, a stacked nn.LSTM on MPS does not apply random dropout and fails to train (PyTorch 2.12). nn.RNN and nn.GRU are not affected. Train that model on the CPU, or set dropout=0. See Chapter 05.
  • float64 has no support. A dtype=torch.float64 fails when you move it to MPS. Use float32 by default.
  • Quantization needs an explicit engine. torch.backends.quantized.engine is 'none' by default here. Thus quantize_dynamic fails with Didn't find engine for operation quantized::linear_prepack NoQEngine until you set it to 'qnnpack'. That is the one backend that this platform supports. Note also that torch.ao.quantization is deprecated, and the separate torchao package replaces it.
  • The FlashAttention backend is CUDA-only. F.scaled_dot_product_attention is still the correct call. It is correct, and it is never much slower. But on MPS, it uses a math or memory-efficient fallback, not a flash kernel. Thus do not expect the published speedups. The notebook of Chapter 10 measures this: the fused path is not measurably faster here, but the memory argument is true on each backend. Keep the general habit. When a library advertises a speedup, check that the fast path exists on your hardware before you give it credit.
  • Time it correctly. MPS is asynchronous. Thus, if you time a forward pass with a clock, you measure the queueing, not the work. Call torch.mps.synchronize() before you stop the clock.
  • MPS can be slower than the CPU on very small models. With only a few examples, the overhead to launch each kernel is larger than the work. The benefit starts at Chapter 03.
  • Watch for silent CPU fallback. With PYTORCH_ENABLE_MPS_FALLBACK=1, an operation without MPS support runs on the CPU. The result is correct, but each occurrence forces a synchronization. One such operation in an inner loop can cost more than everything else together.
  • num_workers=0 is frequently fastest in notebooks. macOS spawns workers and does not fork them. Thus each worker imports your module again.
  • pin_memory=True does nothing useful on unified memory.
  • torch.compile is not worth it here. Its MPS support is less mature than its CUDA support. At these model sizes, it usually costs more in compile time than it gives back.

Rules of thumb#

Initial lossshould be $\approx \ln(\text{n classes})$
Training memory16 bytes per parameter with Adam in fp32
Inference memory4 (fp32) / 2 (fp16) / 0.5 (int4) bytes per parameter
Adam learning rate1e-3 for small models; 1e-4–3e-4 for transformers, with warmup
Transformer FFN width$4 \times d_{\text{model}}$
Attention heads8 or 16; free in parameters, nearly free in compute
Gradient clippingmax_norm=1.0 for any sequence model
Sampling defaultstemperature 0.8, top-p 0.9
LoRA rank4–8 covers most adaptation; higher buys little
Quantization8-bit is free; 4-bit per-channel is usable; below that, per-tensor collapses
Seeds before believing a resultthree, minimum

From scratch to the library#

Each component that this course builds by hand has a production equivalent. When you build it yourself, that is not an argument against the library. It lets you use the library well, because you know what each argument does and what fails when it is wrong. Here is the map:

You builtCh.Production equivalentWhat the library adds
manual backward pass01loss.backward()arbitrary graphs, fused stable kernels
manual SGD update01optim.AdamWper-parameter step sizes, decoupled decay
word vocabulary + <UNK>03tokenizers (BPE)no unknown tokens; any byte string encodes
scaled dot-product attention06F.scaled_dot_product_attentionFlashAttention — the $L^2$ matrix is never materialized
MultiHeadAttention06nn.MultiheadAttentionfused projections, key-padding masks
encoder block08nn.TransformerEncoderLayernorm_first, nested-tensor fast paths
seq2seq model09nn.Transformerboth stacks, mask helpers
training loop10accelerate, Lightningmulti-GPU, mixed precision, checkpoint resume
GPT + sampling + KV cache10transformersgenerate(), beam search, correct cache edges
quantize_symmetric11torchao (or legacy torch.ao.quantization)real int8 kernels — actual savings, not simulated; needs an engine set
per-channel scales11bitsandbytes LLM.int8()outlier channels kept in fp16
4-bit fake quant11NF4, GPTQ, AWQnon-uniform grids, activation-aware calibration
LoRALinear11peftsave/load/merge, hot-swap, every layer type
On Apple silicon specifically bitsandbytes is CUDA-first, and it will not give you 4-bit kernels here. On an M-series Mac, two stacks really give quantized inference: MLX (the array framework of Apple, designed around unified memory) and llama.cpp / GGUF. Both are worth an afternoon. If you implement the GPT of Chapter 10 again in MLX, you see very clearly what PyTorch hides from you.

Reading the literature#

You did the mathematics by hand so that papers become readable. Most machine-learning papers are short. Usually, the contribution is one equation, with experiments around it. Here is how to find it.

A reading order#

  1. Read the abstract, then the figures, then the conclusions. The figures usually carry the real claim. After this, if you cannot state the claim in one sentence, the paper may not be worth a full reading.
  2. Find the one equation. Almost each architecture paper has one new expression. You already know the rest. Find that expression, and write its shapes. If the shapes do not combine, you read it wrong. That occurs more frequently than a wrong paper.
  3. Ask what resource it saves. Almost each modern contribution trades one of these: parameters, activation memory, KV-cache memory, FLOPs per token, wall-clock time or data. When you name which one, that usually explains the full design.
  4. Read the ablations before the main table. The main table compares with the models of other people, and scale and data confound it. The ablation compares with the authors' own model with one thing removed. That is the only controlled comparison in the paper.
  5. Check what the paper does not report. Missing seeds, missing error bars, a baseline that got less tuning than the method, and evaluation on the set used for model selection are all common. Each one decides whether you can trust the result.
Key concept — the shape check

When the notation is too difficult, change it to shapes. Different authors use different notation, but tensor shapes are always the same. "Project the input to a latent of dimension $d_c$, then up-project per head" is ambiguous as prose. When you write it as (B, L, d) → (B, L, d_c) → (B, H, L, d_h), it is clear.

Then count the parameters and the memory for each shape. If the paper claims a saving, your count must give the same saving. If it does not, you read the method wrong, or you found something worth a question. Both results are useful, and the second is how people build reputations.

The papers behind these chapters#

Ch.PaperWhat to take from it

03Joulin et al. (2016), Bag of Tricks for Efficient Text Classificationaveraged embeddings and a linear classifier, the model of Chapter 03, competitive with much deeper models

The modern stack: what changed after 2017#

The transformer of Chapter 08 is the 2017 design. A current frontier model is clearly the same block, with approximately eight changes. Each change is a small idea that is easy to read. When you know all eight, you have most of what separates "can implement a transformer" from "can read the technical report of a frontier model and implement it again".

Each entry below gives what it replaces, the idea, and the resource that it gets back. None of them needs mathematics past Chapter 00.

Normalization: LayerNorm → RMSNorm#

$$\operatorname{RMSNorm}(x) = \frac{x}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{d}\sum_i x_i^2 + \epsilon}}\odot\gamma$$

Remove the mean subtraction and the $\beta$ shift. Keep only the scale. In experiments, the re-centering gives little, and its removal saves one pass over the features and one set of parameters. Gets back: wall-clock time, a little. Llama, Mistral, DeepSeek and almost all current models use it.

Activation: ReLU → SwiGLU#

$$\operatorname{SwiGLU}(x) = \big(\operatorname{Swish}(xW_1) \odot xV\big)W_2 \qquad \operatorname{Swish}(z) = z\,\sigma(z)$$

This is a gated feed-forward block. One projection makes the content. A second projection makes a multiplicative gate, exactly as an LSTM gate does. It needs three weight matrices, not two. Thus implementations decrease the hidden width to $\tfrac{2}{3}\cdot 4d$ to keep the parameter count fixed. It is consistently better for each parameter. Gets back: quality at equal size.

Position: learned/sinusoidal → RoPE#

Do not add a position vector to the embedding. Rotate $q$ and $k$ by an angle proportional to position, in 2-D pairs of dimensions. A dot product depends only on the relative angle. Thus $q_m \cdot k_n$ depends on $m - n$, not on $m$ and $n$ separately. You get relative position at no cost, inside the attention operation.

This directly fixes the hard context limit from Chapter 10. There is no position-embedding table to run out of. Also, if you interpolate or rescale the frequencies, you can extend the context of a model that is already trained. Gets back: length generalization.

KV cache: MHA → GQA/MQA → latent attention#

Chapter 10 showed that the KV cache limits the number of concurrent users. Here are three attacks on it, one after the other:

  • Multi-query attention (MQA): all heads share one key head and one value head. The cache becomes $H$ times smaller. Quality decreases a little.
  • Grouped-query attention (GQA): heads share keys and values in groups, for example of 8. This gives most of the saving and almost none of the loss. It is the current default.
  • Multi-head latent attention (MLA), from DeepSeek-V2: compress keys and values into a low-rank latent vector, and cache that. The model makes the projections for each head again when it needs them. It is the low-rank factorization of Chapter 11, applied to the cache and not to the weights. It is a good example of an idea that you already know, moved to a new place.

Gets back: KV-cache memory, which means serving throughput.

Capacity: dense → mixture of experts#

Replace the feed-forward block with $N$ expert blocks and a router. The router sends each token to the top-$k$ experts (usually $k = 1$ or 2). The total parameters increase by approximately $N$. The active parameters for each token do not. A model can hold much more knowledge than it spends compute on at any one token.

The engineering problem is load balance. If you do not control it, a router sends almost all tokens to a few experts. Classic MoE adds an auxiliary loss for balance, and that loss competes with the language modeling objective. DeepSeek-V3 adjusts a routing bias for each expert, based on the load that it measures. This gets balance without an auxiliary loss term. DeepSeekMoE also divides the experts more finely, and it keeps a few shared experts always on for common patterns. Gets back: knowledge per FLOP.

Attention kernels: FlashAttention#

This is not a modeling change at all. The mathematics is the same, but the kernel calculates it in tiles with an online softmax. Thus it never writes the (B, H, L, L) matrix to memory, and memory becomes linear in $L$, not quadratic. Gets back: context length. Remember this lesson about the field. One of the largest capability increases of the last several years came from a new kernel, not from a new architecture.

Decoding: speculative and multi-token#

Generation is sequential and limited by memory bandwidth, so the GPU is mostly idle. Speculative decoding uses a small draft model to propose several tokens. Then the large model verifies them in one parallel pass, and it accepts the longest correct prefix. The output distribution is provably the same, and it is several times faster. DeepSeek-V3 puts a related idea into training with a multi-token prediction objective. It predicts more than one future token at each position. Gets back: tokens per second.

Post-training: SFT, then preference optimization#

A base model trained as in Chapter 10 continues text. It does not follow instructions. A separate stage changes it into an assistant. First comes supervised fine-tuning on demonstrations. Then comes optimization against preferences: RLHF/PPO in the classic form, DPO without a reward model, and GRPO for reasoning training. (GRPO is the DeepSeek variant. It removes the value network and normalizes advantages within a group of sampled responses.) DeepSeek-R1 is an important demonstration. It shows that reasoning behavior can come from reinforcement learning against answers that you can verify, with little or no supervised start. Gets back: usefulness, which pretraining does not give.

Key concept — the shape of progress Look at that list, and see how few entries are new mathematics. Two are factorizations that you already implemented (the low rank of LoRA, used again for the KV cache). Two are gating (SwiGLU and MoE routing), which is the LSTM idea from Chapter 05. One is a new kernel, one is a rotation, and one is a change of training objective. You can get to the frontier from here. What separates you from it is not mathematics that you have not seen. It is engineering scale, data, and the habit of asking which resource a design gets back.

Making work others will trust#

The technical ability to build these systems is one skill. The ability to make someone believe a result is a different skill, and it is less common. Most of it comes from a few habits. They all occur in other places in this book. Here they are together.

HabitWhy it persuades
Report a spread, never a single numberseed variance often exceeds the effect being claimed (exercise 00.15)
Compare at matched parameters and matched computeotherwise you have measured capacity, not your idea
Tune the baseline as hard as the methodan undertuned baseline is the most common way good-faith work becomes wrong
Ablate one thing at a timethe ablation is the only controlled comparison you will have
Touch the test set oncerepeated selection is overfitting in slow motion
State what you cannot concludereaders who spot an unstated limitation stop trusting the stated ones
Publish the code and the seedsreproducibility is the cheapest credibility available
Show a failure casea method with no reported failure mode reads as unexamined

Before you publish anything, in a paper, a blog post or a pull request, do this test. Suppose that a hostile reader with your data and code tried to break this claim. What would they attack first? Answer that in the text. It is the paragraph with the highest return that you can write. It changes your most probable critic into a reader who trusts the rest.

About this book#

book/build.py builds the book from HTML fragments in book/chapters/, one for each chapter. It uses only the standard library. It concatenates the fragments, gives stable anchors to the headings, checks each cross-reference, and highlights the code blocks. A vendored copy of KaTeX renders the mathematics, so nothing here needs a network connection. The interactive figures are canvas widgets, written by hand in book/book.js. Each one calculates the same arithmetic as the text next to it. Nothing is drawn only to look convincing. 

python3 book/build.py           # rebuild book/index.html
python3 book/build.py --check   # validate fragments and cross-references only

To add or edit a chapter, change a file in book/chapters/ and build again. The filenames sort into reading sequence. Each fragment is one <section class="chapter" id="…"> with an <h1>. Headings without an explicit id get a generated id that comes from the heading text. Thus, if you change the text of a heading, update the cross-references that point to it, or give the heading an explicit id. build.py --check finds each reference that breaks.
